He further stated that opposite party No.3 filled up the land by bringing earth by truck and in doing so he had to spend TK. 2/22 lakh and he also spent TK. 12 lakh for erecting the rooms. In cross-examination, he stated that presently he works. at the colour shop of his maternal uncle. He had no written tenancy agreement with OPW-3 and no receipt of the payment of rent as well. There was no agreement to show that Azad Khandaker used to do business with him jointly, However, he denied the suggestion given by the pre-emptor that he was not tenant in the case land.

50. OPW-5 is Tota Miah. He deposed that opposite party No.3 had been possessing the .case land for 7/8 years. The case land was low land and the same was filled up by bringing earth by truck through him. A sum of taka 3/4 lakh were spent in filling the land: The earth was brought from Gazipur and Monoharer chak. The cost of bringing the earth was paid by opposite party No.3. He further stated that after filling the land opposite party No.3 erected rooms at the cost of Tk.22 lakh. There are 3(three) shops in the case land, one furniture shop, one saloon and one tea shop which have been let out to the tenants. In cross-examination, this OPW stated that he was a man of village Monoharer chak which was 2 kilometers away from his house. He further. Stated that he had no truck of his own and he did not file any receipt of hiring truck. He denied the suggestion that, the rooms in the case land 'were erected after 20-03-1998.

51. In cross-examination he further stated that এর পাশে লাগ পূর্বে দিকে ব্রক্ষ্মপুত্র নদী আছে। সেখান থেকে মাটি ভরাট হয়েছে। (সে নিশ্চুপ ছিল)পরে বলে তা সত্য নয়।” The demeanor of the witness as recorded by the trial Court shows that he was a: partisan witness and he did not tell the truth.

52. OPW-6 is one Haridas. He deposed that he has furniture shop in the case and  he has been doing his business there since 1995 by taking the same on rent at TK.6,00 per year, In cross am in action, he stated that he brings wood for furniture from Araihazar and Narsingdi. The receipt for purchasing wood is given from Narsingdi but he has not filed the same in Court. He further stated that- there was no tenancy agreement with the opposite party No.3.

53. These are the relevant evidence of the witnesses adduced by the parties in the case hind.

<u>54. Sub-section (1) of section 96 of the Act has clearly mandated that if a portion or share of it holding of a raiyat is transferred then a co-sharer tenant of that holding may within 4(four) months of the service of notice given under section 89 of the Act or if no notice has been served under section 89 of the Act within 4 (four) months of the date of know ledge of the transfer, apply to the Court for the said portion or share to be transferred to him. In this case, the pre-emptor categorically asserted in the application for pre-emption that before transfer of the case land no notice was served upon her either in writing or verbally. The pre-emptor further asserted that the case land was transferred secretly beyond her knowledge. On the other hand, the pre-emptee in his written objection asserted that before purchasing the case land, he served notice of the transfer to the pre-emptor and the pre-emptor was aware about the notice and the sale in question. Section 96 (1) of the Act has contemplated two situations as to the limitation for filing an application for pre-emption, one within 4(four) months of the service of the notice given under section 89 of the Act and the other within 4(four) months of the date of knowledge of the transfer if no notice has been served under section 89 of the Act. When the pre-emptee in his written objection specifically pleaded that notice of transfer was given to the pre-emptor onus was squarely upon him, to prove the same. Now let us see whether the pre-emptee proved the said fact.</u>

55. Pre-emptee-opposite party No.3 examined himself as OPW 1. He in his examination in chief asserted that at the time of purchase of the case land notice was given to the pre-emptor. The OPW further asserted that the seller-opposite party informed chase the same. I consider it better to quote the relevant portion of the evidence of PW 1 in this respect বিক্রেতা তরপছানী নালিশী সম্পত্তি বিক্রির সয়ম মজহরকে জানায়। নালিমী সম্পত্তি রাখতে বা ক্রয়ে অস্বঅকার করে। দরখাস্তকারীনিকে নোটিশ দেওয়া হয় নালিশী সম্পত্তি খরিদেও সময় নালিশী সম্পত্তির দক্ষিণ পার্শ্বে আমাদের সম্পত্তি।” But copy of such notice was not filed in the Court. And in cross-examination this PW stated to the আমরা নালিশী সম্পত্তি খরিদেও বিষয়ে মজহরকে জানাই এ বাবত নোটিশ এর কপি আদালতে দাখিল করি নাই। পরে বলে নোটিশ হারিয়ে গেছে।”  Thus it is clear that notice of transfer under section 89 of the Act was not served upon the pre-emptor and the contesting pre- emptee took false plea in the written objection. Therefore,' the case of the pre-emptor that on coming to know  about the transfer in question in the salish baithak held on 20th of March, 1998 she obtained the certified copy of the kabala in question on 6-4-1998 and then came to know definitely about the transfer in question and then filed the case on 27- 05-1998, that is, well ahead of 4(four) months from the date of knowledge has to be considered in the light of the evidence adduced by the parties. In this regard, I am not oblivious of the onus of the pre- emptor to prove the fact of knowledge as to the sale in questions as asserted by her in the pre-emption application as well as by her husband as PW-l.

56. From the judgment of the trial Court, it appears that it considered the evidence of the PWs and then believed the pre-emptor's case of knowledge about the transfer in question on 20th of March, 1998 as disclosed by the seller-opposite party in the salish baithak held on the said date. The trial Court found the PWs trustworthy and no inconsistency in their evidence. The trial Court did not find OPW1 trustworthy as he-made contradictory statements in cross-examination from that of the examination-in-chief. I consider it better to quote the relevant portion of the finding of the trial Court about OPW-1 which is as follows:-

অপর দিকে প্রতিপক্ষের সাক্ষী নং-১ তার জবান বন্দীতে বলে, খরিদের পূর্বে থেকেই দরখাস্তকারীনী জানে। নাঃ সম্পত্তি খরিদের সময়, সে তার জেরায় স্বীকার কওে, আমরা নাঃ সম্পত্তি খরিদের বিষয়ে মজহরকে জানাই এবং এ বাবদ নোটিশে এর কপি। আদালতে দাখিল করি নাই। পরে বলে নোটিশ হারিয়ে গিয়েছে। এ সাক্ষীর জবানবন্দী ও জেরা মধ্যে সামঞ্জস্য খুজে না পাওয়ায় ও এ সাক্ষীর বিশ্বাস যোগ্য নয়।”

57. The trial Court found that though OPW-2 in his examination-in-chief stated that everybody knew about the purchase and that the transfer in question was not made secretly and that after purchase, the purchasers planted seedlings for sometimes, in cross-examination, stated that he was not present during the transfer and he also-could not say whether the people of the village knew about the transfer and finally observed that this witness could not say whether. everybody knew about the transfer and then concluded, by saying that from analysis of the deposition of the witnesses it appeared that the pre-emptor came to know about the transfer for the first time on 20-03-1998. However, the trial Court did not consider it necessary to discuss the evidence of the other OPWS.

58. The appellate Court which his the last Court of fact disbelieved the pre-emptor's case of salish baithak held on 20th of March, 1998 on the ground that no document was filed as to the proof of holding of salish on the said date completely forgetting that neither in the application for pre-emption nor in the deposition of  PW1 any such case of written salish baithak was made but. The other reason given by the -appellate Court to disbelieve the story of salish as deposed by PW-3, an independent Witness is that except him none of the other salishder deposed to the said effect completely ignoring the evidence of PW-4 who categorically deposed about the holding of salish on 20th of March, 1998 and the েfurther fact that he was present at the salish PW1 categorically stated in his examination-in-chief that he was present in the salish aleng with PWs' 2 and '3'. In this regard, the appellate Court else failed to notice section 134 of the Evidence Act which has clearly provided that no particular number of witnesses is necessary to-prove a fact. Thus apples to me that the appellate Court' totally misread as well as failed to consider the material 'evidence' on 'record' and also Misconceived the case of the pre-emptor as made out in the pre-emption application in arriving at the finding of knowledge of the pre-emptor as to the transfer in question. It further appears that the appellate Court disbelieved the evidence of PWs 1, 2 and 4 on the ground that they were the own men of the pre-emptor. Such reason given by the appellate Court in disbelieving PWs 1, 2 and 3 is absolutely fallacious and contrary to the settled principle of law that the testimony of a witness cannot be disbelieved only on the ground of relationship or closeness if his evidence is otherwise found to be true and withstand the test of cross-examination. In this regard, reference may be made to the cases of Samad Sikder @ Somed Sikder vs State reported in 50 DLR (AD) 24, Nowabul Alam vs State reported in 45 DLR (AD) 140, and Anwara Khatun vs Md. Abdul Hye reported in 4 BLC (AD) 14.

59. In support of the case of knowledge about the transfer in question for the first time in the salish baithak held on 20th of March, 1998 the pre-emptor examined 3 (three) witnesses in addition to her husband as  PW1. The evidence of the witnesses to the above effect could not be shaken in cross- examination then what more the pre-emptor could do to prove the knowledge within the meaning of sub Section (1) of section 96 of the Act. So, the appellate Court was absolutely in error when it observed that the pre-emptor could not prove that she did not know about the transfer in question before 20th of March, 1998. It further appears that the appellate Court in a circuitous and negative way disbelieved the pre-emptor's case of knowledge about the transfer in question on 20th of March, 1998 and the development made in the case land including the erection of the shops therein after the said date by posing a question why she did not pray for any injunction after filing of the pre-emption application on 27-05-1998 of the pre-emptees undertook development work in the case land after 20th of March, 1998 in complete disregard to the factual position that the gap between 20th of March, 1998 up to 27th May, 1998 was quite enough to undertake the nature of the development works and erection of the structures on the case land as claimed by the pre-emptees. The appellate Court also failed to consider in its proper perspective that even if it is conceded that the pre-emptees undertook development work after the filing of the pre-emption case and the pre-emptor failed to take any step by way of filing an application to in junco them from undertaking such development work that does not debar the preemptor to pray for pre-emption and for such failure no adverse presumption can be drawn against her. In this regard, law is very much clear which is that the pre-emptees shall be entitled to get development cost till getting notice of the pre-emption application.

60. It is very much striking to state that the appellate Court itself disbelieved the pre-emptee's case of spending TK.5,00,000 for the development of the case land including erection of the structures thereon on the ground that he failed to file any documentary evidence in that respect and found that the pre-emptee spent Tk. 1,50,000 only. From the appellate Court judgment, it further appears that it proceeded with a prior view that since the pre-emption application was filed after 8(eight) years, the same was barred by limitation ignoring the positive evidence on record adduced by the pre-emptor that she had no knowledge about the transfer in question prior to 20th of March, 1998 and whatever development was done in the case land was done after the said date. The appellate Court also failed to consider the fact that the pre-emptee took specific plea in the written objection as well as in Court while he deposed as OPW-1 that notice under section 89 of the Act was served upon the pre-emptor but failed to prove the said fact which shows that the pre-emptee took false plea in his pleading to defeat the case of the pre-emptor and for this reason the appellate Court ought to have drawn an adverse presumption against him. It is true that the pre-emptee developed the case land and erected some shop rooms therein but the pre-emptor specifically stated that those were done after the disclosure of the fact of transfer on 20th of March, 1998.

61. In sifting the evidence of the PWs in arriving at the finding of knowledge of the pre-emptor about the transfer in question, the appellate Court totally failed to consider the pertinent fact that the seller-opposite party No.4 is none else, but his full brother and the father of the pre-emptees Sultanuddin Bhuiyan used to cultivate the, case land as bargadar during the life time of her father and then under them and the seller used to give her the share of the crops, so even if the pre-emptee was in possession of the case land till 20th of March, 1998 the pre-emptor had no scope to know about the transfer in question.

62. In the face of positive evidence adduced by the pre-emptor as to knowledge about the transfer in question as discussed above the pre-emptee was obliged to examine witnesses who as per his own case participated in filling up the case land and erecting shop rooms thereinafter 1994 and before 20th March, 1998. But the pre-emptee failed to examine any such witness in the case. To specify, the pre-emptee did not examine the truck owner or the truck driver in support of his case that he filled up the case land by bringing earth in truck from Gazipur and Monoharer chak. The pre-emptee examined one Total Mia as OPW-5 to prove that earth was brought from Gazipur and Monoharer chak by truck at the cost of taka 3/4 lakh, but in cross-examination he stated that his house was two kilometers away from the case land and that he had no truck and did not submit any receipt of truck fare. The pre-emptee did not examine anyone who erected the shop rooms in the case land. The pre-emptee examined Haridas as OPW-6 who is his alleged tenant in the case land since 1995. This OPW stated in his deposition that he had a furniture shop in the case land since 1995 but in support of his tenancy no agreement was produced. Although OPW-6 stated that he has been doing the business in the case land since 1995 by paying rent of Tk. 6,000 per year, no rent receipt was produced. All these categorically disproved the case of the contesting pre-emptee that he undertook development work in the case land in 1994/1995 rather supported the case of the preemptor that the development in the case hind was done and shop rooms were erected after 20th of March, 1998.

<u>63. I am of the view that by examining 4(four) witnesses in support of the case of knowledge of the transfer in question on 20th of March, 1998 the pre-emptor discharged her onus and then the onus shifted upon the contesting pre-emptee that he developed the case land in 199411995 and then erected the shop rooms therein, but he failed to discharge the said onus. The appellate Court did not at all consider this legal aspect of the case.</u>

64. From the impugned judgment of the High Court Division, it appears that the High Court Division, in fact, did not discuss and consider the evidence on record on the question of limitation on the view that the question of limitation "hinges on the credibility of the witnesses and the trial Court had the advantage to see the demeanor of the witnesses" and as such, its decision in respect of such finding should prevail and accordingly, endorsed the finding of the trial Court on the question of limitation. In this regard, the High Court Division further rob served that "The Court of appeal below, on the other hand, did not have the advantage to see the demeanor of the witnesses and as such the finding arrived at by the Court of appeal below as to limitation cannot get preference."

65. In view of the discussions made herein- above, I do not find anything wrong with the view taken by the High Court Division. Since the trial Court did not consider the question of improvement of the pre-emptees and the appellate Court found the same at TK.1,50,000, the High Court Division considering the admission of the pre-emptor that the pre-emptees made improvement in the case land at the cost of taka 40,000/50,000 fixed the development cost at Tk. 75,000. find the assessment of cost reasonable and based on evidence on record particularly in view of the admitted fact that no documentary evidence was produced in support of the development cost.

66. It is true that the judgment of High Court Division is not that happy as it should have been, but I do not find any error in the ultimate decision arrived at by the High Court Division in making the Rule absolute restoring those of the trial Court considering the judgments of the two. Courts below.

67. In conclusion, I am of the view that the appellate Court rejected the pre-emption application on total misreading, non-consideration of the material evidence of the PWs and the OPWs, with reference to the pleading of the parties as well as the settled principle of law in sifting and weighing the evidence of a witness. I would dismiss the appeal with- out any order as to cost.

Nazmun Ara Sultana J: I have gone through the separate judgments prepared by my learued brother, Surendra Kumar Sinha, J. and my learned brother Md. Abdul Wahhab Miah, J. I agree with the judgment of brother Surendra Kumar Sinha, J.

Muhammad Imman Ali J: I have gone through the judgmerits delivered by my learned brothers Surendra Kumar Sinha, J and Md. Abdul Wahhab Miah, J. I agree with reasons given and the decision arrived at by my learned brother Mr. Md. Abdul Wahhab Miah, J. I would, therefore, dismiss the appeal without any order as to costs.

Muhammad Mamtaz Uddin Ahmed J: I have gone through the separate judgments prepared by my learned brother, Surendra Kumar Sinha, J. and my learned brother, Md. Abdul Wahhab Miah, J. I agree with the judgment of brother Surendra Kumar Sinha, J.

Md. Shamsul Huda J: I have gone through the separate judgments prepared by my learned brother, Surendra Kumar Sinha, J. and my learned brother, Md. Abdul Wahhab Miah, J. I agree with the judgment passed by my learned brother Surendra Kumar Sinha, J.

Courts Order

The appeal is allowed by majority decision without any order as to costs.

End.

Aleka Khatun and others  ------- Petitioners
Vs. 
Government of Bangladesh  -------  Respondent.
full_judgment:
Sharifuddin Chaklader J: At the instance of the petitioners a Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the impugned letter dated 19-4-2002 vide Memo No. BPRH/2L/23/2003-294 issued by respondent No.4, evidenced by Annexure-T to the petition, moved in Court should not be declared to have been made without lawful authority, illegal, without jurisdiction and is of no legal effect and the respondents should not be restrained from disturbing the possession of the petitioners over the scheduled land.

2. It has been stated in the Writ Petition that Government acquired 1.17 acres of land from plot No. 327 under CS Khatian No. 123, belonging to Abul Hossain for making Mohakhali- Tejgaon link road in LA Case No. 66/57-58. The land was recorded in SA and RS Khatian in the name of the Government. Out of the said acquired land, 0.73 acres of land was unutilised. The heirs of Abul Hossain filed an application to the Ministry of Communication for derequisition of the said land and by order dated 26-2-1984 the Ministry of Communication de-requisitioned 0.73 acres of land. On 9-10-1985 the said land was given in possession of Abul Hossain. Noor Hossain, son of late Abul Hossain, transferred 0.035 acres of land to Mofizul Islam by sale deed dated 8-2-1986 and gifted 0.05 acres of land in favour of his wife, Karimunnessa. The heirs of Abul Hossain transferred 0.2997 acres of land in favour of Alef Mia, the predecessor of the petitioners by deed dated 19-2-1987. Alef Miah mutated his name and paid rents to the Government. The said purchased land was demarcated by a sketch map. The petitioners filled up 10 feet deep approaching road to the main road and approached the authority for leasing out the said land and it has been stated that a verbal assurance was given to them for leasing out of the said land. On 27-3-2003 respondent No. 6 filed an application for leasing out 0.32 acres of land from plot No. 327 for establishing a CNG filling station. On 1-4-2003 respondent No. 5 leased out the said land to respondent No. 6. The petitioners challenged this order on the ground that if this land be delivered to respondent No. 6 this would encroach their purchased land and this being violatative of fundamental right granted to a citizen for maintaining property under the Constitution, obtained this Rule.

3. It is also stated in the writ petition that the writ petitioners filed Title Suit No. 191 of 2003 before the learned Assistant Judge, Second Court, Dhaka for the relief prayed for in this writ petition. At the time of hearing of the writ petition, Mr Md Nurul Amin, learned Advocate for the petitioners, when asked about the present position of the said title suit, supplied two certified copies from which it is evidenced that the writ petitioners prayed for withdrawal of the said title suit from the Court of Assistant Judge, Second Court, Dhaka and the learned Assistant Judge by order dated 24-6-2003 allowed the prayer of the writ petitioners and withdrew the Title Suit from his Court.

4. In this writ petition there are several applications for vacating the order of stay as well as several affidavits-in-opposition filed by the parties. Respondent Nos. 5 and 6 contested the Rule by filing two separate affidavits-in-opposition. Government in its affidavit-in-opposition denied the facts disclosed in the writ petition and stated that after leasing out of 0.32 acres of land to respondent No. 6, Government still possess 0.11 acres of land in the disputed area, as such, there is no question of encroachment of the land of the writ petitioners on the part of the Government for installing CNG filling station. Respondent No.5 totally denied the case of the writ petitioners and stated that land measuring 1.17 acres in CS Plot No. 327 was fully acquired by the Government vide LA Case No. 66/1957-58 for constructing Dhaka-Tongi Diversion Road which was published in the Government Gazette notification dated 21-3-1963. After acquisition 0.37 acres of land was used for constructing Dhaka-Tongi diversion road and 0.80 acres of land remained unutilised. Thereafter, 36 decimal of unutilised land was de-requisitioned by the authority in favour of the original owner. Subsequently, writ petitioner purchased 0.29 acres of land out of 0.36 acres of derequisitioned land and 0.43 acres of land still remained vacant unutilised. After leasing out of 0.32 acres of land to respondent No. 6, Government still possess 0.11 acres in excess. So, the allegation of encroachment is totally false. To remove pollution of Bangladesh as well as of Dhaka City, Government has taken a big project to establish CNG re-filling stations in the country to implement the said project. The respondent No.4 leased out 0.32 acres of land from CS Plot No. 327 to respondent No.6. The writ petitioners have no right, title and interest in the land and, as such, instant Rule is liable to be discharged.

5. Respondent No. 6 also filed affidavit-in-opposition wherein he has taken identical ground that after giving 0.32 acres of land to this respondent No.6, Government still possess 0.11 acres of land. Respondent No. 6 also denied the writ petitioners' case and it is his case that, in fact, 1.17 acres of land in CS Plot No. 327 was fully acquired by the Government vide LA Case No. 66/1957-58 for constructing Dhaka-Tongi Diversion Road which was published in the Government Gazette notification on 21-3- 1963. Thereafter, 0.3650 acres of land from the said plot was de-requisitioned in favour of the original owner and the said land was handed over to them in time and they have sold some portion of their derequisitioned land to the petitioners and other persons who have already constructed a four-storied building thereon. But for illegal gain, the petitioners tried to occupy 0.1000 acres of Government acquired land from the said plot. To protect pollution of Dhaka City, Government has taken a project to . establish CNG re-filling stations all over the country step by step and to implement the said project, respondent No.4 leased out the property in dispute to respondent No.6, measuring 0.3200 acres of land from CS Plot No. 327 and there remains 0.4850 acres of the land in that CS Plot No. 327 in excess, excluding aforesaid 0.3200 acres, under possession of the Government as well as under Roads and Highways Department. So, the petitioners filed this writ petition to create obstructions in the implementation of the said nationwide project and to misappropriate the Government acquired land; The petitioners had filed a title suit in the lower Court and obtained orders of temporary injunction, which were vacated as proved false. Thus the Rule is liable to be dis charged with costs for the greater interest of public in general.

6. Mr Khan Saifur Rahman, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioners, submits that on the admitted position of the parties, the land leased in favour of respondent No.6 encroaches purchased lands of the petitioners and, as such, it infringes the fundamental rights of the petitioners in enjoying their purchased land.

7. Mr Zaman Akhter, learned Assistant Attorney-General appearing for the respondent No. 5, argues that the entire writ petition contends disputed question of facts which cannot be resolved in writ jurisdiction, as such, the Rule obtained is liable to be discharged.

8. Mr Rezaul Islam, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondent No.6, endorsed the argument of the learned Assistant Attorney-General.

9. We have heard the learned Advocates for the petitioners, respondent No. 6 and the learned Assistant Attorney-General for the Government, perused the writ petition with annexures, affidavit- in-opposition filed by the parties and also considered the submissions of the learned Advocates.

10. It is the case of the petitioners that they have purchased de-requisitioned land from Noor Hossain. Annexure-L is the photocopy of the deed of purchase. The schedule of the properties appended with the said deed speaks for;

“বার্ষিক খাজনা ২.০০ টাকা আর,সি ও তেজগাঁও সার্কেলে আদায় হয় যাহার বার্ষিক খাজনা আদায় হয় যাহার চৌহদ্দির উত্তরে মেট্রোপলিটনের রাস্তা ও দক্ষিনে মফিজুল ইসলাম পূর্বে ১৪-০ রাস্তা এজমালীসহ পশ্চিমে সরকারী জমি।”

11. It appears from this deed that on the west of the land purchased, there is Government land. Annexure-S is the impugned order. From it, it appears that the Government has given lease of 0.32 acres of land to respondent No.6 from the vacant portion of plot No. 327. It further appears from the affidavits filed by the parties that 1.17 acres of land were acquired by the Government in LA Case No. 66/57-58. Thereafter, Government utilised 0.37 acres of land and 0.80 acres of land remain unutilised and out of unutilised 0.80 acres of land, 0.36 acres of land were de-requisitioned and from this land, the petitioners purchased 0.29 acres of land. It appears that 0.43 acres of land still remain vacant with the Government as unutilised and from this 0.43 acres of unutilised land, respondent No.6 was given lease of 0.32 acres of land for installing CNG filling station. It appears that after giving 0.32 acres of land, 0.11 acres of land still remained vacant with the Government. It appears from Annexure-2 of the application for vacating the order of stay filed by respondent Nos. 5 and 6 that the leased out land (0.32 acres) was given in possession of respondent No.6. By a supplementary-affidavit, the petitioners stated that no possession was delivered and if possession of 0.32 acres of land be delivered that would encroach their purchased land. It is argued by respondent No.5 that the map appended with the writ petition differs from the map appended with the applications filed by respondent Nos. 5 and 6. From perusal of writ petition, we find that writ petitioners stated that it is an admitted position that the leased out land if delivered, that would definitely encroach their purchased land. The respondents differ and stated that Government after leasing out 0.32 acres of land, still possess 0.11 acres of land and no encroachment would be made in delivering the said land to respondent No.6.

<u>12. It is the settled principle of law that disputed question of fact cannot be gone into in writ jurisdiction. What is meant by disputed question of fact? It is not merely confined to one who alleges and other denies. Disputed question of fact is that which requires evidence to prove the fact in issue. Merely controverting an allegation cannot by itself constitute disputed question of fact. This is dispute which could be resolved on affidavits and annexures. But disputed question of fact requires evidence to settle such fact. In the instant case, petitioners allege that the papers annexed with the petition are enough to hold that petitioners' fundamental right has been violated. From the papers filed and submitted by the parties it is an admitted fact that Government de-requisitioned 73 decimals of land out of 1.17 acres of land and out of this 73 decimals of land, petitioners purchased 29 decimals of land. There remains 83 decimals of land in the hand of the Government. It is the petitioners' case that Government made 30-foot road for the hospital, 20 feet left for extension of the road in future, as such, if the Government delivered 80 feet land in length to respondent No.6 then it straight penetrates inside the land of the petitioners, is an admitted position which could be easily seen from the map evidenced (Annexure-N) with the writ petition. But the contesting respondents dispute such contention of the petitioners. Respondent Government as well as respondent No.6, lessee, annexed the same map in their respective applications for vacating the order of stay, evidenced as Annexure- 2 respectively. It is seen from these 3 maps that map of the petitioners (Annexure-N) differs from the maps of the Government and respondent No.6 (Annexure-2). The maps of the contesting respondents are same but both these maps differ from the map of the petitioners. The respondent Government in its affidavit- in-opposition stated that after the lands given to the lessee, there remains at least 11 decimals of land in the hands of the Government, without encroaching into the purchased land by the petitioner and Government from its own land handed over 32 decimals of land to respondent No.6, retaining, if 10 decimals of land given as per oral assurance to petitioners, 2 decimals and if not, then 12 decimals. To find out whose statement is true, in our opinion, evidence is required to find out whether in delivering 32 decimals of land to lessee it actually goes behind the boundary wall of the petitioners which cannot be resolved merely on affidavit. It requires at least local inspection to find out whether leased out land to respondent No. 6 actuality goes behind the boundary of the petitioners and then also the report of the local inspection would be evaluated with the other evidences for settling this dispute. From the writ petition as well as affidavits-in-opposition and also from several applications, it appears that whether the leased out land encroached the purchased land of the petitioners, stands as disputed question of facts which cannot be resolved in writ jurisdiction because it needs evidence as well as a local inspection to ascertain whether in leasing out the land to respondent No.6, Government actually encroached within the purchased land of the petitioners. Such questions as to whether in settling the land with respondent No. 6 by installing a CNG filling station, encroached the land of the petitioners is thus a disputed question of fact better acted upon evidence which can be done more appropriately before a civil Court. In the summary proceeding under Article 102, it is not desirable, more often than not, not possible to record a finding as to a disputed question of fact. There is a long line of decisions in favour of the view that the High Court should not enter into disputed question of fact nor decide any question as to title which require investigation into facts and taking of elaborate evidence.</u>

13. In that view of the matter, we find no substance in the Rule.

14. Before parting with the decision, another question calls for determination. From the writ petitioners' own version it appears that they moved the Civil Court for redressing their grievances and obtained an order of injunction against the respondents of writ petition in that suit. The writ petitioners after obtaining stay order from this Court on 16-6-2003 withdrew the suit from the civil Court on 24-6-2003. The writ petitioners in the instant writ petition on 24-6-2003 obtained an order of injunction against the respondents "from demolishing the structures situated in the schedule land of the petitioner."

<u>15. This fact goes to show that writ petitioner acted mischievously in getting relief without knowing where their remedy lies and when they enforced the writ jurisdiction, their suit was pending and the suit was withdrawn when they got the initial relief from this Court. This is an unholy conduct of the writ petitioners. In invoking the writ jurisdiction, the writ petitioner's conduct must be clear and clean. The seeker of enforcing fundamental right must be of clean hands. The invoker should not move to any jurisdiction before invoking the writ jurisdiction. A writ petition cannot be maintainable if it is found that when the writ petition was moved, the writ petitioner still clung to other jurisdiction as what has happened in the instant case. As such, this conduct of the writ petitioners should not be encouraged. Since the petitioner moved the civil Court earlier before filing of the writ petition, he, under law, cannot move this Court in writ jurisdiction on the ground of violation of fundamental right. As such, we hold that this writ petition is also bad for this reason.</u>

In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to cost.

End.

full_judgment:
D. C. Bhattacharya, J.— In all these petitions a question relating to the jurisdiction and powers of an Election Tribunal set up under the provisions of Union Parishad and Paurashava (Election) Rules, 1973 framed under the Bangladesh Local Government (Union Parishad and Paurashava) Order, 1973 (President's Order No. 22 of 1973) has been raised.

<u>2. The result of certain Union Parishad elections held under the provisions of the aforesaid Election Rules having been declared, election petitions, have been filed in respective Election Tribunals challenging the validity of the said results. Applications have been filed in the said election cases purporting to be under Order 39 rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure for temporary injunction restraining the elected office bearers or members from function as such in all these cases, pending the hearing of the said election cases and the learned Presiding Officers of the respective Election Tribunals have allowed the said applications, granting temporary injunctions as prayed for.</u>

3. The present petitions under Article 102 of the Constitution have been filed challenging the jurisdiction of the Election Tribunal to make such an order of temporary injunction. The contention of the learned Advocates appearing on behalf of the petitioners in these petitions is that the Election Tribunal is not a Civil Court within the meaning of the Code of Civil procedure and it being a statutory tribunal set up for the limited purpose of trying an election dispute has no power to initiate any supplemental proceeding, which has no bearing on the trial of the election dispute. It has also beer contended that, in any view of the matter, having regard to the terms of the provisions of Order 39 of the Code, the said provisions have no manner of application in a proceeding before the Election Tribunal.

4. The learned Advocates on behalf of the respondents, on the other hand, have contended that the Union Parishad and Paurashava (Election) Rules, under which these Tribunal have been constituted, have specifically provide that the election Tribunal shall follow the procedures as laid down in the Code of Civil Procedure as early as possible and that such a Tribunal shall have the powers of a Civil Court trying a suit under the said Code. This contention, as strenuously argued on behalf of the respondents has two fold aspects, namely that firstly, an Election Tribunal is a Civil Court within the meaning of the Code of Civil Procedure and, secondly, the Rule 61B of the Election Rules has specifically laid down that the Tribunal shall have all the powers of a Civil Court trying a suit, which includes the power of issuing temporary injunction and that even if the power of issuing temporary injunction does not come within the terms of Order 39 as provided in the Code of Civil procedure, this power can be exercised by an Election Tribunal for the ends of justice and equity.

5. In order that respective contentions of the learned Advocate may properly be appreciated, it is necessary to refer to the specific provisions of the law under which these Election Tribunals have been constituted and functioning.

6. The Bangladesh Local Govt. (Union Parishad and Paurashava) Order, 1972 (P.O. No. 22 of 1973) which provides for the constitution of a Union Parishad and a Paurashava and also election of its Chairman, Vice-Chairman and members, has laid down in clause (1) of Article 24 that the Government may make rules for carrying out the purpose of that Order and in clause (2) of the said Article it has been further provided that such rules may provide for, along, with other particular items, "the submission, trial and disposal of election petitions". In exercise of this rule-making power, the Government has framed rules which have been called Union Parishad and Paurashava (Election) Rules, 1973. Part V of these, Rules, which consists of rules 56 to 64, relates to election disputes. Rule 56 provides that no election shall be called in question except by an election petition and that any candidate may make an election petition challenging the election at which he was a candidate. Rule 564 provides for joinder of parties, and Rule 57 provides for appointment of an Election Tribunal and is to the following effect :

‘57(1) for the trial of the election petition the Election Commission shall, by notification in the Official Gazette, appoint an officer to be an Election Tribunal for such area as may be specified in the notification ;

(2) Where the person constituting an Election Tribunal is succeeded by another, the trial of a petition shall continue before the person so succeeding and any evidence already recorded shall remain upon the record and it shall not be necessary to re-examine the witnesses who have already been examined and discharged.

7. Rule 58 provides that the Election Commission, either of its down motion or on an application made in this behalf by any of the parties, may at any stage transfer an election petition from one Tribunal to another Tribunal and the Tribunal to which the petition is so transferred shall proceed with the trial of the petition from the stage at which it was transferred.

8. Rule 59 provides for the procedure relating to the filing of an election petition and clause (4) of the said rule provides that an election petition shall set forth clearly the ground on which the petition is filed and the relief sought. Rule 60 provides that the petitioner may claim any of the two kinds of declarations namely, (a) that the election of any returned candidate is void and that the petitioner or some other person has been duly elected or (b) that the election as a whole is void. Rule 61 relates to the signature and verification of the petition.

9. Rule 61A and 61B which have been subsequently added by an amending notification dated 22-2-74 have been the subject of much arguments at the bar in the present case and great reliance has been placed by the learned Advocates for the respondents on the said two rules, in support of the proposition that the Election Tribunal has the necessary jurisdiction to issue temporary injunction in the same manner as a Civil Court. The said rules are in the same manner as a Civil Court. The said rules are to the following effect :

"61A Procedure before Tribunal-subject to the provisions of these rules every election petition shall be tried as nearly as may be in accordance with the procedure for the trial of suits under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. 61-B Power of the Tribunal : The Tribunal shall have all the powers of a Civil Court trying a suit under the Code of Civil procedure, 1908 and shall be deemed to be a Civil Court within the meaning of section 480 and 482 of the Code of Criminal procedure, 1898.

10. Rules 62 relates to the procedure in connection with the trial of election petition and is to the following effect :

"(1) A Tribunal shall upon receipt of an election petition give notice thereof to all the contesting candidates and such other candidates against whom any allegation, if any, of any Corrupt of illegal practice is made at the election to which the election relates.

(2) The Tribunal shall, after giving the contesting candidates and such other candidates, against whom any allegation, if any, of any corrupt of illegal practice is made, an opportunity of being heard and taking such evidence as may be produced before it, make such orders as it may think fit ;

Provided that the Tribunal shall not declare the election of any returned candidate for election as a whole void unless it is satisfied that the result of the election has been materially affected by reason of the failure of any person to comply with or the contravention of these rules.

(3) The decision of the Tribunal on an election petition shall be final.

11. Rule 63 provides for withdrawal of an election petition by the petitioner and abatement of such a petition on the death of the petitioner. Rule 64 provides that the Tribunal may make such order as in costs as it may think fit.

<u>12. From these provisions it appears that the Election Tribunal is appointed by the Election Commission which is a statutory body set up under these very Rules and, as we have seen, according to Rule 57, any officer may be appointed as an Election Tribunal and he need not be a judicial officer, though, as we have found in most cases the judicial officers have been made the Presiding Officers of Election Tribunals. This rule also shows that the specific object for the constitution of an Election Tribunal is to try election petitions and the jurisdiction of such a Tribunal must necessarily be confined to the said object. By an election petition, the validity of an election can be challenged and the relief which can be sought or granted on the basis of such a petition is a declaration with regard to the validity of the said election. Therefore, it is manifestly clear that the purpose for which such a Tribunal has been created is solely the determination of a question relating to the validity of an election held under the aforesaid Union Parishad and Paurashava Election Rules and such a Tribunal, unless specifically empowered under some other provision, cannot be beyond the limits of such an object. Rule 58 is an important provision for the purpose of showing that the Election Commission exercises a kind of supervisory jurisdiction over an Election Tribunal inasmuch as it has the power under the said rule to transfer an election petition pending before one Tribunal to another Tribunal sou motu/ or an application of a party. This points out that the Election Commission which is an administrative body set up under these Rules has a kind of controlling jurisdiction over an Election Tribunal and this fact detracts in an unmistakably manner from the Character of a court. The Election Tribunal is obviously not part of the general judicial system of the country.</u>

13. In support of the petitioners contention that the Election Tribunal has no power of granting temporary injunction, reliance has been placed on their behalf on the case of Venkata Subba Chattiar Vs. Sesha Ayiyar reported in I.L.R. 47 Mad. 700. This case has been sought to be. distinguished on behalf of the respondents by contending that in the Madras case there was a Rule similar to Rule 61A, But there was no rule similar to Rule 61B, which purports to confer all the powers of a Civil Court upon an Election Tribunal. The learned Advocates for the respondents have relied very much upon Rule 61B, which has been quoted above, for the purpose of showing that it has been specifically provided that an Election Tribunal shall have all the powers of a Civil Court trying a suit under the Code of Civil Procedure. It has been contended that a Court trying a suit under the Civil Procedure Code has a power to issue temporary injunction under section 94 read with Order 39 of the Code and an Election Tribunal may, therefore, have similar power.

<u>14. This contention as argued by the learned Advocate for the respondents has not taken note of an important aspect, namely, the basic object for which the Election Tribunal has been constitute under the Union Parishad and Paurashava (Election) Rules and the necessary jurisdiction that the Election Tribunal derives therefrom. The sole purpose for which an Election Tribunal has been constituted is to try an election petition and under the said rules the only relief which an Election Tribunal can great to a party or the only power which it can exercise as is a declaration as has been provided in Rule 60 referred to above, It cannot travel beyond this limit of its jurisdiction and cannot arrogate to itself any other extraneous power. It may be that in these particular cases the Presiding Officers of Civil Court have been appointed as Election Tribunals but that fact will not authorise the Tribunals to exercise those powers which such officers exercise while they act as Presiding officers of a Civil Court.</u>

15. The principle consideration stressed in the aforesaid Madras case (I.L.R. 47 Mad. 700) for the applicability of the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure to an election dispute is the relevancy of such of the provisions to the trial of the dispute, and the provisions relating to temporary injunction having had no relation to the trial of an election dispute, according to the said Madras decision, cannot be invoked. This view has been expressed in the following observation made at pages 702-30 of the report :—

"An interim injunction can only be within the jurisdiction of the judge holding an enquiry into an election petition of that injunction is for the purpose of, and in furtherance, the trial which he is conducting. But a temporary injunction under Order XXXIX, rule 2 is not necessarily for the purposes of a trial. Section 94, Civil Procedure Code, but of which Order XXXIX arises, is framed generally to prevent the ends of justice from being defeated An injunction restraining an elected candidate from taking his) seat, may be in the ends of justice but such an injunction in no way affects the conduct of the trial".

16. The question whether a particular tribunal is a Civil Court or not has given rise to a good deal of judicial controversy and in one of the recent cases, namely IDBP Vs. M/S. Master Industries reported in 26 DLR page 157 to which one of us was a party, this Court had to examine this question and it has been held in the said case that the exercise of judicial power of the State is the determining factor for investigating body with the character of a court and that a Tribunal exercising a judicial power does not mean merely that it is acting with fairness and impartiality on a proper consideration of all relevant materials after giving an opportunity to all contending parties to present their respective cases. In order the exercise of the judicial power or acting judicially may be a sign of acting as a Court, it must be acting as a part of the judicial machinery of the State charged with the duty of determining the rights of the subject against another or the question of rights between the subject and State and discharging its functions according to established form of judicial procedure. If we examine the character of an Election Tribunal in the light of this view of law, it will be found that the Election Tribunal does not at all act as a part of the judicial machinery of the State exercising judicial power of the State and as such, in our view, an Election Tribunal cannot be regarded as a Civil Court.

17. While examining the character of an Election Tribunal and its powers in connection with a trial of an election petition in respect of an election of a member to the Delhi State Legislative Assembly, the Supreme Court of India also has held, in the case of Jagannath Vs. Jaswant Singh, reported in A.I.R. 1954 S.C. page 210, that the Election Tribunal does not possess any power of a Court and it has stated its view in the following manner :

"The general rule is well-settled that the statutory requirement of election law must strictly observed and that an election contest is not an action at law or suit in equity but is a purely statutory provisions unknown to the common law and that the Court possesses no common law power."

<u>18. On the question of applicability of the provisions of Order 39 of the Code of Civil) Procedure in a proceeding before an Election Tribunal, there is no gainsaying the fact that the said provisions have no application in terms to an election dispute tried by an Election Tribunal. A Civil Court is authorised to grant temporary injunction under rules 1 and 2 of Order 39. According to rule 1 of the said Order, a court may grant temporary injunction only when there is a property in dispute which falls in danger of being wasted, damaged or alienated or wrongfully sold or where the defendant has a certain property which he threatens or intends to remove or dispose of with a view to defraud his creditors and rule 2 can be invoked only in a suit which is instituted for restraining the defendant from committing a breach of contract or other injury of any kind. There is hardly any scope for argument to contend that an election dispute is a kind of proceeding analogous to those contemplated in the above two rules. An attempt has also been made to bolster up the respondents contention in this regard independently of Order 39 on the basis section 94 of the Code of Civil Procedure which makes provision for certain supplemental proceedings for preventing the ends of justice from being defeated. The relevant part of section 94 is to the following effect :</u>

<u>"In order to prevent the ends of justice from being defeated the court may, if it is so prescribed</u>

<u>(C) grant a temporary injunction and in case of disobedience commit the person guilty thereof to the civil prison and order that his property be attached and sold.</u>

<u>Section 94 the before does not, relate to the merits involved in a suit but provides for certain supplemental proceedings, not for the purpose of facilitating the trial of a suit., but for the sake of ends of justice.</u>

19. Furthermore, we find from the aforesaid provision that the powers contemplated in section 94 can be exercised, only 'if it is so prescribed' and the word "prescribed" means according to section 2 (16) of the Code, 'prescribed' by rules.' It is therefore clear that the authority, referred to in section 94 can be used only within the limits prescribed by the rules of schedule 1 and cannot thus be exercised independently of Order XXXIX.

<u>20. It has also been contended that in any view of the matter the power of making an order of temporary injunction can be exercised by the Tribunal for meeting the, ends of justice in exercise of the powers analogous to inherent power of a Court. We have already held that an Election Tribunal is not a court and as such the exercise of inherent powers for the sake of ends of justice is not available to it.</u>

21. On the above consideration, we are of opinion that an Election Tribunal cannot make an order which has no relation to the trial of the election dispute, and the passing of an order of temporary injunction restraining the elected representatives from functioning according to law is beyond the jurisdiction of such a tribunal.

The result therefore is that all these rules are made absolute and the orders of temporary injunction granted by the Election Tribunals are hereby set aside. There shall be no orders as to costs in these petitions.

Abdur Rahman Chowdhury, J.— I agree.

End.
