parties:
Amizuddin Ahmed ------ Petitioner.
Vs.
Election Tribunal Narayanganj and ors ------ Respondents.
full_judgment:
Shahabuddin Ahmed J. — In this application under Article 102 of the Constitution the petitioner has challenged the order dated 31.8.74 of the Election Tribunal, Narayanganj (Respondent No. 1) accepting the report of a Pleader Commissioner appointed in connection with an election petition filed under Rule 56 of the Bangladesh Union Parishad and Pourashava Election Rules, 1973, briefly, the Election Rules.

2. The petitioner was elected as Chairman of the Siddirganj Union Parishad by a wide margin of votes over his nearest rival candidate, Respdt. No. 2 and in due course went into office but Respdt. 2 challenged his election by filing an election petition on certain grounds and made an application to the Tribunal for appointment of a Pleader Commissioner to count the ballot papers. The application was allowed and a Pleader Commissioner was appointed by an order dated 25.3.74 in spite of serious objections made by the Petitioner. Thereafter, on three different occasions the petitioner raised objections to the appointment of the Pleader Commissioner and to the counting of ballot papers by him but all his objections were rejected by the Tribunal. The Pleader Commissioner re-opens the ballot boxes, recounted the ballot papers, determined the validity or otherwise of a huge number of ballot papers and submitted his report to this effect. The report was accepted by the Tribunal by its impugned order dated 31.8.74.

3. Mr. Moinul Huq, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner has seriously assailed the impugned order raising three contentions:

(i) Appointment itself of the Pleader Commissioner is illegal, without jurisdiction and arbitrary since appointment of a Pleader Commissioner is not permitted by the Election law or any other relevant law;

(ii) The report of the Pleader Commissioner is in excess of the points referred to the Commissioner in that the Commissioner was directed to simply count the ballot papers' contained in different sealed packets forwarded by the Returning Officer, but he determined the validity of the ballot papers;

(iii) The delegation of the material issue to the Commissioner is entirely without jurisdiction, illegal and beyond the scope of the powers of a Pleader Commissioner.

Mr. Khandkar M. Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing for the respondents has defended the action of the Tribunal and contended that the petition is hit by inordinate delay in that though the Pleader Commissioner was appointed on 25.3.75 the petitioner did not challenge it in this Court but waited till the report of the Commissioner was submitted.

4. The Election Tribunal is the creation of a special law and as such it shall exercise only those powers which are specially given it by law, for it has no common law powers. Before delegating any powers to any other authority, assuming that it has authority to so delegate, the Tribunal must see whether it itself has got any such powers, and if so, under what circumstances. The Election Rules do not provide for recounting ballot papers by the Tribunal and the power to recount ballot papers has been given under rule 41 to the Presiding Officer only. But if recounting of ballot papers is a material issue before the Tribunal and the election petition cannot be determined without such recounting, only then the Tribunal has got power to reopen the ballot boxes and recount the ballot papers in presence of parties. Before doing so it must come to a finding by evidence on oath that this recounting is indispensably necessary. On this view we are supported by established judicial principles. The decisions in Stowe Vs. Jollife (1874), L.R.I.C. P-446 and "G.T. Mudaliar Vs. Sakuntala" AIR 1949 Mad. 835 may be referred to. In the instant case there was no finding by the Tribunal to this effect and it appears that the Pleader Commissioner was appointed for recounting ballot papers at the instance of a party to the election-petition in spite of serious objection by the other party. Under Election Rules, great sanctity is attached to ballot papers and connected documents. As soon as the counting of ballot papers is made by the Presiding Officer the papers are properly sealed and put into separate packets, in presence of the parties, which are then forwarded by the Returning Officer to the Sub-Divisional Officer for safe custody. It is therefore quite in the fitness of things that these sealed packets should be opened by the Tribunal alone and that is also when the Tribunal comes to a finding that these papers should be examined. The Election Rules do not provide for appointment of any Pleader Commissioner for counting ballot papers, far less, for determining their validity. Under Rule 61-A of the Election Rules, a petition is to be tried as far as possible in accordance with the procedure for trial of a suit under the Civil Procedure Code and under Rule 61-B the Tribunal has got all the powers of a Civil Court trying a suit under that Code. Mr. Khandaker M. Ahmed has contended that as the Civil Procedure Code is applicable to the trial of an election petition, so the provision for appointment of a Pleader Commissioner under Order, 26 of that Code shall necessarily apply in an election case. It appears that the provisions of the Civil Procedure Code (briefly the Code) will not necessarily apply in an election case for all purposes, but may apply "as nearly as may be", and this application is subject to the provision of the Election Rules. Under Order 26 of the Code, Pleader Commissioner is appointed for four specific purposes for examination of witnesses, for 'local investigation' for examination of 'accounts' and for making 'partition'. Even if the Code is applicable in full to an election case then also none of these 4 purposes covers the counting of ballot papers. Mr. Ahmed has tried to show that examination of "accounts" includes the counting of ballot papers in that a process of counting is involved in both the cases. We are unable to accept this contention since it is obvious that examination of "accounts" is altogether different from counting of ballet papers.

5. The object of appointing a Pleader Commissioner under the Code is to get elucidation of some points appearing in evidence on records of a case and the Pleader Commissioner is merely to assist the court in such a matter. But a function which can be best discharged by the court itself cannot be delegated to a Pleader Commissioner. A Division Bench of this court expressed exactly the similar view in the case "Sirajuddin Ahmed Vs. Upendra Lala", 22 DLR (Dacca) 827. A material issue in a case cannot be delegated to a Pleader Commissioner. The Privy Council held in Ram Kr. Vs. Ratan, 35 C.W.N. 841: "The decision of a material issue in the case can never be left to the Pleader Commissioner which must be decided by the court itself In the instant case the Tribunal delegated to the Pleader Commissioner the power to count as well as to determine the validity or invalidity of ballot papers. The Writ of Commission was not traceable in the record and when controversy arose as to what were the points referred to the Commissioner appointed under order dated 25-3-5, the Tribunal itself clarified the matter stating in its order dated 31-8-74 that the proposed 'counting of ballot papers' necessarily included determination of the validity of those ballot papers. It is therefore clear that the Tribunal delegated to the Commissioner the most material issue in the election case i.e., to determine the validity of ballot papers. In fact the Commissioner determined the validity of ballot papers; he declared invalid 270 ballot papers of the petitioner which had been held valid by the Presiding Officer; on the other hand, he declared 169 ballot papers of respondent No.2 valid which had been held invalid by the Presiding Officer, and as a result, according to his report, the petitioner's win was reduced to defeat. Determination of such a material point cannot be left to a Pleader Commissioner. Determination of the validity of the ballot papers is a mixed question of law and fact and such a question shall not be delegated to the Pleader Commissioner as has been held by the Privy Council in the case mentioned above.

6. Mr. M. Ahmed has tried to argue that the report of the Pleader Commissioner is a mere opinion which is subject to revision by the Tribunal. But in this case the Tribunal has already accepted the, report of the Pleader Commissioner in full. Acceptance of the report means the end of the whole matter; the petitioner, elected chairman, stands defeated and in his place the defeated candidate stands elected. After acceptance of the report, the Tribunal was left only with the formality of delivering the judgment. For the purpose of determining the most vital issue of a case no Pleader Commissioner shall be appointed such a course of action is not contemplated in the Code. By appointing the Pleader Commissioner, the Tribunal acted entirely without jurisdiction. The ground for appointing the Pleader Commissioner, has given by the Tribunal, is its pre-occupation with other witness of the court. This simply amounts to dereliction of the duty cast upon the Tribunal by law. The counting was held in the court-building; this act could have been done very conveniently by the Tribunal. Instead of doing so, the Tribunal appointed the Pleader Commissioner inspite of serious objections. We, therefore, highly deprecate such a course of action taken by the Tribunal. Again, the appointment of the Pleader Commissioner was made on an application of a party to the case (Respdt. No.2) in the face of strong objection from the other party, If the respondent thought that recounting of ballot papers was very much necessary, he should have prayed for such, recounting by the Tribunal.

7. In a recent case Petition No. 492 of 1974, disposed of on 16-9-74 by a Division Bench of this court presided over by D.C, Bhattacharya, J. it has been held that though the provisions of the Civil Procedure Code are applicable, as far as possible, to the trial of an election petition under Rule 61-A and 61-B, yet the provisions of the Court to temporary injunctions are not applicable and that the Tribunal cannot make an order, which has not relation to the trial of an election dispute, ''Though the Election Tribunal has alt the powers of the Civil Court for the purpose of trying the election dispute, the Election Tribunal cannot be regarded as Civil Court". On this analogy, it appears clearly that the provisions as to appointment of a Pleader Commissioner under the Code are not applicable to an election-petition.

8. As to the contention of inordinate delay in filing this petition, we do not think that there has been any such delay since the election case is still pending before the Tribunal. When an order suffers from want of jurisdiction it can be challenged at any stage.

<u>9. The result therefore is that the Tribunal got no jurisdiction to appoint a Pleader Commissioner for counting ballot papers including the determination of validity of ballot-papers. The impugned order is declared to have been made without lawful authority, and of no legal effect and is set aside. The Rule is made absolute with costs against the contesting respondent No.2. In the circumstances of the case, we assess the costs at Taka one thousand only.</u>

S.M. Hussain, J. — I agree.

End.

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 43 of 2010.
lawyer:
Karunamoy Chakma, Deputy Attorney-General instructed by B Hossain, Advocate-on-Record----- For the Petitioners.
Sheik Mohammad Morshed, Advocate instructed by Syed Mahbubar Rahman, Advocate-on-Record----- For the Respondent.
parties:
Bangladesh and another ----- Petitioners
 Vs.
 Md Abdul Karim ----- Respondent
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated the 7th day of June 2009 passed by the Administrative Appellate Tribunal in Miscellaneous Case No.5 of 2009)
full_judgment:
Md. Abdul Wahhab Miah J: Delay of 72 days in filing this petition for leave to appeal is condoned.

2. This petition for leave to appeal has arisen out of an order dated 6-7-2009 passed by the Administrative Appellate Tribunal, Dhaka in Miscellaneous Case No.5 of 2009.

3. Short facts relevant to disposal of this petition for leave to appeal are as follows:

The respondent, Upazila Food Controller, Munshiganj, filed Administrative Tribunal Case No. 170 of 2000 before the Administrative Tribunal No. 2, Dhaka under section 4 of the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1980 against the present petitioners for declaration that the order dated 14-9-2000, issued by present petitioner No.2, namely the Director General Directorate of Food, Khadya Bhaban, Dhaka imposing penalty for recovery of Tk 1,68,131.44 from the respondent and the order dated 13-8-2001 issued by present petitioner No.1 rejecting his appeal as illegal, void and of no legal effect and also for further direction upon the present petitioners not to recover the said amount from him. Subsequently, the case was re-numbered as Administrative Tribunal Case No. 106 of 2003. The present petitioner No. 2 contested the said Administrative Tribunal Case by filing written objection. Eventually, the Administrative Tribunal No.2, Dhaka by its order dated 8-8-2004 allowed the case declaring the order dated 14-9-2000 imposing penalty for recovery of Tk 1,68,131.44 from the respondent and the dated 13-8-2001 rejecting his appeal as illegal, void and is of no legal effect and not binding upon him .

<u>4. Against the order of the Administrative Tribunal the present petitioners filed Appeal No. 43 of 2005 before the Administrative Appellate Tribunal, Dhaka. The appeal was dismissed for default on 19-1-2001 as none appeared for the appellants when the same was called on for hearing. The petitioners filed an application before the Administrative Appellate Tribunal, Dhaka for restoration of the appeal after setting aside the order of default. The Appellate Tribunal by the impugned order rejected the application on the ground that the same was f led out of time by 7 days. The Appellate Tribunal further observed that the appeal being under special statute, it had no power to condone the delay; hence this petition for leave to appeal.</u>

5. 	Heard Mr Korunamoy Chakma, learned Deputy Attorney General for the petitioners and Mr Sheikh Mohammad Morshed, learned Advocate for the respondent.

<u>6. In the back-ground of the case as stated hereinbefore, the only point to be decided in this petition for leave to appeal is whether any limitation has been prescribed for in the relevant laws, namely, the Administrative Tribunal Act. 1980 (the Act) and the Administrative Tribunals Rules. 1982 framed under the Act for filing an application for restoration of an appeal dismissed for default and whether the Administrative Appellate Tribunal was justified in rejecting the application for restoration as being barred by limitation. The point has also some public importance as there has been no pronouncement by this Division.</u>

7. Section 5 of the Act has dealt with the provisions of establishment of the Administrative Appellate Tribunal. The provision for filing appeal by an aggrieved person against the order or decision passed by the Administrative Tribunal has been provided for in section 6 of the Act, but provisions have not been provided therein as to how an appeal shall be filed, registered and disposed of. Similarly provisions have not been made in the Act as to how the Administrative Tribunal shall deal with a case filed before it under section 4 of the Act right from its filing and registration. We consider it beneficial to quote section 6 of the Act in its entirety which is as under:

6. Jurisdiction of Administrative Appellate Tribunal-(1)

The Administrative Appellate Tribunal shall have jurisdiction to hear and determine appeals from any order or decision of an Administrative Tribunal.

(2) 	Any person aggrieved by an order or decision of an Administrative Tribunal may, within (three months) from the date of making of the order or decision, prefer an appeal to the Administrative Appellate Tribunal.

(2A) Notwithstanding the provisions of subsection (2), an appeal may be admitted after the period of three months specified in that sub-section but not later than six months, if the appellant satisfies the Administrative Appellate Tribunal that he had sufficient cause for not preferring the appeal within three months.

(3) 	The Administrative Appellate Tribunal may, on appeal, confirm, set aside, vary or modify any order or decision of an Administrative Tribunal, and the decision of the Administrative Appellate Tribunal in an appeal shall subject to section 6A, be final.

8. Thus, a reading of sub-section (2) of section 6 of the Act shows that an appeal has to be filed by an aggrieved person before the Administrative Appellate Tribunal within three months from the date of making of the order or decision and sub-section (2A) has given the power to the Administrative Tribunal to admit an appeal after the period of three months as specified in sub-section (2), but not later than 6(six) months, if the appellant satisfies it that he had sufficient cause for not preferring the appeal within three months.

9. Section 12 of the Act has provided that the Government may, by notification in the official gazette, make rules for carrying out the purpose of the Act, Sub-section (2) of section 12 of the Act has further provided that in particular and without prejudice to the generality of the foregoing power, such rules may provide for all or any. of the following matters, namely;-

(a) Form and manner in which and the fee on payment of which an application or appeal may be made;

(b) Registration of an application or appeal; (c) Procedure to be followed by a Tribunal in hearing an application or appeal, as the case may be;

(d) 	Form and service of notices, summonses and requisitions;

(e) Prescription of records and reports to be maintained or prepared by a Tribunal:

(f) 	Execution of decisions and orders of a Tribunal;

(g) 	Any other matter which is to be or may be prescribed.

10. Pursuant to the provisions of section 12 of the Act the Government made rules under the name Administrative Tribunal Rules, 1982 (the Rules) which were published in the official gazette on 12th of March, 1982 vide SRO 92-L/82- JIV/IT-3/81. In the Rules detailed provisions have been made as to how an application shall be filed before the Administrative Tribunal, registered and disposed of by it including the provisions for restoration in case an application is dismissed for default and to set aside any order made ex-parte. In the Rules no separate procedure has been provided for in respect of filing of an appeal before the Administrative Appellate Tribunal, its registration and disposal by it. Rule 11 has provided that the provisions of the Rules shall, mutatis mutandis, apply to an appeal to the Administrative Appellate Tribunal under sub-section (2) of section 6 of the Act, Rule 11 runs thus: Appeals-Save as otherwise provided in the Act, the provisions of these rules shall, mutatis mutandis, apply to an appeal to the Administrative Appellate Tribunal under sub-section (2) of section 6.

11. Since the provisions of the Rules made in respect of disposal of an application by the Administrative Tribunal have been made applicable in case of disposal of an appeal by the Administrative Appellate Tribunal by Rule 11 of the Rules as quoted hereinbefore as of necessity for restoration of an appeal dismissed for default, the appellants are to fall back upon Rule 6 of the Rules. For ready reference we consider it relevant to quote sub-rules (4) (5) (6) and (7) of Rule 6 for the purpose of the present case (the other sub-rules not being relevant to the case are not quoted). The said sub-rules read as follows:

(4) Where on the day so fixed neither party appears and it is found that the notices to appear have been served upon the par- ties to the dispute, Tribunal may make an order dismissing the application.

(5) Where on the day so fixed the applicant appears and the opposite party does not appear, Tribunal may, if it is found that, the notice to appear has been served, hear the application ex-parte.

(6) Where on the day so fixed the opposite party appears and the applicant does not appear the Tribunal may make an order dismissing the application; Provided that where the opposite party admits the claim of the applicant or from the materials on record it is found that the relief claimed by the applicant should be allowed, the Tribunal shall make an order granting the relief to such extent as it deems fit.

(7) Any party to the dispute aggrieved by an order made under sub-rules (4), (5) and (6) may apply to the Tribunal for an order to set aside the dismissal or the order made ex-parte and if the Tribunal is satisfied that there was sufficient cause for the non-appearance of the party, the Tribunal shall make an order setting aside the dismissal or the order made ex-parte on such conditions as it deems fit.

<u>12. Sub-rule (6) as quoted hereinbefore clearly shows that on the day fixed for hearing of an application if the opposite party (in case of appeal it is to be read as respondent) appears and the applicant (in case of appeal it is to be read as the appellant) does not appear, the Tribunal may make an order dismissing the application (here the appeal). Sub-rule (7) has clearly provided that any party to the dispute aggrieved by an order made under sub-rules (4) (5)(6) may apply to the Tribunal for an order to set aside the dismissal or the order ex-parte, and if the Tribunal is satisfied that there was sufficient cause for non-appearance of the party the Tribunal shall make an order setting aside the dismissal or the order made ex-parte on such conditions as it deems fit. A plain reading of sub-rule (7) shows that no period has been prescribed for filing an application for setting aside an order of dismissal or an order made ex-parte. What has been provided for in sub-rule (7) is that it is the satisfaction of the Tribunal whether there was sufficient cause for non-appearance of the party when the application was called on for hearing or the order was made exparte. When in the Rules no period has been prescribed for filing an application for setting aside an order of dismissal which is also applicable in case of an appeal because of Rule 11 of the Rules as quoted hereinbefore, the question of treating an application for restoration of an appeal as time barred does arise at all. It may be stated that in sections 4 and 6 of the Act, specific period of limitation has been provided for filing an application and an appeal by an aggrieved person before the Administrative Tribunal and the Administrative Appellate Tribunal respectively.</u>

13. Besides the Rules framed under section 12 of the Act, section 7 of the Act is also relevant to the present context. In section 7 powers and procedure of the Tribunals have been spelt out, In sub-section (1) of section 7 it has been clearly provided that for the purpose of hearing of an application or appeal as the case may be, a Tribunal shall have all the powers of Civil Court, while trying a suit under the Code of Civil Procedure in respect of the following matters, namely:

(a) 	Summoning and enforcing the attendance of any person and examining him on oath;

(b) 	Requiring the discovery and production of any document;

(c) 	Requiring evidence on affidavit;

(d) 	Requisitioning any public record or a copy thereof from any office;

(e) 	Issuing commissions for the examination of witnesses or documents;

(f) 	Such other matters as may be prescribed.

14. So the Tribunals have been equated with the civil Court for a very limited compass. In section 7, there are 7 other sub-sections. And of those subsection (8) is on the point at issue. We consider it necessary to quote sub-section (8) which is as follows:

(8) Subject to the other provisions of this Act, a Tribunal shall, for the purpose of hearing an application or appeal, as the case be, follow such procedure as may be prescribed;

Provided that where, in respect of any matter no procedure has been prescribed by this Act or by rules made thereunder, a Tribunal shall follow the procedure in respect thereof as may be laid down by the Administrative Appellate Tribunal.

15. A reading of sub-section (8) shows that subject to the provisions of the Act, a Tribunal shall for the purpose of an application or appeal, as the case may be, follow such procedure as may be prescribed. Proviso to sub-section (8) has further provided that where, in respect of any matter, no procedure has been prescribed by this Act or by Rules made thereunder, a Tribunal shall follow the procedure in respect thereof as may be laid down by the Administrative Appellate Tribunal. So, when in the Rules detailed procedures have been laid down as to the power of dismissal of an appeal by the Administrative Appellate Tribunal and then restoration of the same on the basis of an application, the Administrative Appellate Tribunal has no other option but to follow the same.

<u>16. From a close study of the above mentioned provisions of the Act as well as the Rules, it appears to us that no period has been prescribed for filing an application for setting aside an order of dismissal of an appeal, so the question of rejection of an application on the ground of limitation does not arise at all. But unfortunately the Administrative Appellate Tribunal has failed to consider this legal aspect of the case in passing the impugned order. The Appellate Tribunal has also not stated the provisions of law under which the appellant was required to file an application for restoration within a specified time when it mentioned that the application was filed out of time by 7(seven) days. What appears to us is that an Administrative Tribunal or the Administrative Appellate Tribunal, as the case may be, may rejected application for setting aside an order of dismissal or an ex-parte order even if the same is filed within the shortest possible period, if the applicant or the appellant fails to give sufficient cause to the satisfaction of the concerned Tribunal for failure to appear when the case or appeal was taken up for hearing.</u>

17. For the discussions made above, we hold that the Administrative Appellate Tribunal acted illegally in passing the impugned order rejecting the application for restoration of the appeal in question as being barred by limitation, consequently the impugned order cannot be sustained. However, since the Administrative Appellate Tribunal rejected the application on the ground of limitation only without going in to the merit of the application we refrain ourselves from making any comment about its merit and leave the matter to the Administrative Appellate Tribunal for its decision.

18. In the backdrop of the case as discussed above, we find no other alternative but to send the case back on remand to the Administrative Appellate Tribunal for disposal of the application for restoration of the appeal on merit as expeditiously as possible. Accordingly, this leave petition is disposed of in the following terms;

(a) 	The impugned order dated 6-7-2001 passed by the Administrative Appellate Tribunal, Dhaka in Miscellaneous Case No.5 of 2009 is set aside.

(b) 	The Administrative Appellate Tribunal, Dhaka is directed to dispose of the application filed by the appellants for restoration of the appeal on merit as expeditiously as possible keeping in view sub-rule (7) of Rule 6 of the Administrative Tribunal Rules ) 982 and the observation made and the findings  given hereinbefore.

Let a copy of the order be sent to the Administrative Appellate Tribunal, Dhaka.

End.

lawyer:
Akram Hossain Amin, with Aftab Hossain ------ For the Petitioner.

B.N. Chowdhury ------ For the opposite party.
parties:
Rokya Begum  ------ Petitioner.
Vs.
Radha Gobinda Das  ------ Opposite Party.
full_judgment:
This Rule arises out of a proceeding for preemption which was originally started under section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act.

2. The property in question belonged to two brothers, namely, Gopal Chandra Das and Radha Gobinda Das, of whom Gopal Chandra Das was insane. Radha Gobinda Das having sold the disputed land by a kabala dated 14.11.60 for a sum of Tk. 400/- to the petitioner, an application under section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was filed on the 22nd July, 1965 by Gopal Chandra Das through one Suren Chandra as his next friend on the allegation that Gopal Chandra was insane and the applicant's date of the knowledge about the sale under pre-emption was the 23rd April, 1965. On the 28th March, 1966 the said Suren Chandra Das was removed as the next friend of the applicant, who was thereafter represented by one Promatha Nath Sarker as his next friend. At the time of the hearing Suren Chandra Das was examined as a witness on behalf of the opposite party in the said case. The pre-emption proceeding was ultimately dismissed by the trial Court on the grounds that the formalities enjoined under section 96 of the Act as to the statement about the total quantity of the land in possession of the applicant was not complied with and also that the story that the purchaser having not been in possession of the purchased land, the applicant was not at all aware of the sale under pre-emption, was not believable and as such the proceeding was barred by limitation. The purchaser's further case that she made an improvement of the land costing about Tk. 1200/ was also not accepted. The application having failed, an appeal against the said order of dismissal was filed, and the appeal was allowed by the Subordinate Judge, Rajshahi on the finding that the applicant had no knowledge of the sale earlier than the date alleged in the application and as such the application was not barred by limitation. The learned Sub ordinate Judge further held that it being stated in the application that the applicant had not more than 20 bighas of land and this statement having not been denied in the written objection, it cannot be said that the requirement of section 96 as to the ceiling of the land in possession was not complied with.

3. As against the said order the present rule has been obtained on behalf of the purchaser.

4. Mr. Akram Hossain Amin, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner submits that although the application has been purported to have been filed under Section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, this application should be treated as an application under section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act in as much as the right of pre-emption has accrued at the time when the provisions of Bengal Tenancy Act were in force in the area in which the lands under pre-emption are situated. The learned Advocate has contended that the period of limitation under section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act in case of a non-notified co-sharer is 3 years from the date of the sale, and that the present application having been filed long after three years from the date of the sale, the Court of appeal acted illegally in the exercise of its jurisdiction in allowing the said application.

5. It has been stated in the application that Part V of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 which includes section 96 of the Act came into operation on the 1st August, 1963 in the District of Rajshahi wherein the land under. Pre-emption lies. The right of pre-emption accrued in the present case on the 14th November, 1960, the date of the Kabala under pre-emption, when Section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was not brought into operation but section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act was in force. In the circumstances the learned Advocate for the petitioner has submitted that the application for pre-emption should be deemed to be an application under, section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act, although the same has been purported to have been filed under section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act.

<u>6. Sattar, J, (as he then was) sitting singly in the case of Huzzat Ali Vs. Imamuddin Bepari 13 D.L.R. (Dhaka) page 819 held that an application for pre-emption filed after Chapter V of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act had come into operation must be governed by the rule of limitation prescribed by Section 96 of the said Act. This view of the warned Judge has been over ruled by a Division Bench of Dacca High Court in the case of Abdul Malek Vs. Abdur Rahman 19 D.L.R. (Dacca) page 318 in which the following view was expressed :—</u>

<u>"We are of the view that a right of pre-emption accrued before the repeal of the Bengal Tenancy Act does not cease to be a right under the repealed Act by virtue of section 8 of the Bengal General Clauses Act, 1899 and that the said right can in no manner be affected by the new act, since in terms of the Act of 1899 the new Act is to be considered as if it has not been passed. An applicant seeking to enforce his right of pre-emption accrued under section 26F of the old Act, is, therefore, entitled to the rule of three years limitation as was available to him before the repeal".</u>

<u>Although the application was described as under section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, I do not think that such a mis-description of the provision of law or misquotation of a particular section of an Act will stand in the way of the said application being considered to be under the relevant law which is applicable to the case in question. I am, therefore of the view that the learned Advocate for the petitioner is correct in con-tending that this application for pre-emption should regarded as an application under section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act and the provisions of the said Act should be applied for the purpose of determining the question of limitation raised in the case.</u>

7. Mr. Akram Hossain Amin, the learned Advocate for the petitioner next contends that the application being under section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act and the co-sharer applicant having claimed that he was a non-notified co-sharer the period of limitation in such a case is not 4 months from the date of the knowledge as prescribed under section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, but three years from the date of sale as has been laid down by a Special Bench of the Calcutta High Court in the case of Asmat Ali Sharif Vs. Mujahar Ali Sardar and another 52 Calcutta weekly Notes page 64. It has been held in the said case that the case of non-notified cosharers having not been provided in the Bengal Tenancy Act nor there having been any specific provision in regard to such a case in the Limitation Act, the residuary provision of Article 182 of the Schedule to the Limitation Act shall apply. The learned Advocate for the petitioner contends that the starting point of limitation being the date of sale which was the 14th November, 1960 the period of limitation has come to an end on the expiry of three years from the said date and the present application having been filed after more than four years 7 months is hopelessly barred by limitation.

8. Mr. B. N. Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite parties has not seriously disputed the applicability of the provisions of the Bengal Tenancy Act to the present application for pre-emption, but he has contended that the period of limitation as prescribed under Article 182 of the Schedule of the Limitation Act shall be extended in the present case as the applicant had been suffering from a disability as contemplated in section 6 of the Limitation Act during the entire period from the date of accrual of the cause of action till the filling of the application.

9. The contention of the learned Advocate has raised a question of limitation of some nicety. The period of limitation prescribed under the Bengal Tenancy Act is of only 4 months from the date of service of the notice and it was a special or local law within the meaning of section 29 of the Limitation Act. Section 29(2) embodies the following provisions:

"Where any special or local law prescribes for any suit, appeal or application a period of limitation different from the period prescribed therefor by the first schedule, the provisions of section 3 shall apply, as if such period were prescribed therefor in that schedule, and for the purpose of determining any period of limitation prescribed for any suit, appeal or application by any special or local law—(a) the provisions contained in section 4, sections 9 to 18 and section 22 shall apply only in so far as, and to the extent to which, they are not expressly excluded by such special or local law; and (b) the remaining provisions of this Act shall not apply."

10. Mr. Akram Hossain Amin, the learned Advocate for the petitioner contends that having regard to the aforesaid provision of Limitation Act, section 6 of the said Act has no application to the present case. We are to see how far the contention of the learned Advocate is borne out by the aforesaid provisions.

<u>11. The said provision has application only in the case where any special or local law prescribes for any suit appeal or application a period of limitation different from the period prescribed therefor by the First Schedule in the limitation Act. The Bengal Tenancy Act does not provide for any period of limitation in respect of any application made by a non-notified co-sharer. According to the Special Bench decision of Calcutta High Court in Asmat Ali's case the period of limitation shall be three years, as prescribed under Article 182 of the First Schedule of the Limitation Act. The present case is that of a non-notified co-sharer. It is therefore, clear that it cannot be said that the Bengal Tenancy Act prescribes in respect of this particular application a period of limitation different from the period prescribed therefor by the Limitation Act.</u>

12. In the case of Province of Bengal Vs. Amulya Dhon Addy, in 54 Cal. Weekly Notes page 297 the question arose whether section 5 of the Limitation Act could be made applicable to an appeal preferred to the High Court under Calcutta Improvement (Appeal 1911 Act XVIII of 1911). Section 3 of the said Act confers a right of appeal to the High Court against a decision of the Board of the Trustee but it does not prescribe any special period of limitation and therefore Article 156 of First Schedule of the Limitation Act was held to be applicable in respect of an appeal preferred to the High Court under section 3 of the said Act. On the question whether the provisions of section 5 of the Limitation Act could be made applicable to such an appeal in view of section 29 of the Limitation Act, the learned Judges of the Calcutta High Court held that as the special Act did not prescribe any period of limitation other than that prescribed in the Limitation Act, section 29(2) of the Limitation Act had no application and therefore the provision of section 5 of the Limitation Act would be available to an appellant under section 3 of the said Act for the purpose of making out a case for condonation of delay on the ground of sufficient cause.

13. In the case of Mutyala Venkatramayya Vs. Tanguutri Venkata Subbaya and others, decided by Wordsworth and Patanjali Sastri, JJ of Madras High Court reported in A.I.R. 1946 Madras page 351, the law as to applicability of section 29(2) of limitation Act, was laid down in the following manner:

"All that section 29(2) lays down is that where a special or local law prescribes a special period of limitation, the excluded provisions of the Limitation Act shall not apply. For instance, it has been held that under section 20, Madras Act IV(4) of 1936, a special period of Limitation is laid down for the filing of an application under section 19 by a person who has obtained a stay under section 20 and consequently section 5 of the Limitation Act, cannot be applied to extend the period therefor prescribed under the Special Law. In section 25A, newly introduced into this Act, though a right of appeal is given, no period of limitation different from the period prescribed by Schedule 1, Limitation Act, is indicated. Therefore the provisions of section 29(2) have no application so as to exclude the provisions of section 5, Limitation Act, from being applied to appeals under the special law".

<u>14. It is thus quite clear that the provision of section 29(2) has no application to a case where no different period of limitation has been prescribed by a special or local law for an application which may be filed to enforce a right created or declared under the said law and the person making such an application is entitled to the benefits of those provisions of the Limitation Act which operate to extend the period of limitation for such an application in certain cases.</u>

15. Section 6 of the Limitation Act was amended in Pakistan by Central Ordinance XLIII of 1962, according to which the words, "a proceeding" were inserted in the first sentence of sub-section (1) of the said section after the word "suit" in two places and after amendment the said sub-section of section 6 stands as follows :

"Where a person entitled to institute a suit or proceeding or make an application for the execution of decree, is at the time from which the period of limitation is to be reckoned a minor, or insane or an idiot, he may institute the suit or proceeding or make the application within the same period after the disability has ceased, as would otherwise have been allowed from the time prescribed therefor in 'the third column of the first schedule".

Mr. B. N. Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite party submits that the original co-sharer applicant Gopal Chandra was insane at the time when the sale took place and the application was filed through a next friend on 22.7.65 when he was still an insane person and therefore he is entitled to exclusion of the entire period under sub-section (1) of section 6 of the Limitation Act.

16. A single Bench of Calcutta High Court in the case of S. Radharani Dasi Vs. Atul Chandra Mondal and another in 55 Calcutta Weekly Notes page 501 had an occasion to consider a similar question when the provision of section 6 was pleaded on behalf of the applicant under section 26F of the B. T. Act for exclusion of certain period due to minority of the applicant and held that the applicant was not entitled to claim the benefits of the said section on the ground that it did not come within the terms of section 6 as was in force in India because section 6 of the Indian Limitation Act has not been amended for the purpose of making it applicable to a proceeding. Murshed C. J. of Dacca High Court sitting singly in the case of Debendra Chandra Dev Nath Vs. Bharat Chandra Singha and others 19 D.L.R. (Dacca) page 514 had to consider a similar question but it does not appear that the question of applicability of section 29(2) of the Limitation Act was raised in the said case. The learned Chief Justice has held there that a period of three years limitation as provided in Art. 182 of Schedule 1, Limitation Act is applicable to the case of a non-notified co-sharer and has further observed that the scheme of the Act'is that the guillotine should be applied in the manner as indicated in the said Act with such exceptions as have been provided by sections 5, 12, 14, 15, 16 and 18 thereof and period of Limitation could not be extended on any other account. (Section 5 is apparently a misprint or mistyping for section 4 in the above-sentence). It was not considered in the said case that the exception as provided in section 6 of the Act may also be attracted in a certain circumstances.

<u>17. Mr. Akram Hossain Amin, the learned Advocate for the petitioner further submits that the provision of section 6 of the Limitation Act as amended cannot be invoked in the present case in view of the provisions of section 8 of the Limitation Act which provides that nothing in section 6 applies to a suit to enforce the right of pre-emption. The learned Advocate submits that though the word 'suit' has been used in section 8 it should be understood in the wider sense to include also a proceeding for pre-emption. I am unable to accept the contention of the learned Advocate in this regard. The provision of section 6 as amended clearly brings a proceeding for pre-emption within the purview of that section. It is obvious, that the words 'suit' and 'proceeding' have not been used in synonymous sense and therefore when section 8 was not amended by adding 'proceeding' in the same manner as in section 6 of other Act, it must be taken that the Legislature did not do so deliberately. I, therefore, hold that it having not been disputed that the original applicant Gopal Chandra was insane at the time of the sale under pre-emption as well as at the time the application was filed, he was entitled to exclusion of the period under the provisions of section 6 of the Limitation Act.</u>

18. The learned Advocate for the petitioner has also contended that the opposite party No. 1. who has been substituted in place of the original applicant is no other than the Vendor himself who was responsible for the sale under pre-emption and in that view of matter he is not entitled to step into the shoes of his brother and prosecute the pre-emption case. It is no doubt very curious that the original vendor has after lapse of several years become a heir to the original applicant and has purported to exercise the preferential right of purchase of the property which he himself sold. But I do not find any provision of law by virtue of which his claim of pre-emption can be defeated. He has succeeded to the interest of his brother and has inherited all the rights of his deceased brother including the right of pre-emption. 'There does not appear to be any question of estoppel in this case.

19. Mr. Akram Hossain Amin, the learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that the original vendor purported to sell the land as a including the share of his brother and therefore he sound not be allowed to claim the right of pre-emption as a co-sharer. On a perusal of the document, however, I find that although he purported to sell the entire land, it was made clear in the deed that the property belonged to two brothers and the purchaser purchased the property with his eyes open.  We are not concerned here with any case as to whether, in view of the recitals in the Kabala, the opposite party No. 1 was not entitled succeed to the property of his deceased brother. This question cannot be decided in a summary proceeding like this under section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act 1, therefore, do not find any substance in this contention of the learned Advocate.

20. Although this case has been argued in this court on a new basis, namely that this application should be considered to be one under section 26F of the B. T. Act and the learned Advocate is correct in this contention but on a consideration that the provision of section 6 is applicable to the facts of this case, I do not find that the application is barred by limitation. In that view of the matter, I am of opinion that this application cannot succeed and the Rule is therefore discharged without any order as to costs.

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 17th February, 1997 passed by the  administrative Appellate Tribunal, Dhaka in Appeal No.29 of 1991).
full_judgment:
Mahmudul Amin Chowdhury CJ: These two appeals are taken up for disposal which arose out of judgment and order dated 17th February. 1997 passed by the Administrative Appellate Tribunal. Dhaka in Appeal No.29 of 1995 allowing the same with certain observations

2. The short fact leading to these appeals are that Md Anwarul Islam, former Police Sergeant appellant in Civil Appeal No.61 of 1997 filed Administrative Tribunal Case No.107 of 1991 alleging that earlier he was posted at eastern Police Post. Dhaa and on 20-6-1984 at dead of night while he was returning home from duty station at East Dhanmondi Police outpost he found a Microbus bearing No. Dhaka-Cha-1456 moving suspiciously and after a chase he arrested the driver and found two bales of Indian cloth in the Microbus. He then escorted the driver and the Microbus and cloths to Dhanmondi Police Station with the help of another police sergeant and handed over the driver the Microbus and two bales of Indian cloth and lodged First Information Report which was recorded as Dhanmondi PS Case No.61(6) 84 under section 156(4) of the Customs Act. It is the case of the petitioner that thereafter he was transferred to Khulna on 8-7-1984 by the Inspector General of Police where he joined on 15-7-1984. It is his further case that Assistant Commissioner of Dhaka Metropolitan Police investigated the case and submitted a report on 16-7-1984. On 30-7-1984 respondent-petitioner was suspended by the Metropolitan Police Commissioner, Dhaka on he basis of that report and a proceeding drawn up against him under the Police Officers (Special Provisions) Ordinance, 1976 on a charge of corruption on the allegation of illegally releasing 18 bales of Indian cloth seized by him. A show cause notice was served upon him on 15-10-1984 to which he submitted a written statement in his defence on 27-10-1984 denying all the charges brought against him. In that proceeding was fixed for personal hearing before the inquiry officer where he appeared but was not heard. Then the inquiry officer completed the inquiry but the copy of the charge sheet of the Dhanmondi Police Station case was not supplied to him and thereby he was denied the opportunity of defence. Then by order dated 17-11-1984 he was compulsorily retired from service. Then the respondent preferred appeal which was rejected on 7-3-1985 Then again revisional application was filed on 30-3-1985 which was also rejected on 16-1-1991 and thereafter the aforesaid case before the Administrative Tribunal was filed on 28- 4-1991.

3. The case was contested by appellant No.2 the Inspector General of Police by filing a written statement denying the material allegations. It was the case of the contesting party that from the Microbus 20 bales of Indian cloths were seized but after producing only two bales to the duty officer the first information report was lodged stating that only two bales were seized consequent to which a depart-mental proceeding was started against the respondent on charge of misconduct and corruption under Clause 4(1) and 4(IV) of the aforesaid Ordinance of 1976 and after observing the formalities including second show cause notice respondent was compulsorily retired from service on 17-1-1984 under the aforesaid Ordinance.

4. Before the Administrative Tribunal both the parties adduced evidence and the Tribunal on consideration of the same by judgment dated 18-2-1995 dismissed the case on two counts, firstly that the case is time barred and secondly that no illegality has been committed in passing the order of compulsory retirement.

5. On being aggrieved by the order of dismissal of the case respondent preferred Appeal No. 29 of 1995 before the Administrative Appellate Tribunal and the Appellate Tribunal on hearing allowed the appeal, set aside the order of the Administrative Tribunal and declared that the respondent is still in service and entitled to all benefits upon setting aside the order of compulsory retirement. The Administrative Tribunal however observed that the competent authority will be at liberty to proceed against the respondent afresh on the same allegation if they so desire and the appellant will continue to remain in suspension till final order is passed. The present appellant and the respondent on being aggrieved by the same judgment of the Administrative Appellate Tribunal filed two Leave petitions and leave was granted to consider the following:

"It appears from the impugned judgment that the Appellate Tribunal took the view that since opposite party No.3 drew up proceeding against the petitioner after he had joined District Police force, Khulna on transfer he (of No.3) had no jurisdiction for taking disciplinary action against the petitioner because: the provisions of Regulation No.859 of PRB, and section 9 of the DMP Ordinance (IIl of 1976) provide that when a police detachment is transferred to another jurisdiction the authority or taking disciplinary action against that detachment will lie with the competent authority or the latter jurisdiction for all purposes and the jurisdiction of the authority of former station will cease. The Appellate Tribunal also found that the application of the petitioner was not time barred and the decision of the Tribunal below on that point as wrong.

6. Mr B Hossain, learned Deputy Attorney General appearing for the opposite party petitioner (Civil Petition No.326 of 1997) submits that the learned Appellate Tribunal upon a misconception or law and facts wrongly held that the Metropolitan Police Commissioner, Dhaka cased to have jurisdiction for taking disciplinary action against the petitioner (respondent) causing failure of justice he also submits that the order of compulsory retirement passed against the petitioner is protected by section 8 of the Police Officers (Special Provisions) Ordinance, 1976.

7. Mr Amir-ul-Islam, learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner (In Civil Petition No.330 of 1997) submits that the learned Appellate Tribunal acted in excess of its jurisdiction by making the observation in the judgment as above causing prejudice to the petitioner. The observation is liable to be deleted from he said impugned judgment, he submits."

8. From the perusal of the judgment it appears that the Administrative Tribunal also dismissed the case on the ground of limitation which was set aside by the Administrative Appellate Tribunal but leave was not granted on the point of limitation. Leave was granted on he competency of appellant No.3, Metropolitan Police Commissioner to pass the impugned order of compulsory retirement of the respondent Leave was also granted in the Civil Petition filed by the respondnent No. Anwarul Islam against certain observations made by the Administrative Appellate Tribunal. The first point raised by the Additional Attorney General is that the Administrative Appellate Tribunal committed wrong and illegality in holding that drawing up of the proceeding against the respondent by appellant No.3 i.e. Metropolitan Police Commissioner, Dhaka after transfer of the respondent from Dhaka to Khulna and joining there is contrary to law and discipline and it is the Superintendent of Police of Khulna where the respondent was posted on the date of drawing up proceeding was competent to proceed with the inquiry.

9. Admittedly the respondent was charged for misconduct alleging that on 20-6-1984 while he was posted as Sergeant in Dhaka Metropolitan Police he apprehended a Microbus with a driver and actually recovered 20 bales of Indian cloth but while lodging the First Information Report he showed recovery of only two bales and misappropriated the remaining. The occurrence took place within Dhaka Metropolitan area where the respondent was posted at the relevant time. On receipt of the First Information Report from the respondent Dhanondi PS Case No.61(6) 84 was started. Thereafter on 8-7-1984 the respondent was transferred by the Inspector General of Police to Khulna where he joined on 15-7-1984. It is also an admitted fact that on 30-7-1984 the respondent was placed under suspension and proceeding was drawn up against him under Police Officers (Special Provisions) Ordinance, 1976 ona charge of corruption. It is also an admitted fact that show cause notice was served upon the respondent on 15-10-1984 and he submitted his written statement in his defence on 27-10-1984. He was to be heard in person on 4-11-1984 by appellant 0.3 Subsequently on completion of inquiry report was submitted and ultimately respondent was compulsorily retired from service on 17-11-1984. Now the Administrative Appellate Tribunal found that after transfer of the respondent from Dhaka to Khulna the Metropolitan Police Commissioner, Dhaka has no authority to initiate proceeding and to pass any disciplinary order compulsorily retiring the respondent. This proceeding was initiated under the Police Officers (Special Provisions) Ordinance, 1976. The Administrative Appellate Tribunal placing reliance on regulation 859 of Police Regulation observed that the proceeding ought to have been initiated and conducted by the Superintendent of Police of Khulna where at the relevant time the respondent was posted. Admittedly the occurrence took police while respondent was posted in Metropolitan Police at Dhaka. Section 6 of the Ordinance provided that when a police officer is to be proceeded for any or the offences mentioned in section 4 the authority concerned shall frame a charge and specify therein penalty proposed to be imposed and communicate it to the police officer hereinafter called "accused" requiring him to show cause within specified time which shall not be less than 7 days and not more than 10 days from the date the charge has been communicated to him why penalty proposed to be imposed shall not be imposed and also to state whether he desires to be heard in person. Now section 2(A) of the Ordinance defined "authority" as the authority specified in column 2 of the schedule. In column 2 of the schedule it has been provided that in case of a sergeant the authority would be Deputy Inspector General of Police and in case of Metropolitan area Police Commissioner or Additional Police Commissioner. Admittedly the respondent was acting' as Sergeant in the Dhaka Metropolitan Police and as such as per this Ordinance it is the Metropolitan Police Commissioner, Dhaka or the Additional Commissioner who was competent to draw up proceeding and that has been done in the present case. Admittedly when the proceeding was initiated by the Metropolitan Police Commissioner the respondent was posted in Khulna. In this Ordinance there is nothing that in case of transfer before drawing up of proceeding the same should be drawn up or initiated or proceeded with at the place where the accused is posted. This Ordinance indicate that the proceeding may be initiated/drawn up when the alleged offence has been committed. Though in Regulation 859 of PRB it has been provided that the Superintendent of Police where such an officer is posted will be fully competent to take any disciplinary action for an offence committed by such an officer when he was posted outside his jurisdiction but in view of section 3 of the Ordinance this Regulation 859 has lost its force as section 3 provided that this Ordinance shall have effect notwithstanding anything contained in any law, rules and regulations relating to police force not shall prejudice operation of any other law, Rules and regulations including service conditions of the said police force. When a proceeding is drawn up against a police official under this Ordinance the plea that his case is to be decided under any other law will have no effective force. So in the present case regulation 859 cannot be a bar in proceeding with the disciplinary action against the respondent by the Metropolitan Police Commissioner in Dhaka. It is an admitted fact that the accused respondent was transferred to Khulna by the Inspector General of Police and he has been charged and proceeded with for an offence committed by him while posted in Dhaka Metropolitan Police by the Police Commissioner of Dhaka Metropolitan Police and in view of the clear provision of the Ordinance we hold that no illegality and wrong has been committed in this case. in he Ordinance there is nothing to show that in case of such a nature the concerned authority is required to send the record of the proceeding to the Superintendent of Police where the accused has been subsequently transferred and when there is no such provision in the Ordinance and when this Ordinance override all other laws, rules and regulations we hold that the Administrative Appellate Tribunal committed wrong and illegality in allowing the appeal holding that appellant No.3 i.e. the Police Commissioner of Dhaka Metropolitan Police had no jurisdiction in taking disciplinary action against the respondent. In such a case provision of regulation 859 of PRB and section 9 of the DMP Ordinance (III of 1973) will have no effect and bar in holding an inquiry and punishing an accused.

10. Having given our anxious consideration to the materials on record and after hearing the learned Advocate of both the sides we hold that the Administrative Appellate Tribunal committed wrong and illegality in allowing the appeal.

11. The respondent also filed Civil Appeal No.61 of 1997 against certain observation made in the judgment by the Administrative Appellate Tribunal. It appears that while disposing of the appeal the Administrative Appellate Tribunal observed as follows

"In view however of the' facts and circumstances of the case we are inclined in the interest of justice to allow the competent authority an opportunity to proceed fresh against the appellant on the same allegations."

<u>12. Mr Amirul-Islam learned Counsel appearing on behalf of appellant of Civil Appeal No.61 of 1997 submits that the Administrative Appellate Tribunal committed gross illegality in passing the aforesaid order. It is submitted that under the Administrative Tribunal-Act the appellate authority has no jurisdiction to pass ush an order and in support of his submission he placed reliance in the case of Quazi Nazrul Islam vs BHBFC reported in 45 DLR (AD) 106 wherein it has been held that the Administrative Tribunal and the Administrative Appellate Tribunal have been established with a limited jurisdiction and limited powers. The Tribunal cannot grant gratuitous relief and if such a relief is granted the same should be construed as relief granted in excess of jurisdiction. The Administrative Tribunal Act has not provided for any such authority to the Tribunal to give Such a relief as has been given to the authority in the present case before us.</u>

13. In view of this we hold that illegality and wrong has been committed in making the aforesaid observation which require interference and accordingly we are inclined to allow the appeal and delete the aforesaid observation.

14. Civil Appeal No. 60 of 1997 is allowed without cost as aforesaid. Judgment and order passed by the Administrative Appellate Tribunal in the aforesaid appeal is hereby set aside and these of the Administrative Tribunal is restored.

15. In Civil Appeal No.61 of 1997 the observation made by the Appellate Tribunal as aforesaid is hereby deleted and the appeal is accordingly disposed of.

No order as to cost.

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 22-7-2001 passed by the High Court Division in First Appeal No. 40 of 1994).
full_judgment:
Mr. Syed J. R. Mudassir Husain, C. J.:- have perused the judgment written by Mr. Arnind Kabir Chowdhury. I and I agree with his findings and decision.

2. Mr. Mohammad Fazlul Karim. J.- I have gone through the judgments in the matter written by my brothers, Amirul Kabir Chowdhury, J and Md. Joynul Abedin, J. In view of the judgment and decree of the Trial Court decreeing the suit on merit and those of the Court of Appeal below allowing the same without considering the facts and circumstances of the case and rejecting the application for amendment and an application under Order 41 Rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure without considering in its real perspective, ends of justice has not been secured by rejecting those applications, Thus, in the facts and circumstances of the case and for reasons aforesaid, ends of justice would best be served, while agreeing with my learned brother. Amirul Kabir Chowdhury 1, to send back. the case on remand for giving opportunity to both the parties upon allowing the applications for amendment of the plaint and under Order 41 Rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure and  permitting both the parties to take necessary steps in the suit for disposal of the sui accordance with law.

<u>3. Mr. Amirul Kabir Chowdhury, J.- This appeal at the instance of the plaintiff arises out of the judgment and order dated 22 July 2001 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division in First Appeal No.40 of 1994 reversing the judgment and decree dated 02.11.1993 passed by the. First Court of the learned Subordinate Judge, Dhaka is Title Suit No.18 of 1985 decreeing the suit declaring the suit property to have been purchased in the benami of the defendant (respondent No.1). The appellant as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No.578 of 1979 in the 4th Court the Subordinate Judge, Dhaka, renumbered as Title Suit No.1283 of 1981 and being transferred to the First Court of the Subordinate Judge, Dhaka again renumbered as Title Suit No.18 of 1984t stating, inter-aria, that the appellant and the respondent No.1 when were reading M.B.B.S Course in Dhaka together, intimacy developed between them and that the respondent was a Hindu window named Kamala Rani wife of late Promode Sunder Roy who died in 1950 in Assam leaving the respondent as his widow and two daughters Bithi Roy and Sathi Roy. The children were staying at Karimganj, Assam in India with their maternal grandparents. After passing the M.B.B.S examination he went to Karachi for obtaining M. Phil degree and was attached to Jinnah Hospital when the respondent used to maintain contact with him through letters. In 1964 the respondent No.1 flew to Karachi and got married with the -appellant. They thereafter returned to Dhaka and the appellant served as Medical Officer in different hospitals including Post Graduate Medicine Research Hospital, Dhaka and also was Medical Officer in 31- different organizations and also was doing private practice. The respondent was then living with the appellant in Dhaka. The appellant was also Professor of Pathology in Dhaka Medical College Hospital and thus he was earning a lot of money. The respondent No.1 also managed a job in the Motijheel Central Government Dispensary as Medical f Officer and that the appellant purchased a t plot of land measuring 5 kathas together with one storied building at Pallabi being Plot No.4, Block 1/A from the Eastern Housing Society Ltd. in benami of his wife, the respondent No.1 at a cost of Tk.54,000/- in August, 1968. He paid part of the consideration money from his own savings and balance Tk.30,000/- was paid by taking loan from the House Building Finance Corporation (HBFC). The appellant thereafter purchased the suit plot in Gulshan Model Town in 1970 from its original 4 allottee. The consideration money was paid from his own fund and with the sale proceeds of his house at Pallabi after repaying the loan of House Building Finance Corporation and at that time also at the influence of the respondent No. 1, and because of bondage of love and affection, for the respondent Not, the appellant purchased the disputed property in Gulshan in benami of his wife, the respondent No.1 by deed of sale dated 16.01.1970. The appellant, thereafter, started construction of a two storied building upon 4 the land in Gulshan.</u>

4. The appellant was awarded scholarship for higher studies in England leading to M.R.C.P. in Pathology and he left for U. K. in the month of September, 1970 after making all arrangement for completing the construction of the house in Gulshan. After completion of the construction the house was let out to the Hoechst Pharmaceuticals Co, Ltd., Dhaka. The respondent No.1 during the liberation period in 1971 left Bangladesh for India and thereafter the appellant took her to U.K. in early 1972 from India and they were residing there at their own house in London together. The eldest daughter of the respondent namely Bithi Roy and her husband were brought to London in 1974 and their settlement was managed in U.K. Later on the second daughter of the respondent No. 1 namely Sathi Roy and her husband were also brought to U.K. by the appellant and he met their matrimonial expenses and made arrangement for their settlement there. There was no issue out of the wedlock between the appellant and the respondent No. 1. It is also the contention of the appellant that the disputed property at Gulshan was purchased by his own money in the benami of the defendant respondent No.1 but because of the attempt of the respondent No. 1 to sell the suit property and because of their strained relationship as husband and wife the suit has been filed.

5. The suit has been contested by the respondent No.1 by filing a written statement contending, inter-alia, that the suit property has been purchased by the money of the Respondent No.1 herself and she denied that it was purchased by the appellant in the benami of the respondent No. 1 at the expenses of the appellant. The respondent contended further that the appellant used to maintain a large paternal family of him with his small income and as such he had no means or money to purchase the disputed property.

6. Further case of the respondent No.1 is that she herself paid consideration money for the disputed property and purchased the same in her own name, for her own interest and it was never purchased by the appellant in benami, in her name and the appellant did not pay the consideration money.

7. The learned Subordinate Judge examined witnesses of the parties, received documents in evidence and decreed the suit.

8. The defendant-respondent preferred First Appeal No.40 of 1994 before the High Court Division. 40. In a transaction where a person purchased the property in the name of another person, the person who pays the Consideration money acquires the property for his own benefit, and the person whose name appears in the deed of transfer, he merely lends his name as a transferee but he acquires no interest in the suit property. The initial presumption in the case of a transfer concluded by a registered deed is in favour of the person whose name appears as the transferee in the deed but this presumption is rebuttable.

<u>41. Normally the disputed question of benami cannot be determined only on consideration of source of consideration money and it also becomes incumbent for the court to fall back upon other surrounding circumstances of the transaction. The essential ingredients of a benami transaction are as to who has paid the consideration money, who is in possession of the suit property, who has the custody of title deeds and also how the property is dealt with in the sense who enjoys the property and collects the rent. The onus of proof of these ingredients lies upon him who claims certain transaction as benami. In other words, the motive of benami transaction as well as the conduct of the parties including their dealings and enjoyment of the property also become factors for consideration.</u>

42. In the case of Musammat Bilas Kunwar Vs. Desraj Ranjit Sing, 42 I.A. 202, apart from adopting the principle as laid down in Gopeekrist Gossain's case, it is held that the source of purchase money is not only an important qualification but this was and is always considered to be the only criterion in the absence of all other relevant circumstances in a case where ownership is keenly disputed. The Privy Council in lmambandi Begum Vs. Kumleshwari Pershad (1886) 13 I.A. 160 held as under: "where there are benami transaction, and the question is who is the real owner, the actual possession or receipt of rents of the suit property is most important". Similarly in the case of Ram Narain Vs. Muhammad Hadi (1898) 26 I.A. 38 the Privy Council laid stresses on the factum of possession of the property and the collection of rents.

43. In order to discharge this onus plaintiff is required to prove his ownership by adducing very strong and formidable evidence particularly with regard to the payment of consideration money from his own fund.

<u>44. The plaintiff in order to- prove his ownership to the suit property examined himself as P.W.1 and also examined P.W.2 and P.W.3 to corroborate his evidence. He did not even call any of his brothers or the family members to prove that it was the plaintiff who purchased the Pallabi house property with his own money. , The claim of purchase of the Pallabi house property by the plaintiff in the benami of his wife, defendant No.1, is a very important and material fact in deciding the issue involved in the suit. The mere assertion of P.W.1 that the plaintiff purchased the Pallabi house property prior to purchasing the suit property at Gulshan without any corroboration by any other evidence as indicated above remains unproved.</u>

If we advert and look into the evidence on record led by both the parties it is found that the construction works of the one-storied house at Gulshan were carried out by, the defendant No.1 and not by the plaintiff. The plaintiff as P.W.I deposed that he left for U.K. in September, 1970. But before his departure he authorized his brother to look after the construction work on the suit property.
