case_source: (From the Judgment and Order dated April 9, 2003 passed by the High Court Division in First Appeal N9. 186 of 1999).
full_judgment:
Md Ruhul Amin J: This appeal, by leave, is by the plaintiff against the judgment and decree dated April 9, 2003 of the High Court Division in First Appeal No.186 of 1999 allowing the same and thereby setting aside the judgment and decree dated January 31, 1999 of the 3rd Court of Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Chittagong in Other Suit No.136 of 1996 decreeing the same.

2. The ordering portion of the judgment of the High Court Division reads as follows:

"In the result this appeal is allowed and the impugned judgment and decree are set aside. The appellant is directed to pay Taka 4,00,000 together with 6% interest thereon from 28-4-93 to the respondent No.1 and the respondent No. 1 is directed to execute and register a sale deed in favour of the appellant and respondent No.2 within 60 days and in default of the appellant in making the payment as directed above this appeal shall stand dismissed. There shall be no order as to costs".

3. The decree passed by the trial Court was to the effect:

"অত্র মোকদ্দমা দোতরফা সূত্রে ১নং বিবাদীর বিরুদ্ধে এবং একতরফা সূত্রে অন্য বিবাদীপক্ষের বিরুদ্ধে বিনা খরচায় শর্ত মতে ডিক্রি প্রদান করা হইল। তৃতীয় অর্থঋণ আদালতের ২৬/৯০ মামলা ২৮-৪-১৯৯৩ইং তারিখের সোলে ডিক্রি বাতিল ও অকার্যকরী বলিয়া ঘোষিত হইল। বাদীপক্ষ আগামী ৩০ দিনের মধ্যে ৫৬,০০,০০০ (ছাপ্পান্ন লক্ষ) টাকা দাখিল প্রদান সাপেক্ষে নালিশী সম্পত্তির খাস দখলের ডিক্রি প্রদান করা হইল। বাদীপক্ষ উক্ত টাকা দাখিলের ৩০ দিনের মধ্যে নালিশী সম্পত্তির দখল বাদী বরাবর প্রদানের নির্দেশ দেওয়া গেল। অন্যথায় বাদীপক্ষ আদালতযোগে আইনানুযায়ী দখল দিতে পারিবেন।”

4. The Other Suit No. 136 of 1996 was filed seeking the relief primarily:

"অতএব প্রার্থনা যে,

(ক) চট্টগ্রাম ৩য় অর্থঋণ সাব জজ আদালতের ১৯৯৩ ইংরেজী ২৬ নং অপর মোকদ্দমার ২৬-৪-১৯৯৩ ইং (সিক) সোলে ডিক্রি বাতিল ও অকার্যকর হইয়া গিয়াছে ঘোষণা পূর্বক তপশীলোক্ত সম্পত্তি বাদীর বরাবরে খাস দখলের ডিক্রি হয়।”

5. It may be mentioned that respondent Nos. 1 and 2 herein filed Other Suit No. 26 of 1990 before the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge; Chittagong and the same was later on re-numbered as Other Suit No. 26 of 1993, of the 3rd Court of Subordinate Judge, Chittagong seeking decree for specific performance of contract for sale of the property described in the schedule attached to the plaint of Other Suit No. 136 of 1996. The said suit i.e, Other Suit No. 26 of 1993, was decreed on compromise.

6. The reliefs sought in Other Suit No. 26 of 1993 were as follows:

"a) Plaintiffs be given a decree for specific performance of the Contract directing the defendant No.1 to execute and admit registration of the deed of sole/Kabala on receipt of the balance consideration of Taka 3,87,588/88 (Taka three lac eighty seven thousand five hundred eighty eight and paisa eighty eight only) by paying transfer fee and obtaining approval as per Memo No. 515/26- 92(H)/30 dated 31-7-1985 of defendant No.2.

b) On failure of the defendant No. 1 to execute the sale deed/kabala within the time specified by the learned Court be pleased to execute and present for registering of the sale deed/kabala on behalf of the defendant No. 1 and in favour of the plaintiffs on taking deposit of the balance consideration money.

c) that the defendant No. 1 be restrained by an order of temporary injunction from creating any fraudulent, forged document till the disposal of the suit.

d) that the cost of the suit be decreed against the contesting defendant.

e) that the plaintiffs be given any other relief or reliefs he is entitled so in law and equity".

7. As against the aforesaid reliefs the suit on compromise was decreed in the following terms:

"(ক) ১নং বিবাদী নালিশী প্লট ও তদস্থিত দালানের ১৭-৬-১৯৮৭ ইংরেজি তারিখের বিক্রয় চুক্তির মূল্যের আন্দর বাদীগণ হইতে মোট ৫৬,০০,০০০ (ছাপ্পান্ন লক্ষ) টাকা বায়না স্বরূপ গ্রহণ করা স্বীকার করেন।

(খ) ৩নং মোকাবিলা বিবাদী দি চিটাগাং কো-অপারেটিভ হাউজিং সোসাইটি লিঃ কর্তৃক ১নং বিবাদীগণের বরাবরে ইস্যুকৃত ৩১-৭-১৯৮৯ ইংরেজী তারিখের স্মারক নং ৫১৩/২৬-বি-২(ক)/৮৯ইং এ উল্লেখিত নালিশী প্লট হস্তান্তর ফি ৩নং মোকাবিলা বিবাদীকে বাদীগণ পরিশোধ করিবেন।

(গ) অত্র সোলেনামা মঞ্জুর হওয়ার ৩০ দিনের মধ্যে ১নং বিবাদী কবলা মূল্যের উপর সরকারকে দেয় ৬% হারে উৎস কর বা গেইন টেক্স নিজে পরিশোধ করিয়া বাদীপক্ষের বরাবরে রেজিস্ট্রি কবলা করিয়া দিবেন।

(ঘ) অত্র সোলেনামা মঞ্জুর হওয়ার ৬০ দিনের মধ্যে যদি ৬% হারে উৎস কর পরিশোধ করিয়া কবলা রেজিস্ট্রি করিয়া দিতে কোন কারণে ব্যর্থ হয় তবে বাদীপক্ষ বিক্রয় মূল্যের আন্দর বাকি ৪,০০,০০০ (চার লক্ষ) টাকা হইতে গেইন টেক্স বা উৎস কর বাদ দিয়া তাহা সরকারকে প্রদান পূর্বক অবশিষ্ট টাকা আদালতে দাখিল করিয়া আদালত যোগে কবলা পাইতে ক্ষমতাবান হইবেন এবং তখন মামলার যাবতীয় খরচ ১নং বিবাদী বহন করিবেন।

(ঙ) ১ নং বিবাদী মামলার সম্পত্তি হস্তান্তরের ব্যাপারে শুধু মাত্র "গ" শর্তে বর্ণিত গেইন টেক্স পরিশোধ করিবে অন্যান্য যাবতীয় খরচ তথা রেজিস্ট্রি খরচ ও তৎ সংশ্লিষ্ট কবলা সম্পাদনের স্ট্যাম্প খরচ ইত্যাদি যাবতীয় খরচ ও ব্যয় বাদীগণ বহন করিবে।

(চ) বাদীগণ অত্র সোলেনামা মঞ্জুর হওয়ার ৪ মাসের মধ্যে নিজে অবশিষ্ট টাকা পাওনা নিষ্পত্তি করিয়া কবলা সম্পাদন করাইয়া নিতে বাধ্য থাকিবেন এবং বিবাদী ও কবলা রেজিস্ট্রি করিয়া দিতে বাধ্য হইবেন। কোন পক্ষ বিনা কারণে উক্ত মেয়াদের অধিক বিলম্ব করিতে পারিবে না।

(ছ) অত্র সোলেনামা ডিক্রির একাংশ হিসাবে গণ্য হইবে।”

8. The ordering portion of the judgment passed in Other Suit No. 26 of 1993 runs as:

"It is ordered that

অত্র মোকদ্দমা সোলেনামায় শর্ত মোতাবেক ডিক্রি হইল এবং সোলেনামা ডিক্রি একাংশ হিসাবে গণ্য হইল।”

9. The plaintiffs of the Other Suit No. 26 of 1993 having had failed to perform their obligation in terms of the compromise decree passed in Other Suit No. 26 of 1993, appellant filed Other Suit No. 136 of 1996 impleading the respondent Nos.1 and 2 herein as the principal defendants seeking the relief as mentioned hereinbefore. It was the case of the plaintiff-appellant that he proposed to sell the property described in the schedule attached to the plaint of Other Suit No. 136 of 1996 and the defendants agreed to purchase the same for Taka 60,00,000 and an agreement was executed on June 17, 1987 and on that date principal defendants i.e. respondent Nos.1 and 2 herein, paid Taka 45,00,000 to the plaintiff and thereupon plaintiff parted with the possession of the land in suit in favour of the principal defendants, that subsequent to the date of contract the defendants paid further amount of Taka 11,00,000 towards the consideration money, that the defendants i.e. respondent Nos. 1 and 2 herein, filed Other Suit No. 26 of 1993 (previously numbered Title Suit No. 26 of 1990) seeking decree for specific performance of contract. The said suit i.e. Other Suit No. 26 of 1993 was decreed on compromise in the light of the terms and conditions set forth in the petition for compromise.

10. The plaintiff filed the Other Suit No. 136 of 1996 averring that in terms of the compromise decree defendants, i.e. respondent Nos.1 and 2, upon paying balance of the consideration money within the stipulated time failed to get the kabala registered and, consequent thereupon, the compromise decree having become infructuous the defendants were not entitled to get the kabala registered. As because of the laches and negligence of the defendants they failed to get the kabala registered within the time specified in the compromise decree and consequent thereupon, contract between the plaintiff and the defendants as having became unenforceable the earnest money paid by the defendants to the plaintiff stood forfeited and, as such, defendants were legally under obligation to deliver the possession of the land described in the schedule attached to the plaint to the plaintiff. It was the contention of the plaintiff that he demanded possession from the defendants but they avoided on different pretexts to deliver possession of the land in suit. Hence the suit.

11. The suit was contested by the defendant No. 1 i.e. respondent No.1, by filing written statement denying the material averments made in the plaint and stating, infer alia, that the plaintiff agreed to sell the land in suit to the defendant Nos.1 and 2 for a consideration of Taka 60,00,000 and upon executing an agreement for sale on June 17, 1987 received Taka 45,00,000 and delivered the possession of the land as well as the structures therein to the defendants, that subsequent to the date of contract the plaintiff received further amount of Taka 11,00,000 from the defendants and thus the plaintiff in total received Taka 56,00,000 but in spite of receiving the said amount plaintiff was reluctant to register the kabala. Thereupon the defendants i.e. respondent Nos. 1 and 2 herein, filed Other Suit No. 26 of 1993 seeking the decree for specific performance of the contract for sale of the land in suit, that the said suit was decreed on compromise, that in terms of the compromise decree as the kabala could not be executed and registered, period of validity mentioned in the solenama for getting the kabala executed and registered was extended with the consent of the plaintiff but later on plaintiff, on different pretexts, delayed the execution and registration of the kabala and in the background of the said fact defendant No. 1 requested the plaintiff to register the kabala and although the plaintiff agreed to execute and register the kabala but finally did not act accordingly, that defendants served legal notice on the plaintiff and in reply thereto plaintiff disclosed about the filing of Other Suit No. 136 of 1996 upon making statements which were not true and that the suit has been filed by the plaintiff only to harass the defendants, that plaintiff is entitled to get Taka 4,00,000 from the defendants and except the said amount plaintiff is not entitled to any other amount and also is not entitled to get back the land.

12. The trial Court decreed the suit on the finding that the suit so framed is maintainable and that there is cause of action for filing the suit, that the defendants were required to obtain kabala on payment of the balance of the consideration amount by August 28, 1993 but they did not do the same that in case of reluctance on the part of the plaintiff to execute and register the kabala the defendants had the remedy as per terms 'gha' of the soleh decree, but in spite of that defendants did not take any step for obtaining kabala from the plaintiff, that as the defendants did not take step for obtaining kabala in terms of the soleh decree and consequently defendants having had defaulted in obtaining the kabala  from the plaintiff the plaintiff cannot be compelled after the expiry of the time i.e. after August 28, 1993, to execute and register the kabala, that after the expiry of the period in which i.e. by August 28, 1993, defendants having had not obtained the kabala from the plaintiff the compromise decree has become unenforceable and as such is liable to be rescind, that the plaintiff' after the expiry of the stipulated time i.e. after August 28, 1993, is not bound by the soleh decree and the defendants are not entitled to obtain kabala from the plaintiff as regard the land in suit, that the soleh decree has become unenforceable after the expiry of 4 months from the date of decree passed in Other Suit No. 26 of 1993 and as the stipulated time expired on August 28, 1993 the decree that was passed in Other Suit No. 26 of 1993 became unenforceable and consequent thereupon, the plaintiff is entitled to the relief sought in the suit i.e, Other Suit No.136 of 1996, that defendants having had not put the decree passed in Other Suit No. 26 of 1993 into execution within 3 years from the date of decree i.e. 28-4-1993, the soleh decree became void and inoperative, that the plaintiff has filed the suit within 12 years from the date on which the soleh decree became unenforceable seeking recovery of khas possession and, as such, plaintiff's suit is not barred by limitation, that plaintiff's prayer for confiscation of the earnest money and for return of the amount, received as rent from the land in suit is not legally well founded and as such the relief so sought cannot be granted, that it will be consonant to justice if plaintiff is directed to return the earnest money to the defendants and thereupon would get the land in suit back in his possession. On the aforesaid findings and decision the trial Court decreed the suit in the manner, as stated hereinbefore.

13. As against the judgment and decree of the trial Court the respondent No.1 went on appeal before the High Court Division in First Appeal No. 186 of 1999.

14. The High Court Division upon allowing the appeal set aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court and thereupon directed the plaintiff- Respondent to execute the kabala in favour of the appellant and respondent No. 2 On receiving Taka 4,00,000/- from the appellant within 60 days and in case of default on' the part of the appellant the appeal shall stand dismissed. It may be mentioned the order of the High Court Division has already been quoted hereinbefore.

15. It was the contention of the defendant-appellant before the High Court Division that the trial Court was in serious error in not holding that the defendant-appellant and the respondent No. 2 were all through willing to perform their part of the contract dated June 17, 1987 and also were all through willing and ready to perform their part required to be performed as per compromise decree dated April 28, 1993 in Title Suit No. 26 of 1993, previously Title Suit No, 26 of 1990, but for sufficient reason and for unavoidable circumstances as stated in the written statement defendant No. 1 could not perform his part of contract, that appellant paid Taka 56,00,000 out of the consideration of Taka 60,00,000/- and the same shows willingness and readiness of the appellant and the respondent No, 2 to perform their part in respect of the contract for sale of the land in suit. It was also the contention of the appellant that because of the provision of section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act he is entitled to continue his possession of the land in suit and the plaintiff-respondent is not entitled to get the possession' back of the land nor can he assert any title in the land other than claiming the balance of the consideration money which is Taka 4,00,000 after deducting the amount to be paid as gain tax. Lastly, it was contended by the appellant that since no consequence was provided in the agreement in case of default on the basis of which plaintiff-respondent delivered possession to the defendant- appellant and, as such, the plaintiff is not entitled to the decree as sought in Other Suit No. 136 of 1996.

16. As against the aforesaid contentions of the appellant it was contended on behalf of the plaintiff respondent that the decree in Other Suit No. 26 of 1993 was passed on 28-4-1993 and thus decree became infructuous and non-enforceable after lapse of 3 years and the suit (Other Suit No, 136 of 1996) having been filed on September 10, 1996 the trial Court rightly found that the decree that was passed on. April 28, 1993 became ineffective in view of Article 182 of the Limitation Act. It was also the contention of the plaintiff-respondent that defendant- appellant is not entitled to get the benefit of the provision of section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act since he failed to satisfy the requirement of the provision of the said section of the Transfer of Property Act that he was willing to perform his part of the contract.

17. As seen from the judgment of the High Court Division that the said Division proceeded on the premise upon taking the agreement dated June 17, 1987 as the basis the defendant-appellant and respondent No.2 on payment of substantial amount of the consideration money got possession of the land in suit and that subsequent to the execution of the agreement for sale paid Taka 11,00,000 and thereupon continuing possession of the land in suit in part performance of the contract dated June 17, 1987 and that defendant-appellant and the respondent No.2 being willing to perform their part of the contract instituted Other Suit No. 26 of 1993/ Other Suit No. 26 of 1990 for the specific performance of the contract that was entered into on June 17, 1987 and for obtaining kabala in respect of the land in suit, The High Court Division was of the view that although Other Suit No. 26 of 1993 ended on compromise on April 28, 1993 but the same was not a new contract "rather by this compromise the respondent has acknowledged the receipt of Taka 56,00,000 from the purchaser and also it contemplates to extension of time for the performance of the contract", that as the defendant did not put the compromise decree into execution and thereupon obtained the kabala from the plaintiff-respondent and thus defendant is on the land not on the basis of compromise decree but on the basis of agreement dated June 17, 1987, that because of the provision of section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act the plaintiff-respondent is not entitled to get back the possession of the land and that defendant is quite entitled to protect his possession under the said provision of law. The High Court Division has observed "...................the plaintiff cannot get back the land already sold to the defendant-appellant and the defendants are entitled to continue in possession provided they are willing to perform their part of the contract".

18. It may be mentioned the plaintiff in support of his case examined one witness and he was cross-examined by the contesting defendant No. 1 (appellant before the High Court Division). The defendant No.1 except filing written statement did not examine any witness.

<u>19. It is seen from the judgment of the High Court Division that the said Division placing reliance on the written statement was of the view that since defendant was in jail and that whereabouts of defendant No.2 were not known and that defendant was all along ready to perform his part and that a legal notice was served upon the plaintiff respondent to do his part and that provision of section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act "willing to perform of the contract" is referable to the agreement dated 'June 17, 1987 since on the basis thereof defendant paid Taka 56,00,000 and continuing possession of the land in suit and that the defendants are not in possession of the land in suit on the basis of compromise decree. The High Court Division while decreeing the suit allowing the appeal and passing decree in favour of defendant has observed that the appellant "performed substantial part of their obligation" and that filing of the suit for specific performance of contract demonstrates willingness of the defendant appellant to perform his part of the contract, that defendant- appellant served a legal notice on the plaintiff-respondent asking him to receive the balance consideration money and to register the document but in the meantime the suit i.e. Other Suit No. 136 of 1996, was filed and because of the aforesaid state of the matter "we find that the appellant is entitled to get the benefit of section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act but since the appellant is seeking protective possession under section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act he cannot get the same unless he pays back the balance money of Taka 4,00,000/- because this is the right of the respondent expressly provided by the terms of agreement".</u>

20. It may be mentioned the High, Court Division itself observed that the compromise decree because of the provision in Article (82 of the Limitation Act has become unenforceable but held "this decree did not create any independent right to the parties rather it is an acknowledgment of the original, contract other than of course the extension of time but there is no novation of contract", The High Court Division held "respondent is liable to execute and register the document in favour of the appellant, the principal defendant No. 1 and the defendant No.2". It may be mentioned that the appellant was taken into custody on September 26, 1993 i.e. at a time when the decree dated April 28, 1993 became unenforceable because of lapse of 4(four) months time from that date and that the aforesaid decree also became unenforceable having not been put into execution within 3 years from the date of decree i.e. 3 years from April 28, 1993. It may also be mentioned that the suit i.e. Other Suit No. 136 of 1996, was filed on September 10, 1996 and the legal notice, on which the High Court Division placed reliance to show willingness of the defendant-appellant to perform his part of the contract was sent on January 29, 1997 and the plaintiff respondent replied to the said legal notice on 4-2-1997.

21. Leave was granted to consider the submissions that the respondent Nos.1 and 2 being defendants in the Other Suit No. 136 of 1996 and having not prayed for a decree of specific performance of contract which legally could not have prayed for in plaintiff's suit, the High Court Division was in error in passing a decree for specific performance of contract in favour of the said defendants, that after passing of the compromise decree dated April 28, 1993 the agreement dated June 17, 1987 between the parties became inoperative and the rights and liabilities of the parties would be governed by and determined, with reference to the compromise decree only the High Court Division committed an error in holding otherwise i.e, that the rights and liabilities of the plaintiff and the defendant Nos.1 and 2 would be governed by the terms and condition as in the agreement dated June 17, 1987, that defendant Nos. 1 and 2 having not paid the balance of the consideration money in terms of the compromise decree the High Court Division was wrong in holding that the said defendants were ready and willing to perform their part of the contract entitling to the benefit of section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act overlooking the position of law that after passing of the compromise decree, the defendant Nos.1 and 2 cannot press in the provision of section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act when ex- facie defendant Nos.1 and 2 defaulted in making payment in terms of compromise decree for long over 3 years.

<u>22. The learned Counsel of the appellant submits that the High Court Division was wrong in passing the decree for specific performance of the contract for sale of the land in suit in the suit filed by the plaintiff, although the defendant Nos.1 and 2 in whose favour the High Court Division has passed the decree for specific performance of contract did not ask for the said kind of relief the High Court Division granted to the defendant Nos.1 and 2. It was also contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court Division upon wrongly placing reliance on the legal notice dated January 29, 1997 arrived at the finding that the defendant Nos.1 and 2 were willing and ready to perform their part of the contract and accordingly, the defendants are entitled to the protection provided in section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act, since legal notice was sent after the institution of the suit on September 10, 1996 i.e. long after the institution of the suit. The learned Counsel continued that after the passing of the compromise decree in Other Suit No. 26 of 1993/ Other Suit No. 26 of 1990 there was no other option for the defendants other than acting as per terms of compromise which they did not perform or in other words did not act as the terms of compromise required to do, as such, there was no occasion for the defendants to take advantage of section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act, since the transferee can retain the possession of the property when he performs his part under the agreement or is willing to perform his part but the said condition i.e. ready to perform or willing to perform his part the transferee. under the contract was required to be performed being absent the defendant Nos. I and 2 are not entitled to the protection of section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act for retaining their possession of the land in suit, that the High Court Division was wrong in proceeding with the premise that the defendants were ready find willing to perform their part although any evidence was not brought on record to establish the said fact. It has also been submitted on behalf of the appellant that in the compromise decree specific provision was made for the defendant to obtain the kabala in respect of the land under suit and that the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 having not done so and that the defendant Nos.1 and 2 having not put the decree passed in Other Suit No. 26 of 1993 into execution within the period of 3 years and consequently, the decree passed in Other Suit No. 26 of 1993 having become barred and that after the passing of the compromise decree rights and liabilities of the parties to the compromise decree as were to be governed by the terms of the said compromise decree and that decree having had become barred and there being no provision in the Limitation Act for reviving a decree that' became barred the High Court Division was wrong in setting aside the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court decreeing the suit of the plaintiff on the view that in spite of the compromise decree parties' rights and liabilities relating to the land in suit would be governed by the agreement dated June 17, 1987 and consequently, defendant Nos.1 and 2 are entitled to the benefit of the provision as in section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act or in other words they have right to protect their possession in the land in suit and the plaintiff is not entitled to claim return of possession of the land in suit to him. It is also the contention of the appellant that there was nothing in the written statement where from it can be gathered that the defendants were ready and willing to perform their part in the light of the compromise decree passed in Other Suit No. 26 of 1993 and that the finding of the High Court Division that the defendants were always ready and willing to perform their part and thus entitled to protect their possession in the land in suit as per provision of section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act is based on no evidence.</u>

23. As against the aforesaid contentions of the appellant, it has been submitted on behalf of the respondent No.1, i.e. defendant No. 1, that appellant having had not performed his part as per term 'ga' of the compromise decree, he is not entitled to the relief sought in the suit.

24. For the appreciation a the aforesaid contention of the respondent No. 1, who was plaintiff in Other Suit No. 26 of 1993, we may refer to the terms 'ga', 'gha' and 'cha' of the compromise decree, On reading the aforesaid terms it is seen that respondent No. 1 could have obtained the document from the appellant through the Court in execution of the compromise decree even if the plaintiff was reluctant to perform his part as in clause 'ga' of the compromise decree, but the defendant for the reason best known to him did no go tor that and allowed the decree that was passed in Other Suit No. 26 of 1993 to become barred by limitation for execution. The aforesaid state of the matter clearly shows that the defendant was not ready and willing to perform his part in the contract that was effected through the compromise decree and that being so he is not entitled to the protection of the section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act by way of retaining the possession of the land in suit.

25. It was also contended by the respondent that plaintiff having had asked for rescission of the contract that was entered into between the appellant and the respondent Nos.1 and 2 on June 17, 1987 within 3 years on the expiry of 4 months as in clause 'cha' of the compromise decree the suit so filed by the plaintiff seeking the relief for recovery of possession was barred by limitation.

26. To appreciate the aforesaid contention of the respondent No.1, we may refer to the relief plaintiff sought in a suit. The plaintiff prayed primarily the following relief:

"অতএব প্রার্থনা যে,

(ক) চট্টগ্রাম ৩য় অর্থঋণ সাব জজ আদালতের ১৯৯৩ ইংরেজির ২৬ নং অপর মোকদ্দমার ২৬-৪-১৯৯৩ ইং (সিক) সোলে ডিক্রি বাতিল ও অকার্যকর হইয়া গিয়াছে ঘোষণা পূর্বক তপশীলোক্ত সম্পত্তি বাদীর বরাবরে খাস দখলের ডিক্রি হয়।”

27. On going through the averments made in the plaint and the relief sought as quoted hereinbefore it is clear that the plaintiff sought for declaration that the sole decree has become void and inoperative and in the background thereof prayed for recovery of possession of the land. In the light of the provision of the Limitation Act it is seen that the relief so sought is quite within the period of limitation or in other words the plaintiff's suit or for that matter the reliefs sought in the suit were not barred by limitation.

28. The learned Counsel for the respondent has submitted that decree passed in a suit for specific performance of contract being both in favour of the plaintiff and the defendant the plaintiff could go to the Court for execution of the decree that was passed on compromise in Other Suit No. 26 of 1993. The contention so made is not a merited one since looking to the terms of the compromise it is seen that if for any reason defendant in the suit wherein the compromise decree was passed was reluctant to execute and register the kabala in that case right was given to the defendant alone i.e. respondent Nos.1 and 2 in the instant appeal to go to the Court for obtaining the kabala, which defendants of the instant suit, i.e. the respondent Nos. 1 and 2 herein, had not done for the reason best known to them. It was also the contention of the respondent that the plaintiff's suit was not maintainable since as per provision of section 35(c) and the last clause of that section of Specific Relief Act he was required to file an application before the Court that passed the decree on compromise for specific performance of the contract. It was also submitted on behalf of the respondent that plaintiff was required to file an application before the Court that passed the decree for specific performance of contract before the expiry of 3 years of the compromise decree, which plaintiff did not do, and that to avoid the bar of the said 3 years plaintiff has filed the suit in the different Court for rescission of the contract dated June 17, 1987 or for that matter contract in the light of the compromise decree dated August 28, 1993.

29. The learned Counsel for the respondent in connection with his submission that the respondent Nos.1 and 2 were ready and willing to perform their part of the contract, has referred to the averments made in the plaint of Other Suit No. 26 of 1993/ Other Suit No. 26 of 1990. Suffice it to say, with the passing of the compromise decree the defendant Nos.1 and 2 in Other Suit No. 136 of 1996, who were plaintiffs in Other Suit No. 26 of 1993, were required to establish their readiness and willingness to perform their part in the light of the compromise decree since with the passing of the compromise decree the agreement for sale which was entered on June 17,1987 was no longer available to the parties thereto. The learned Counsel finally submitted that in the background of the materials on record noticed by the High Court Division contract between the plaintiff and the respondent Nos.1 and 2 cannot be rescinded and that the suit filed seeking rescission of the contract was barred by limitation and that the suit tiled seeking recession of the contract was filed in the wrong Court since as per provision of section 35(c) and the last paragraph of the said section of the Specific Relief Act the plaintiff was required to approach the Court that passed the decree in Other Suit No. 26 of 1993 and the respondent Nos.1 and 2 are entitled to retain the possession of the land in suit as per provision of section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act since they are ready and willing to perform their part of contract as found by the High Court Division. It was also submitted that the High Court Division was quite correct in refusing the relief sought by the plaintiff against the defendant Nos.1 and 2 or, in other words, seeking declaration as to the compromise decree in Title Suit No. 26 of 1993.

30. The learned Counsel of the respondent tried to substantiate his submission as to the correctness of the decree, particularly the part whereby decree for specific performance of contract was passed in favour of the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 by the High Court Division, upon referring to the provision of Order VII, rule 7 of the Code of Civil Procedure but having felt difficulty that no case Was made out in the written statement or no prayer was made from the defendant's side for the relief of the specific performance of contract in their favour abandoned his contention in support of the decree for specific performance of contract in favour of the defendant and submitted that his purpose would be served if the first part of the decree i.e. "appeal is allowed and the impugned judgment and decree are set aside" is maintained. As to the extent of power of the Court to grant relief in the light of the provision of Order VII, rule 7 of the Code of Civil Procedure reference may be made to the case of Smt. Thakamma Mathew vs M. Azamathulla Khan and others reported in AIR 1993 (SC) 1120 wherein it has been held that the power conferred by the said provision of law on the Court does not enable it to override the statutory limitations precluding the Court from granting of the relief. In the instant appeal, the defendant respondent under the compromise decree passed in Other Suit No. 26 of 1993 could go for execution of the decree so passed in the said suit for obtaining the kabala within 3 years from April 28, 1993 but did not do so and thereby decree so obtained by them in Other Suit No. 26 of 1993 having become barred the High Court Division was in serious error in passing the decree for specific performance of contract in the plaintiff's suit in favour of the defendant Nos.1 and 2.

31. It has been submitted by the learned Counsel for the appellant that if the decree passed by the High Court Division in the manner as contended on behalf of the respondent Nos.1 and 2 is maintained then the same will create an anomalous situation in that defendant without obtaining any title because of his laches and negligence will enjoy the property of the plaintiff or in other words defendant will have the premium of his intentional default in the performance of his part under the compromise decree and that having had allowed the compromise decree to become unenforceable they will be allowed to enjoy the property to the deprivation of the plaintiff when the plaintiff was not at fault or stood against, in any respect, as to the enforcement of the decree in Other Suit No. 26 of 1993 by the defendant.

32. In the background of the materials on record it appears to us there is substance in the submission so made.

33. It was the contention of the learned Counsel for the respondent No.1 that suit filed by the plaintiff seeking declaration in respect of the decree passed in Other Suit No. 26 of 1993 because of the provision of section 35 of the Specific Relief Act was not maintainable since in view of the last paragraph of section 35 of the Specific Relief Act plaintiff was required to file the application before the Court that passed the decree i.e. the decree passed in Other Suit No. 26 of 1993 seeking rescission of the decree.

34. The provision of section 35 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877 reads as follows:

"35. When Rescission may be adjudged- Any person interested in a contract in writing may sue to have it rescinded, and such rescission may be adjudged by the Court in any of the following cases, namely,

(a) where the contract is voidable or terminable by the plaintiff

(b) where the contract is unlawful for causes not apparent on its face, and the defendant is more to blame than the plaintiff;

(c) where a decree for specific performance of a contract of sale, or of a contract to take a lease, has been made, and the purchaser or lessee makes default in payment of the purchase-money or other sums which the Court has ordered him to pay.

When the purchaser or lessee is in possession of the subject-matter, and the Court finds that such possession is wrongful, the Court may also order him to pay to the vendor or lessor the rents and profits, if any, received by him as such possessor.

In the same case the Court may, by order in the suit in which the decree has been made and not complied with, rescind the contract, either so far as regards the party in default, or altogether as the justice of the case may require".

35. The learned Counsel for the respondent in support of the contention that for seeking rescission of the decree as the plaintiff did not approach the Court that passed the decree and, as such the suit i.e. Other Suit No. 136 of 1996 is not maintainable has referred to the case of Kanhaiyalal vs Mulla Abdul Hussain (deceased by LRS) and others reported in AIR 1985 (Madhya Pradesh), 24, wherein it has been held "It is settled law that a decree in a suit for specific performance of contract for sale is not a final decree but it is in the nature of a preliminary decree which is clear from the provisions of section 35 itself as the original Court retains control over the matter by having full power to make any just and necessary orders therein including the power to extend the time fixed by the decree. On this analogy it, therefore, follows that if the decree is in the nature of preliminary decree and the Court retains full control over the matter having power to make any just and necessary orders can also pass a decree for rescinding the contract under section 35 of the Specific Relief Act". From the reported decision it is seen that the learned Judges in support of the aforesaid view noticed the decisions in the cases of Kurpal Hemraj and others vs Shamrao Raghunath Raote and others reported in AIR 1923 (Bombay) 211. Tribeni Tewary and others vs Ramratan Nonia and others reported in AIR 1959 (Patna), 460 and the case of Anandilal Poddar vs Gunendra Kumar Roy and another reported in AIR 1966 (Calcutta), 107. In the Bombay case it has been observed "The Court is empowered to make an order in the suit in which a decree has already been made, to rescind the contract, instead of putting the opponent to file another suit for rescission". In the Calcutta case the learned Judges agreeing with the view expressed in the Bombay case observed "that not only does a suit lie for rescission of a contract after a decree for specific performance if the purchaser makes default in payment of any money which the Court has ordered to pay; but the rescission can also be effected by making an application in the suit in which a decree for specific performance has been passed and that such an application lies under section 35(c) of the Specific Relief Act" In the case of Shri Murti Parasnathji through Sarbarakar Singhai Motilal and another vs. Gulabchand s/o Mithulal Jain and others reported in AIR 1943 (Nagpur), 111, the learned Judges expressed the view similar to the Bombay Case. In the case of Narayan Gangadhar Deshpande and others vs Rango Krishna Dixit reported in AIR 1960. Mysore, 175 it has been observed "The true effect of this provision is that the Court, which passed the decree for specific performance, is given power to rescind the contract and consequently set aside the decree which it had passed earlier if the successful plaintiff fails to comply with the terms of the decree".

<u>36. The learned Counsel for the appellant in the background of the aforementioned submissions of the respondent submitted that no where in the reported cases it has been held or observed that a separate suit for rescinding the decree for specific performance of contract for the default of the plaintiff who obtained the said kind of decree is barred because of the provision of section 35 of the Specific Relief Act, rather from the reading of the aforesaid decisions it is seen that person who intends to rescind the contract because of the non-performance of the direction in the decree for specific performance of contract for sale of the land can either approach the Court that passed the decree or can file independent suit for rescinding the contract for sale or for declaring the decree not binding on the party who has approached the Court for avoidance of the decree for non-performance of the part by the plaintiff, who obtained the decree in the suit for specific performance.</u>

37. The learned Counsel for the respondent also referred to the case of Onkar Nath and another vs Basheer and others reported in AIR 1986 Punjab and Haryana, 152. This case is of no help to the respondent No.1 since the same has been decided in the light of the provision of section 28 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963. Section 28 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 has enacted in the modified form sub-section (c) of section 35 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877 (Act No. 1 of 1877) and in the said section 28 there is specific bar for filing separate suit for the relief provided in section 35(c) of the Specific Relief Act.

<u>38. About the maintainability of the suit it has been submitted by the learned Counsel for the appellant that question of rescinding of contract would come when contract for sale remain valid or in other words decree passed in the suit for specific performance of contract for sale of land would remain valid or for that matter has not become unenforceable or non operative or that has not become barred by limitation or only when the contract for sale of land would remain valid or that the decree obtained in the suit for specific performance of contract is enforceable then, and then only provision of section relating to rescission of contract would come. It has been submitted by the learned Counsel for the appellant that with the passing of decree in Title Suit No. 26 of 1993 the contract which was entered between the parties on June 17, 1987 had superseded and that the decree passed in Other Suit No. 26 of 1993 will be the only agreement/instrument relating to the land in suit. It is the contention of the learned Counsel that there is no occasion after the decree passed in Other Suit No. 26 of 1993 to refer or to put reliance on the agreement that was entered between the parties on June 17, 1987. In the background of the relief sought in the Other Suit No. 136 of 1996 as well as in the light of the observation made in the cases referred to hereinbefore, except the case reported in AIR 1986 P and H, we are of the view plaintiff's suit was very much maintainable or in other words was not barred because of the provision of section 35(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1877.</u>

39. It was the contention of the learned Counsel for the respondent that the plaintiff's suit was barred under Article 114 of the Limitation Act. In our opinion, the contention so made is not legally well founded since the plaintiff has sought for a declaration that the decree passed in Other Class Suit No. 26 of 1993 has become void, inoperative and unenforceable and for recovery of khas possession of the land in suit which the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 are possessing on the basis of the decree passed in the aforementioned suit. It may be mentioned plaintiff's suit is governed by the Article 120 as well as by the Article 144 of the Limitation Act. It is seen from the materials on record that the suit has been filed quite within time seeking the relief as mentioned hereinbefore.

<u>40. It is the contention of the plaintiff since the defendants i.e. respondent Nos.1 and 2, had failed to perform their part as contemplated by the provision of section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act plaintiff is entitled to get back the possession of the land which was the subject matter of the agreement for sale dated June 17, 1987 and later on of the decree dated April 28, 1993 in Other Suit No. 26 of 1993 through the decree sought in the suit i.e. in Other Suit No. 136 of 1996. As against that it was the contention of the contesting defendant i.e. respondent No.1, that since the transferees i.e. the respondent Nos.1 and 2, were ready and willing to perform their part of the contract dated June 27, 1987 they are entitled to retain possession since they obtained possession from the transferor on payment of the considerable part of the consideration money. It may be mentioned the High Court Division allowed the appeal taking the view that since the defendants i.e. respondent Nos. 1 and 2 herein, were willing and ready to perform their part as evidenced by filing of Other Suit No. 26 of 1993, previously numbered Other Suit No. 26 of 1990, is entitled to retain possession and also to have a decree for specific performance of contract for sale of the land in suit. The High Court Division, on the aforesaid view, passed the decree in favour of the respondent Nos.1 and 2 directing the plaintiff to execute the document for sale on receiving the amount mentioned in the judgment of the High Court Division.</u>

41. To appreciate the aforesaid contention of the parties the provision of section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act is quoted below:

"53A. Part performance-Where any person contracts to transfer for consideration any immovable property by writing signed by him or on his behalf from which the terms necessary to constitute the transfer can be ascertained with reasonable certainty and the transferee has in part performance of the contract, taken possession of the property or any part thereof, or the transferee, being already in possession, continues in possession in part performance of the contract and has done some act in furtherance of the contract and the transferee has performed or is willing to perform his part of the contract then notwithstanding that the contract, though required to be registered, has not been registered, or, where there is an instrument of transfer, that the transfer has not been completed in the manner prescribed therefor by the law for the time being in force, the transferor or any person claiming under him shall be debarred from enforcing against the transferee and persons claiming under him any right in respect of the property of which the transferee has taken or continued in possession, other than a right expressly provided by the terms of the contract:

Provided that nothing in this section shall affect the right of a transferee for consideration who has no notice of the contract or of the part performance thereof.

<u>42. The learned Counsel for the appellant upon referring to the 3rd paragraph "and the transferee has performed or is willing to perform his part of the contract" of section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act submitted that pursuant to the decree passed in Other Suit No. 26 of 1993 the respondent No.1 or for that matter respondent Nos.1 and 2 having had not taken any step for obtaining any kabala upon putting the decree passed in that suit into execution and finally having had allowed the decree passed in Other Suit No. 26 of 1993 to be barred by limitation and consequently making the said decree unenforceable, the plaintiff is entitled to the relief sought in the suit. It has been submitted by the learned Counsel that a transferee who obtained possession of the land in part performance of the contract for sale of land can only retain possession so long he is willing and ready to perform his part of the contract or has performed his part of the contract. In support of the aforesaid submission the learned Counsel has referred to the case of Mohan Lal (deceased) through his LRs. Kachru and others vs Mira Abdul Gaffar and another reported in AIR 1996 (SC) 910 (same case has been reported in (1996) 1 Supreme Court Cases (639) wherein it has been held "the transferee has performed or is willing to perform his part of the contract, he would be entitled to retain possession and to continue, in possession which he has already received from the transferor so long as he is willing to perform his part of the contract Equally, when the transferee seeks to avail of section 53A to retain possession of the property which he had under the contract, it would also be incumbent upon the transferee to plead and prove his readiness and willingness to perform his part of the contract. He who comes to equity must do equity. The doctrine of readiness and willingness is an emphatic way of expression to establish that the transferee always abides by the terms of the agreement and is willing to perform his part of the contract. Part performance, as statutory right, is conditioned upon the transferee's continuous willingness to perform his part of the contract in terms covenanted thereunder". It may be mentioned the defendant No. 1 contested the suit by filing written statement but did not lead any evidence. In the written statement there is no averment to show that he was willing and ready to perform his part under the compromise decree which was passed in the suit filed by the respondent Nos. 1 and 2 seeking enforcement of the agreement for sale of the land in suit on the basis of agreement dated June 17, 1987. The learned Counsel for the appellant has also referred to the case of Atauddin Khan and another vs Md Hafizullah Bhuiyan and others reported in 1 B.C.R 1981 (AD) 207. The short fact of the reported case is that transferor as plaintiff filed a suit seeking declaration that the agreement between him and the defendant stood cancelled, earnest money stood forfeited and for recovery of possession and for compensation. It may be mentioned defendants pursuant to a contract for sale of land on payment of part of the consideration money took possession of the land agreed to be sold and purchased in part performance of the agreement and stipulation in the agreement was that in case of failure to obtain kabala within the specified time the earnest money would be forfeited and the transferee would restore vacant possession of the land, agreed to be sold, to the transferor. It was the contention of the transferor that transferee failed to pay balance of the consideration money and to obtain the kabala within the specified time and the transferee having had not done so the transferor served notice on the transferee asking him to vacate the land and also informed that the earnest money has been forfeited. The Courts of fact concurrently held that the transferee failed to perform his part. In the afore state of the matter it was held "He must show that he has done his part of the bargain. He was supposed to pay the balance consideration money. It has been concurrently found that he did not do so. Since he has not performed his part of the contract, nothing inhered in him to confer any right under section 53A and the rider clause "other than a right expressly provided by the terms of the contract" comes into play he has not performed his part of the bargain. He cannot, therefore, claim any right under section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act, and in terms of the contract his earnest money stood forfeited and he is obliged to restore possession of vacant land to the plaintiff'.</u>

<u>43. The learned Counsel for the appellant upon referring to clause 'Gha' and 'Cha' of the compromise decree has submitted that in terms of the aforesaid compromise decree defendants i.e. respondent Nos.1 and 2, having had not taken any step in obtaining kabala in respect of the land in suit, the said facts clearly demonstrate that the transferees i.e. respondent Nos.1 and 2, failed to perform their part of the compromise decree i.e. the contract, and consequently the plaintiff is very much entitled to have the decree in suit. Although defendant- appellant contended before the High Court Division that he was and is willing and ready to perform his part but no evidence was led to establish the said contention. As stated hereinbefore the High Court Division while allowing the appeal referred to the matter of defendant's going to jail and to the legal notice served by the defendants. The defendant was taken into custody on September 26, 1993 i.e. after compromise decree passed in Other Suit No. 26 of 1993 became unenforceable and he served the legal notice on January 29, 1997 i.e. after the institution of the Other Suit No. 136 of 1996 on September 10, 1996. In the background of the said fact it is clearly seen that the High Court Division was in serious error in holding that the aforesaid fact of serving notice clearly shows that the respondent No. 1 who contested the suit as defendant No. 1 but did not lead any evidence, was ready and willing to perform his part under the compromise decree dated April 28, 1993. It may be mentioned after the compromise decree dated April 28, 1993, there was no occasion to refer to the agreement for sale dated June 17, 1987 for any purpose or in respect of anything relating to the land seeking return back of possession in Other Suit No. 136 of 1996 was filed.</u>

44. The learned Counsel for the respondent in support of his submission that provision of section 53A clearly provides that when the transferee is ready and willing to perform his part the transferor cannot make demand from the transferee to return the land possession whereof was taken by the transferee in part performance of the contract and in support thereof has referred to the case of Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Works and others vs Kazi Ashrafuddin Ahmed reported in 55 DLR (AD) 16. The facts of the case is that the owner of the property in question entered into an agreement for sale of the said property on April 21, 1968 and upon executing an agreement for sale received part of the consideration money, that on the basis of the agreement the transferee went into possession of the land, that while the document of transfer was yet to be executed and registered the property was declared abandoned and the abandoned property authority served notice on the transferee. The transferee submitted his paper in support of his claim of the property in question, but that was not accepted by the abandoned property authority. It may be mentioned the property in question was not listed as abandoned property. It is pertinent to mention that the agreement for sale being of April 21, 1968 it was held by this Division that the same was binding on the Government in the same way as upon the original owner but the same may be cancelled, amended or terminated by the Government if the Government chooses to do so and that the abandoned property authority could ask for surrendering possession under the provision of President's Order No. 16 of 1972, In the reported case the contract was not terminated. In the background thereof it was held "The respondent admittedly is in possession of the property on the basis of agreement for sale dated 21-4-1968 and has the protection of the provision of section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act alleging that the abandoned property authority could not disturb his possession asking to surrender it as he has been claiming the possession legally duly protected by the provision of section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act". In the background of the facts of the instant case the case so referred to by the learned Counsel for the respondent has no relevancy. The learned Counsel has also referred to the case of Mir Abdul Ali vs Md Rafiqul Islam reported in 40 DLR (AD) 75. The fact of the case is that plaintiff filed a suit for declaration of his title to the land in suit and by subsequent amendment he prayed for permanent injunction. The suit was dismissed by the trial Court since plaintiff had not the possession of the land in suit. It was established from the defendant's side that he entered into an agreement to purchase the land in suit and he got the delivery of possession of the suit land upon the execution of the agreement for sale. In the background of the said fact it was held "The equitable principle as given in section 53A can be invoked by the defendant for protecting his possession..................". In the background of the fact of the present case the decision so referred to appears to us of no help to the respondent. The learned Counsel has also referred to the case of Progati Industries Ltd vs Shahida Khatun and others reported in 43 DLR 429. The plaintiff filed the suit seeking declaration of title and recovery of possession of the property measuring 1.50 acres of land with buildings and structures thereon. The suit ended in compromise but the plaintiff failed to comply with the terms of the compromise and at one stage the plaintiff entered into a contract for sale with the third party but ultimately failed and the defendant took possession of the property. The defendant tried to protect its possession upon resorting to the provision of section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act. In the background of the facts of the aforementioned case it was held "that when a transferor has delivered possession of his property to the transferee in part performance of a written contract neither the transferor nor anyone claiming under him will be permitted to assert his title to the said property or to recover possession of the same from the transferee or anyone claiming under him so long the transferee or person claiming under him has done some act in furtherance of the contract and has performed or is ready and willing to perform his part of the contract". We have already observed that no material was brought on record from contesting defendant's side to establish or to show that he was ready and willing to perform his part of the contract that came into existence on the disposal of the Other Suit No. 26 of 1993 upon compromise. It was observed by the High Court Division that on the basis of the contract dated June 17, 1987 the defendant is entitled to protect his possession since the decree passed in Other Suit No. 26 of 1993 "did not create any independent right to the parties, rather it is an acknowledgment of the original contract other than of course the extension of time but there is no novation of contract". The High Court Division in our view was in serious error in holding that the decree passed in Other Suit No. 26 of 1993 did not create "any independent right" in favour of the parties since' the terms of the compromise decree clearly show that under the said decree the defendant in case of delay on the part of the plaintiff was quite competent to obtain the kabala through Court, but for the reason best known to the defendant he did not do the same, rather he allowed the decree passed on compromise in Other Suit No. 26 of 1993 to be barred by time and consequently, making the decree unenforceable. This fact alone clearly shows that the defendant was not ready and willing to perform his part under the contract and in that state of the matter certainly defendant is not entitled to have the protection of section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act. It has been submitted by the learned Counsel for the Respondent upon referring to the case of Quazi Din Mohammad vs Alhaj Arzan Ali and another reported in 47 DLR (AD) 48 that very filing of the Other Suit No. 26 of 1990 (subsequently numbered Other Suit No. 26 of 1993), shows that the plaintiff who is now defendant in Other Suit No. 136 of 1996 was ready and willing to perform his part of the contract. We have already held that defendant having had not gone for obtaining the kabala in respect of the land in suit on the basis of the compromise decree passed in Other Suit No. 26 of 1993 and that having had allowed the decree to be barred by limitation and unenforceable and consequently, it being clear that he failed to show his readiness and willingness to perform his part of the contract, he is not entitled to have the protection of section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act and is bound to restore possession of the land in suit to the plaintiff. The submission that filing of Other Suit No. 26 of 1993 demonstrated ready and willingness of the transferee (in Other Suit No. 136 of 1996 defendant) is of no merit since there is nothing on record to show that after the compromise decree the decree holder was ready and willing to perform his part under the decree rather plaintiff has sufficiently established his right to have the relief sought in the suit.

45. In the background of the materials on record, it is seen that the plaintiff did not create any hindrance or obstruction preventing the defendant from having the kabala in respect of the land in suit in pursuant to the terms of compromise decree as mentioned hereinbefore and thereupon plaintiff filed the suit to get back the possession.

46. In the light of the discussions made hereinabove we find merit in the appeal.

47. Accordingly, the appeal is allowed with costs.

End.
