full_judgment:
SK Sinha J : These appeals, by leave, arise out of the same judgment and accordingly these appeals are disposed of analogously by this judgment. Points involved in these appeals are whether, an acquisition proceedings would abate under section 12 of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinances, 1982 (the Ordinance) if the requiring body failed to deposit the compensation money within the stipulated period of one year from the date of decision of the acquiring authority, or from the date of award of compensation and secondly, a previous decision based on different cause of action and also on a provision of law which is not applicable will be barred by their principle of res judicata in a subsequent writ petition on the same subject matter. It would be profitable if we narrate the facts out of which these appeals arise.

2. Respondent No.1, Rabitat Al-Alam-al-Islami, (Rabitat) filed Writ Petition No. 2746 of 2001 challenging the Gazette Notification dated 17th May, 2001, by which, the writ respondent No 3 cancelled the proceedings of LA Case No. 1/89-90. The case of Rabitat, in short, is that it is a Non- Government International Islamic Organization providing assistance in the fields of education, culture, social welfare, health care etc. In 1989 it applied to the Government to arrange them 1(one) acre of land in exchange of money at Gazipur, for the purpose of establishment of it's building complex and the writ respondent No.2, the Deputy Commissioner, after fulfillment of the requirements approved the proposal and started LA Case No. 1/89-90. After receiving the notice under section 3 of the Ordinance, 6(six) objections were raised by the owners of the property within the stipulated time as per section 4(1) and the said 6(six) objections were heard by the Land Acquisition Officer on 9th July, 1990. The writ respondent No.2 approved the proposed acquisition on 17th July, 1990. Writ Respondent No.2 request- ed the Secretary, Ministry of Land to approve the proposed acquisition on 20th July 1990. The writ respondent No.2 finally approved the said acquisition on 18th August, 1990. On 28th August, 1990 the Land Acquisition Officer published a notice under section 6(1) of the Ordinance asking the affected persons to produce their claims of compensation and on 7th April, 199 L the writ respondent No. 2 estimated the price of disputed land at Taka 17,03,625.45, and on 21st April, 1991 the acquiring authority asked Rabitat to deposit the said compensation money with in 18th August, 1991, as per section 12(1) of the Ordinance. Rabitat by a letter dated 24th July, 1991 requested the writ respondent No.2 to extend the time up to 31st December, 1991 for depositing the said compensation money. Against the said letter the writ respondent No. 3 intimated that there was no scope to extend the time under the said Ordinance. Thereafter Rabitat deposited Taka 1,00,000 (Taka one lakh) on 18th August, 1991. The Land Acquisition Officer by a letter dated 7th October, 1991 requested Rabitat to pay the balance compensation money.

3. Thereafter on 23rd December, 1991 the award of compensation was prepared and the writ respondent No.3 issued notice under section 7(3) of the Ordinance, which was served upon the affected persons to receive their award of compensation. After delivery of possession writ respondent No.5 Dr Malik Mehdi Kabir and 2 others filed Writ Petition Nos. 462, 529 and 2639 of 1992 respectively, challenging the acquisition proceedings. All the said three Petitions were heard analogously and the Rules were discharged, by judgment and order dated 8th March, 1998. Against the said judgment and order the writ respondent No.7 preferred Civil Petition No. 829 of 1998 and the same was dismissed by this Division by judgment and order dated 19th August, 1999. The writ respondent No.3 thereupon cancelled the LA Case No. 1 of 1989-90, which was published in the Gazette Notification on 17th May, 2001. After publication of the said Gazette Notification, the writ respondent No.3 directed Rabitat on 12th June, 2001, to return the land to the owners.

4. Writ respondent Nos. 1, 5, 8, 9, 16, and 17 contested the writ petition by filing separate affidavit-in-opposition denying the material allegations made in the petition and claimed that the impugned Notification was passed legally as Rabitat failed to deposit the compensation money within the stipulated time in accordance with law and therefore the proceedings stood abated. The High Court Division upon hearing the parties and by the impugned judgment made the rule absolute but it did not declare the impugned Gazette Notification, Annexure-S to the writ petition, canceling the acquisition of the disputed property in LA Case No. 1 of 1989-90 without lawful authority and also did not give direction upon the Deputy Commissioner to declare the acquisition of the property in the official Gazette under section 11 of the Ordinance as prayed. Therefore, the cancellation of the acquisition proceedings by the impugned Gazette Notification stands despite making the rule absolute.

5. The High Court Division though made some superficial observations regarding the writ petitioner's failure to deposit the compensation money in accordance with law but made the rule absolute mainly on the reasoning that in view of the earlier judgment of the High Court Division passed in writ petition Nos.462, 529 and 2639 of 1992 and affirmed by this Division in civil petition No. 829 of 1998, the claim of the writ respondents is barred by the "general principle of res judicata." The High Court Division failed to notice that though writ respondent Nos. 5, 6 and 7 instituted the earlier writ petitions but the writ respondent Nos. 8, 9, 16 and 17 who are appellants in CA No.60 of 2006 are not parties in the said petitions.

6. When the earlier writ petitions were filed, the acquiring authority did not record order for abatement of the proceedings. On the point of abatement of the proceedings the High Court Division in the earlier Judgment observed the Deputy Commissioner as per provision of section 5 of the Ordinance made decision as regards acquisition on 18th August, 1990 vide Annexure B to the affidavit-in-opposition of respondent No.5. Award under section 7 for payment of compensation to the petitioners was made by the Deputy Commissioner on 8th April, 1991 and thereafter the requiring body deposited the entire amount of award on 23rd December, 1991. So it is seen that com pensation that to be 'paid' to the petitioners or to be 'deposited' in case of petitioners not accepting the same, in the public account as per provision of section 10 of the Ordinance was available with requiring body well within the period of one year as referred in section 12 of the Ordinance. This being the position of the view that contention of the petitioners that the requiring body did not deposit the amount awarded as compensation for payment to the petitioners within the period as referred to in section 12 of the Ordinance and consequent thereupon LA Case No.1 of 1989-90 started for acquiring petitioners' land stood abated is not well founded."

<u>7. So, the decision of the High Court Division is based on the fact that the award for compensation was made on 8th April, 1991 and as the compensation money having been deposited by Rabitat on 12th December, 1991 within one year from the date of award for compensation, the deposit was made in time, the proceedings not abated. This finding is based on misconception of law, inasmuch as, the High Court Division made the above observation on the basis of the substituted section 12 of the Ordinance, which provision would not be applicable in the said writ petitions. The Deputy Commissioner after hearing objection approved the proposal of the Land Acquisition Officer under section 5 of the Ordinance by order dated 17th July, 1990. The earlier writ petitions were filed in 1992. In the premises, it is the unamended provisions of section 12- would hold the field but the High Court Division wrongly considered the amended provision. Section 12 as stood on the date of acquisition reads as follows:</u>

<u>"12. Abatement or Revocation of Acquisition Proceedings--(1) Notwithstanding anything contained in this Ordinance, where in any case compensation has not been paid or deposited within a period of one year from the date of decision of the Government. [the Divisional Commissioner or the Deputy Commissioner, as the case may be, for acquisition of the property under section 5 or the proviso to section 4(3)(b), as the case may be], for no fault of the person interested, all proceedings in respect of such acquisition shall, on the expiry of that period, stand abated and a declaration by the Deputy Commissioner to that effect shall be published in the official Gazette."</u>

8. This section has been substituted by Act XX of 1994 which reads as under:

"12. Abatement or revocation of acquisition proceeding-Notwithstanding anything contained in this Ordinance, where in any case the estimated amount of the award of compensation has not been deposited by the requiring person for acquisition of any property under section 5 within the period specified in section 7(4), all proceedings in respect of such acquisition shall, on the expiry of that period, stand abated and a declaration by the Deputy Commissioner to that effect shall be published in the Official Gazette."

<u>9. There are substantial differences between these two provisions. The difference is that under the old provision the compensation has to be deposited within one year from the date of decision of the acquiring authority under section 5, whereas, under the new provision the compensation has to be deposited within one year from the date of making estimated amount of the award of compensation under section 7(4). Naturally the period of limitation to deposit the compensation would reckon from the date of the final decision regarding acquisition under the earlier provision, whereas, under the amended provision, the period would be counted from the date of award of compensation. Therefore, there is apparent error in the earlier judgment on the point of limitation to deposit the compensation which has resulted in the decision that the deposit has been made within a period of one year. The High Court Division was totally confused as to the applicability of the law during the relevant time and this might be due to the fact that when the writ petitions were disposed of on 8th March, 1998 the substituted provision of section 12 was in force. If this change of law was brought to the notice of the High Court Division, the decision would have been otherwise. While affirming the judgment this Division through looked at the change of law but dismissed the leave petition relying upon the views taken in Ministry of Land Administration vs Subash Chandra Das, 46 DLR (AD) 63 on the reasoning that "it is not the case of the petitioner (writ respondent No.7) that he was not paid compensation or that his compensation money was not deposited within one year from the date of decision to acquire under section 5 or proviso the section 4(3)(b) of the Ordinance".</u>

<u>Therefore, the earlier decision of this Division was based on a completely different point although the exposition of law as regards the deposit of compensation within one year from the date of decision to acquire under section 5 was correct but did not express any opinion in that regard.</u>

10. In the impugned judgment, the High Court Division has failed to appreciate the reasons on which Writ Petition Nos.462, 529 and 2639 of 1992, and Civil Petition No. 829 of 1998 have been dismissed. In the impugned judgment the High Court Division observed the grounds of violation of sections 15 and 12 were agitated in the earlier writ petitions and rejected by the High Court Division and this Judgment was approved by the Appellate Division in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.829 of 1998 mentioned above. The Appellate Division concluded the judgment be saying it is not the case of the petitioner that he was not paid compensation or that this compensation money was not deposited within one year from the date of decision to acquire under section 5 or the proviso to section 4(3 ) (b) of the Ordinance. As such he has no business to enquire when the requiring body paid the amount of compensation to the government." There is no gainsaying the fact that the High Court Division based its decision relying upon the earlier judgments without applying its judicial mind to the issue and law point decided in the earlier writ petitions.

11. Admittedly Rabitat did not deposit the compensation money in accordance with section 12(1) of the Ordinance is apparent from its statement in paragraph 3 of the concise statement wherein it is stated that "on 18th August, 1990, the Deputy Commissioner approved the acquisition" and "on 18th August, 1991, the respondent herein initially deposited Taka 1,00,000 (taka one lakh) by bank draft. Thereafter on 8th October, 1991 the LA Officer asked the respondent immediately to pay the rest of the money, i.e. Taka 16,03,647.45 (Taka sixteen lakh three thousand six hundred seventy four and fifty paisa) in favour of Deputy Commissioner, which the respondent paid by bank draft on 21st December, 1991," So, Rabitat admitted that the final decision regarding acquisition was made on 18th August, 1990 and as per section 12 Rabitat was required to deposit compensation within one year from the date of final decision regarding acquisition. This is the requirement of law and the Court has no power to hold otherwise.

12. In Subash Chandra Das, MH Rahman, J argued:

"The provision of section 12 will come into play only when the compensation is not paid to the persons interested or not kept in a deposit account of the Public Account of the Republic under sub-section (1) of section 10. Under section 12 no obligation as such is placed on the requiring body to deposit compensation money within six months from the date of decision of acquisition."

13. While endorsing the above views Mustafa Kamal J added as under:

"Under section 15, when any property is proposed to be acquired for any person other than the Government, such person shall enter into an agreement with the government in a prescribed form before a notice under section 3 is published. The Deputy Commissioner has to tender and pay compensation to "the persons interested", before taking possession, to be assessed in terms of sections 8 and 9. The payment of compensation is regulated by section 10. It is either "paid" in terms of section 10(1) or "deposited" in terms of section 10(2). It is this "payment" and "deposited" in section 10 which is attracted in section 12, not the deposit of compensation by the requiring body. Reading all the sections together, sections 8, 9, 10, 12 and 15, it is clear that abatement will take place if the acquiring authority fails to "pay" or "deposit" compensation in terms of section 10 within one year from the date of decision of the Government (which in section 5 in the case of acquisition)

14. In Subash Chandra Das two views have been expressed as regards the date of deposit of compensation by the requiring body. MH Rahman, J was of the opinion that no obligation is placed on the requiring body to deposit compensation within one year from the date of decision for acquisition where as, Mustafa Kamal, J, on the other hand, was of the opinion that the requiring body will deposit the compensation well ahead of expiry of one year from the date of final decision for acquisition. Let us now examine the correct position of law. Section 15(1) of the Ordinance provides that "when any property is proposed to be acquired for any person other than the Government, such person shall enter into an agreement with the Government in such form as may be prescribed before a notice under section 3 of the Ordinance is published."

15. The purpose for entering into such agreement is to initiate the process of acquisition so that the person on whose favour the land will be acquired gets possession from the Government on payment of compensation. The obligation of the requiring body under the agreement is to deposit compensation money within the time specified therein and the obligation of the acquiring authority is to acquire the land after performance of formalities and then to handover possession to the requiring body. If the latter does not deposit the compensation money within the specified time, the acquiring authority will not be able to pay the compensation to the affected person under section 10 and if the compensation is not paid, the Deputy Commissioner has no power to take possession from the affected person. The payment of compensation is a precondition for taking over possession of the land. Thus there is no scope on the part of the acquiring authority to complete the process of acquisition as per provisions of the Ordinance unless the requiring body deposits the compensation money as per agreement. It is only on payment of the compensation to the affected person the land or property "shall stand acquired and vest absolutely in the Government free from all encumbrances" under section 11 of the Ordinance. The High Court Division did not express any independent opinion on the point of violation of sections 12 and 15 on simple reasons that this Division has settled the point in Subash Chandra Das and in Civil Petition No. 829 of 1998.

<u>16. Section 5 of the Ordinance relates to the final decision regarding acquisition of land by the acquiring authority i.e. the Government or the Divisional Commissioner. The proviso to section 4(3)(b) authorizes the Deputy Commissioner to make decision about the acquisition of the property instead of submitting the records of the proceedings to the Divisional Commission if no objection is raised by any interested person in the property. It is admitted by the writ petitioner in its concise statement that six objections have been filed from persons interested in the property. Therefore, the Deputy Commissioner had no authority to give final decision regarding the acquisition under the proviso to sub-section (3) of section 4. In view of this admitted position of the case, the final decision regarding acquisition made by the Deputy Commissioner was also without jurisdiction.</u>

<u>17. Section 15 is a mandatory provision of law to be complied with by the requiring body before the acquiring authority proceeds for acquisition of the land if such acquisition is made not for public purposes of the Government but the question is when the compensation in to be deposited by the requiring body? As noticed above, there are conflicting opinions in Subash Chandra Das on this point. "The requiring body, therefore, will deposit the consideration money with the Government well ahead of expiry of one year from the date of decision of the Government, but within what date, is subject matter of agreement between the Government and the requiring body under section 15" argued by Mustafa Kamal, J. We would like to add that while fixing the date in the agreement it should be kept in mind sections 5, 10, 11 and 12, because if the requiring body does not deposit the compensation within a period of one year from the date of decision for acquisition, the proceedings shall stand abated. Secondly, how the Deputy Commissioner will take possession from the affected person unless the requiring body pays compensation? The possession will be delivered if it pays the compensation in time.</u>

18. In view of the above, with due respect, we find ourselves unable to agree with the understanding of section 12 in Sub ash Chandra Das on the points as to whether there is obligation on the part of the requiring body to deposit the compensation, and whether on the .failure on the part of the requiring body to deposit the compensation within one year from the date of decision for acquisition, the proceedings of the acquisition shall stand abated. MH Rahman, J. argues that no obligation is placed on the requiring body to deposit the compensation money within one year (inadvertently mentioned within six months) from the date of decision of acquisition, while Mustafa Kamal, J. is of the opinion that the abatement will take place if the acquiring authority fails to payor deposit compensation in terms of section 10 within one year from the date of the decision of the Government. We find inconsistency in the above arguments. There is no ambiguity on a plain reading of section 12 that the obligation to pay or deposit the compensation within the specified date is upon the requiring body because if it defaults in complying with such obligation, the acquisition proceedings for the acquisition of the property which was started in its favour, shall stand abated. The Government is under no obligation to pay the compensation money to the affected person.

<u>19. Section 12 is a non-obstante clause which contains the expression 'Notwithstanding anything contained in this Ordinance. The provision containing such clause prevails despite anything to the contrary in the Ordinance is contained. When the non-obstante clause refers to the provision of a statute the intention of the legislature must be determined and the clause has to be construed accordingly. It is often used by way of abundant caution, but mainly used as a legislative device, in case of conflict, to give the provision containing non-obstante clause an overriding effect over any other provision. Therefore, there is no doubt that this provision will prevail other over provisions of the Ordinance. This section should not be read 'subject to' other provisions in the Ordinance. The arguments that no obligation is placed on the requiring body to deposit the compensation money within one year from the date of acquisition and that abatement will take place if the acquiring authority fails to pay or deposit the compensation in terms of section 10 are contrary to the mandate of law for, it is the obligation of the person for whose interest the land is acquired to deposit the compensation within time in order to avoid abatement.</u>

20. In New  Ideal Engineering Works Ltd vs Bangladesh Shilpa Bank, 42 DLR (AD) 221, ATM Afzal, J argued "it is to be observed that a non-obstante clause is usually used in a provision to indicate that, that provision should prevail despite anything to the contrary in the provision mentioned in such non-obstante clause". In Chandavarkar Sita Ratna Rao vs Ashalata S Guram, Air 1987 SC 117 Sabyasahi Mukhcrji, J argued for the Supreme Court as under:

"A clause beginning with the expression "notwithstanding anything contained in this Act or in some particular provision in the Act or in some particular Act or in any law for the time being in force, or in any contract" is more often than not appended to a section in the beginning with a view to give the enacting part of the section in case of conflict and overriding effect over the provision of the Act or the contract mentioned in the non-obstante cause. It is equivalent to saying that inspite of the provisions of the Act or any other Act mentioned in the obstante clause or any contract or document mentioned the enactment following it will have its full operation or that the provisions embraced in the non-obstante clause would not be an impediment for an operation of the enactment. "

21. Similar views have been expressed in South India Corpn. (P) Ltd. vs Secretary. Board of Revenue, Trivandrum, AIR 1964 SC 207 at page 215: (1964) 4 SCR 280. "In Narcotics Control Bureau vs Kishan Lal, AIR 1991 SC 558 it is observed "the non-obstante clause must be given its due importance".

22. The object of the Ordinance is to empower the acquiring authority to acquire land only for a public purpose affecting proprietary right of citizens. Article 42 (1) of the Constitution states subject to any restrictions imposed by law, every citizen shall have the right to acquire, hold, transfer or otherwise dispose of property, and no property shall be compulsorily acquired, nationalized or requisitioned save by authority of law." The underlying idea of this provision is that a citizen shall not be deprived of his land otherwise than in accordance with law and if he is deprived of for public purpose, compensation at the market rate is given to him. No beneficial object of the acquisition can exonerate the government from the restrictions imposed by law and payment of compensation at the market rate. The Ordinance is required to be expounded liberally in favour of the citizen whose land acquired and strictly against the Government. When statutory rights of an exceptional character have been created the conditions prescribed by the statute for exercise of such rights should be strictly fulfilled.

23. The general principle of construction that the object of the legislature has to be kept in view and a construction in conformity with the object has to be placed on the words used. It is contrary to all rules of construction to read words into the Ordinance unless it is absolutely necessary to do so. A statute is to be expounded according to intent of them that make it and that must be gathered from the words actually used in it. This rule of strict construction now requires that where equivocal words leave a reasonable doubt as to meaning which the canons of interpretation fail to solve. the benefit of doubt be given to the affected person.

24. On consideration of the relevant provisions our conclusion is that where the compensation has not been paid or deposited by the requiring body within a period of one year from the date of final decision of the acquiring authority for acquisition of the property under section 5 or the proviso to section 4 (3) (b), the proceedings in respect of such acquisition shall, on the expiry of one year shall stand abated. Similar views have been taken by this Division in the review petition filed by Subash Chandra Das (50 DLR (AD) 106) against the earlier judgment reported in 46 DLR (AD) 63. This Division while disposing of the review petition accepted the contention of the learned counsel for the review petitioner observing that "as far as the exposition of section 12 is concerned, we entirely agree with Mr Pal that an acquisition proceeding shall stand abated if compensation has not been paid or deposited within 6 months (now one year) from the date of the decision of the authority concerned for acquisition of the property notwithstanding anything contained in the Ordinance", Therefore, there is no dispute that the requiring body was bound to deposit the compensation money within one year from date of the decision for acquisition. In this case the Deputy Commissioner approved the acquisition on 18th August, 1990, and as per provisions of law, Rabitat was required to deposit the compensation money within one year from that date but it failed to deposit the money within the statutory period and thus the proceedings stood abated on 17th August, 1991 by operation of law.

25. Section 12 states that in case of default on the part of the requiring body to deposit the compensation within the period mentioned therein the proceedings in respect of such acquisition shall 'stand abated'. A self executory expression has been used in the section for non-compliance of the obligation to deposit the compensation. The Deputy Commissioner in such case has no power to extend the time other than to publish in the Official Gazette the result of abatement of the proceedings. In other words, the acquisition proceedings will be put to an end and the Deputy Commissioner has no power to pass any order extending the time other than publishing the abatement order in the Official Gazette as soon as the period of one year expired. The Deputy Commissioner becomes functus Officio with regard to the said proceedings after the expiry of one year. He retains no power in the said proceedings. The intention of the legislature is clear that the abatement order will operate automatically without any further order of the Deputy Commissioner concerned.

26. In Shah Wali vs Golam Din, 19 DLR (SC) 143, the question arose as to the jurisdiction of the Court to extend the time in respect of self executory order passed by it. H Rahman, J argued:

"in the context of section 148 of the Code of Civil Procedure for extension of time where the time limit has been fixed by any order of the Court to perform certain act by the party. It is argued in the present case, the decree of the trial Court used the words that in the event that default the suit "will be dismissed". These are not words of automatic operation, for, they contemplate a further order dismissing the suit. But the District Judge in the appellate decree made good this defect by stating in the event of default the suits "will be treated as dismissed".

These words were capable, in my view of operating automatically without any further order by Court. In a statute or order where the expression 'stand dismissed' "is used, it indicates that the default clause was to operate automatically without any further order from the authority of the Court."

27. Therefore, as soon as one year period expired from the date of final decision regarding acquisition if the requiring body fails to deposit compensation money the acquisition proceedings will automatically terminate. There is natural death of the acquisition proceedings and after its natural death there is no scope to revive this proceedings. In view of the above, we find no merit in the contention of Mr Abdur Razzaq that this Division having approved the views of the High Court Division, the proceedings have not been abated and that there is no scope to reopen the issue of abatement. The High Court Division, in the premises, committed the same error in holding that this point could not be reopened since it had been decided in the earlier cases.

28. As regards the point of res judicata, Mr Mahrnudul Islam contends that the findings of the High Court Division that the appellants in Civil Appeal No. 60 of 2006, who were not parties in the earlier writ petitions were also bound by the earlier decision, is based on misconception of law. Mr Islam argued that the earlier writ petitions were dismissed on the reasonings that it was not the case of the writ petitioners that they were not paid compensation or that the compensation money was not deposited within the statutory period but in this case, the point in issue is that the compensation money had not been deposited or paid within one year from the date of final decision regarding acquisition and thus, this point had not been heard and finally decided. We find substance in the contention of Mr Islam for, the question raised by these appellants was not considered by this Division in Civil Petition No. 829 of 1998 and the High Court Division in the earlier writ petitions.

29. What is more, in the said petitions the relevant provision of law which was applicable to them was not considered and decided. Before a plea can be held to be barred by the principles of res judicata, it must be shown that the plea had not only been raised but it had been heard and finally decided by the Court. It is further necessary that it must have been in issue directly and substantially. When the plea of res judicata is founded on general principles of law all that is necessary to establish is that the previous adjudication must have been between the same parties and that it must have also been with respect to the same point. What we found is that the earlier writ petitions were decided on the basis of the amended provision of section 12, although the said provision was not applicable in the cases. The High Court Division though noticed that the present writ petition was filed on different cause of action, even then, it had held that the previous decision on the point would be hit by the doctrine of res judicata, relying upon the case of Aditya Kumar Singh vs RM College, AIR 1971 SC J005 which was not applicable in the case. The High Court Division failed to notice that the expression 'any matter' used in section II of the Code of Civil Procedure means matter arising out of the same causes of action.

30. In that case the writ petition was filed by a student of a medical college against order of principal striking off his name from college roll because he had not passed physics paper of B.Sc. Part-1 Examination. The petition impleading only principal and the state government was allowed on the ground of violation of the principles of natural justice. In the subsequent writ petition by the same student against order of the Registrar of University not allowing that student to appear in the 1st MBBS examination, the question arose whether the university was bound by the decision in previous writ petition. It was held that the principle of res judicata shall not apply. ID Dua, J. speaking for the Court argued :

"Besides, the question directly raised in the previous case was confined to the grievance relating to violation of the principle of natural justice as the appellant had not been given adequate opportunity of placing his case before the authorities. He was accordingly held entitled to an opportunity to show cause against the action sought to be taken against him so as to satisfy the requirements of the rule of natural justice. The appellant, as the facts noted earlier in this judgment show, was given notice to show that he had actually passed in physics as claimed by him. The previous decision is thus of no assistance to the appellant in the present case."

31. We fail to understand how the High Court Division applied this case in the present case, which instead supporting the case of the writ petitioner supports the appellants? Though the point of abatement was decided in the earlier writ petition but the decision was given on a wrong premise of law. In AK Mahbub Co. vs State of MP AIR 1966 SC 1637.the question was whether the decision given the earlier case on the right of the parties visa vis an enactment would be res judicata in view of the change in law on the same subject. In the earlier decision it was held that contracts and agreements, such as the one held by the petitioner from were in essence and effect licences granted to the transferees to cut, gather and carry away, the produce in the shape of the tendu leaves, lac, or timber or wood". The decision was given in the light of Act 1 of 1951. Subsequently another legislation on the same subject was promulgated in 1964 namely, Madhya Pradesh Tendu Parra (Vypar Viniyaman) Adhiniyam, 1964 to make provisions for regulating in the public interest the trade of tendu leaves by creating State monopoly in such trade. The Division Commissioner then informed the petitioner firm that the right to collect tendu leaves was abrogated by the State Government. The writ petition was filed challenging the restriction. It was argued by Hidayatullah,J. as under:

"The petitioner firm like others had a licence to go to the forests to pick and carry away tendu leaves but had no other right. The attention of the Divisional Bench was not directed to this difference. Such a decision can not constitute a bar on the principle of res judicata when new circumstances have come to exist which require a reappraisal of the true legal position."

<u>32. The last point urged by Mr TH Khan is whether the acquisition of property for construction of office complex by a Non-government Organization is at all fall within the meaning of 'Public purpose' or 'public interest' within the meaning of section 3 of the Ordinance. Admittedly, Rabitat is a Non-Government Organization. This acquisition cannot be taken for public purpose within the meaning of section 3, which authorizes the Deputy Commissioner to issue notice for acquisition if any property is needed for "any public purpose" or in public interest". The entire scheme of the law is acquisition of the private property for public purpose. The power to acquire property is a power to acquire it only for a public purpose. There is no power in the acquiring authority to acquire private property in order to give it to private persons because if this process is allowed every Non-Government Organization, there are about a million or more working in the country, on influencing the Government or the Deputy Commissioner would acquire any private property for their office buildings. This is not the purpose of the law. 'Public purpose' is contained of the power itself. In Willoughby's constitutional law it is stated:</u>

<u>"As between individuals, no necessity, however great, no exigency, however imminent, no improvement, however valuable, no refusal, however unneighbourly, no obstinacy, however unreasonable, no offers of compensation, however extra vagrant, can compel or require any man to part with an inch of his estate.</u>

<u>33. To constitute public purpose it is necessary that the land when taken should be in general interest of the community as opposed to the particular interest of individuals, is directly and vitally concerned. According to modern view "public use" means useful to the public. In Cooleys Constitutional Limitation, it is said:</u>

<u>"No satisfactory definition of the term "public use" has ever been achieved by the Courts. Two different theories are presented by the judicial attempts to describe the subjects to which the expression would apply. One theory of "public use" limits the application to "employment"  "occupation". A more liberal and more flexible meaning makes it synonymous with "public advantage", "public benefit". A title investigation will show that any definition attempted would exclude some subjects that properly should be included in, and include some subjects that must be excluded from the operation of the words "public use". As might be expected, the more limited application of the principle appears in the earlier cases. and the more liberal application has been rendered necessary by complex conditions due to recent development of civilization and the increasing density of population. In the very nature of the case, modern conditions and the increasing interdependence of the different human factors in the progressive complexity of a community make it necessary for the Government to touch upon and limit individual activities at more points than formerly".</u>

34. In Corpus Juris, VoI.XX, under the caption 'what is a public use. It is said-

"No general definition of what degrees of public good will meet the constitutional requirements for a "public use" can be framed, as it is in every case a question of public policy. The meaning of the term is flexible and is not confined to what may constitute a public use at any given time, but in general it may be said to cover a use affecting the public generally, or any number thereof, as distinguished from particular individuals. Some Courts have gone so far in the direction of a liberal construction as to hold that "public use" is synonymous with "public benefit", "public utility", or "public advantage", and to authorise the exercise of the power of eminent domain to promote such public benefit, etc., especially where the interests involved are of considerable magnitude, and it is sought to use the power in order that the natural resources and advantages of a locality may receive the fullest development in view of the general welfare".

35. In Hamabai Frangee vs Secretary of State, 421A 44 the judicial committee explained meaning of the word 'public purposes' as under:

"General definitions are, I think, rather to be avoided where the avoidance is possible, and I make no attempt to define precisely the extent of the phrase 'public purposes' in the lease; it is enough to say that, in my opinion, the phrase whatever else it may mean, must include a purpose, that is, an object or aim, in which the general interest of the community, as opposed to the particular interest of individual, it directly and vitally concerned."

<u>36. The explanation public purpose, is therefore, construed according to the times in which particular legislation is enacted is so construed. The acquisition of the immovable property has to be held to have been made for a public purpose and not otherwise. In this particular case, it is seen that the acquisition has been made not for any public purpose rather it is meant for private purpose for office complex of a Non-Government Organization and the acquisition is not needed for public purpose. The High Court Division has totally over looked this aspect of the matter.</u>

37. Both the appeals were filed by two sets of writ respondents against the same judgment of the writ petition which challenged the impugned Gazette Notification revoking the acquisition proceedings. We found that the writ respondent No.3 committed no illegality in revoking the proceedings in respect of acquisition of the land. Therefore, the decision in one appeal will cover the other appeal as well.

Civil Appeal No. 60 of 2006, is therefore, allowed without any order as to costs. The other appeal being Civil Appeal No. 59 of 2006 is disposed of with the above observations.

End.

full_judgment:
Sharif Uddin Chaklader J: This Appeal by the plaintiffs directed against judgment and decree dated 22-11-2000 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Noakhali dismissing Title Suit No. 19 of 1994.

2. Appellants as plaintiffs instituted the aforesaid suit with prayer for a decree that suit property as described in schedule 'Ka', Kha, Ga, Gha, Uma, Cha, Chcha, Ja and Jha to the plaint are not vested and non-resident property.

3. It is the case. of plaintiffs that, suit property originally belongs to Chandra Kumar Loadh, Raj Kumar Loadh, Mohendra Kumar Loadh and Debendra Kumar Loadh. Chandra Kumar Loadh died leaving two sons, Kamini Kumar Loadh and Nalini Loadh; Mohendra Kumar Loadh died leaving two sons, Vobesh Chandra Loadh and Dhirendra Kumar Loadh and Raj Kumar Loadh died leaving three sons, Horendra Kumar Loadh, Jogendra Kumar Loadh and Monaranjan Loadh. Debendra Kumar Loadh died unmarried and his share was recorded in the name of original owner, Chandra Kumar Loadh and in the name some of their heirs at Revisional survey, MRR Khatian No.30. Said property, after gradual devolution, devolved upon their heirs i.e Horendra Kumar Loadh, Jogendra Kumar Loadh, Monaranjan Loadh. Horendra Kumar Loadh, Jogendra Kumar Loadh and Mohendra Kumar Loadh sold the suit land to plaintiff Nos. 1-8. Plaintiff No. 9, Habib Ullah sold his purchased land of khatian No. 19 and dag No.533 to plaintiff No. 19, Nalini Kumar Loadh, Jamini Kumar Loadh and one of the original owner by Saf kabala deed dated 10-4-1970 and 11-4-1970 sold 0.16 acres from 'Ka' schedule of dag No. 533 and 1.64 acres of land of dag No. 535, in total, 1.80 acres of land to Mohammad Shah Alam and plaintiff No. 10 Fazlul Hoque. Thereafter, Mohammad Shah Alam died leaving brother, plaintiff No. 25, plaintiffs Nos. 26/27 are sisters and one wife, plaintiff No. 28. While Shah Alam was alive, he sold 6 decimals of land by Saf kabala deed dated 8-1-1979 from dag No. 535 to plaintiffs Nos. 17 and 19. Plaintiff No. 10 by Safkabala deed dated 30-6-1976 sold 0.04 acres of land from 'Ka' schedule of dag No. 535 and 24 decimals of land of dag No. 535, in total, 28 decimals of land to plaintiff No. 22. Plaintiff No. 10, Fazlul Hoque, by registered deed dated 29-6-1976 sold 28 decimals of land from the aforesaid dag to plaintiff No. 14. Plaintiff No. 10 by another saf kabala deed sold, 29 decimals of land out of dag No. 505 to plaintiff No. 29. Vobesh Chandra Loadh son of Mohendra Kumar Loadh, Omreta Kumar Loadh, son of, Jamini Kumar Loadh, Jogendra Kumar Loadh, son of, Raj Kumar Loadh, Nolini Kumar Loadh, son of, Chandra Kumar Loadh and Devendra Kumar Loadh, son of, Mohendra Kumar Loadh by registered saf kabala deed dated 13-10-1978 and 5- 1-1979 sold 2.35 acres of land from 'Ka' schedule from dag 536, khatian No. 19, from dag No. 565, 17 decimals, from dag No. 534, 7 decimals of land, in total, 89 decimals of land to plaintiff Nos. 11 and 12. The aforesaid heirs of original owners by registered saf kabala deed dated 19-1-1979 sold, in total, 1.07 acres of land from dag No. 535, 556,465 to plaintiff No. 10. Aforesaid heirs of the original owners by registered saf kabala deed dated 29-1-1979 sold, 5 decimals of land from dag No. 536, 5 decimals of land from dag No. 534 and 5 decimals of land from dag No. 465, in total, 15 decimals of land to plaintiff No. 13. Aforesaid heirs of the original owners sold 4 decimals of land from dag No. 534, 2 decimals of land from dag No. 365, 6 decimals of land from dag No. 536, in total, 12 decimals of land by registered saf kabala deed dated 23-10-1978 to plaintiff No. 17 and also to the predecessor-in-interest of plaintiffs Nos. 25-28 i.e. Shah Alam. Aforesaid heirs of the original owners by registered saf kabala deed dated 7-2-1979 sold in total 53 decimals of land to plaintiff Nos. 24 and also to the predecessor-in-interest of plaintiff Nos. 25-28. The aforesaid heirs by registered saf kabala deed dated 7-2-1979 sold 43 decimals of land to plaintiff Nos. 19, 17 and 23. Plaintiff No. 10 by registered saf kabala deed No. 3120 dated 11-4-1970 sold 28 decimals of land to plaintiff No. 22. Plaintiff No. 10 by registered saf kabala deed dated 6-7-1976 sold 28 decimals ofland to plaintiff No. 14. Plaintiff No. 31 by registered saf kabala deed dated 5-2-1973 sold 22 decimals of land to plaintiff No. 9, Habib Ullah.

4. In this way plaintiffs Nos. 1-10, 11, 12, 14, 17, 19,23,24,25-28 and 31 purchased in total 4.57 acres of land and in possession. This property along with other properties have been recorded in the khatian as per description made in the plaint. Plaintiff Nos. 2-11 purchased land from plaintiff No. 15 and 20 in total 1.24 acres of land by registered safkabala deed dated 15-2-1976. Plaintiff No. 15 purchased 1.22 acres of land from plaintiff No. 16 and plaintiff No. 17 sold his land to plaintiff No. 18. Plaintiff No. 20 by amicable settlement in between predecessor of dag No. 534 and 537 got in total 29 decimals of land, sold the same to plaintiff No. 11 and 14. Nolini Kumar Loadh, son of, Chandra Kumar Loadh sold 1.20 acres of land to plaintiff No. 15,20,21 and 22 from suit dag. Thereafter, plaintiff No. 20 on amica- ble partition got 29 decimals of land of dag No. 543/537 and by registered safkabala deed dated 21- 6-1976 sold the said land to plaintiff No. 11 and 14. Jamini Kumar Loadh and Nalini Kumar Loadh, sons of, Chandra Kumar Loadh on amicable partition got 29 decimals of land from dag No. 532, 15 decimals of land from dag No. 609 and 2 decimals of land from dag No. 521/1458, in total, 46 decimals of land, sold by registered saf kabala deed dated 20-3- 1970 to Mohammad Shah Alam who in turn sold 15 decimals of land of his purchased land by registered safkabala deed dated 4-3-1971 to plaintiff No. 16, 17 and 18. 9. 10. In this way aforesaid schedule properties are owned by purchase by registered saf kabala by the plaintiffs, they mutated their names in the respective khatian spaying rents regularly. Subsequently they have got notice that the suit land has been recorded by the defendants as enemy and nonresident property. They filed Title Suit No. 149 of 1986 with the aforesaid prayer.

11. Defendant Nos. 1-5 contested the suit by filing written statement. They have denied all the material allegations of the plaint. It is their Case that the Hindu original owners of the suit property left this country on the eve of Pak-Bharat War of 1965, as such, schedule property has been recorded in the name of Government as enemy property in VP Case No. 2/81-82 and by paying lease money lessees of the Government possessing the suit land.

12. Learned Judge by the impugned judgment dismissed the suit holding that the suit property as enemy property.

13. Mr Delwar Hossain, learned Advocate, for the appellant canvassed only one ground that is the suit property cannot be treated as enemy property as the law under which the property has been enlisted and vested in the government already been deed naturally, as such, learned Judge committed illegality in holding the suit property as enemy property. Learned Advocate relied on the decisions of Saju Hossain vs Bangladesh, 58 DLR (AD) 177, the case of Aroti Rani Paul vs Sudarshan Kumar Paul, 56 DLR (AD) 73, the case of Laxmi Kanta Roy vs Upazilla Nirbahi Officer, 46 DLR 1 36, the case of MIS Dulichand Omraolal vs Bangladesh, through the Secretary, Ministry of Industries, 33 DLR (AD) 30, the case of Nittya Gopal Roy Barmon vs Pran Gopa/ Nandi, 32 DLR 11. In these decisions it has been held that, "Since the law of enemy property itself died with the repeal of Ordinance No. 1 of 1969 on 23-3-1974, no further Vested Property case can be started thereafter on the basis of the law which is already dead."

14. It appears that, defendant only produced only one file and no other document. It appears that defendant tried to treated the suit property as enemy property first time in LA Case No. 2/81-82, not before that. It appears that defendant did not give any explanation as to why they did not take step as to the character of the suit property as enemy property after 1965 and before death of the law on this subject. We are of the view that, the learned Judge committed gross illegality in holding that the suit property as enemy property. We find substance in the Appeal.

15. In the result, the Appeal is allowed.

16. The impugned judgment and decree dated 2-11-2000 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Noakhali in Title Suit No. 19 of 1994 is set aside, Title Suit No. 19 of 1994 is decreed.

<u>17. Before parting with the decision it is desirous that Government should act in the benefit of Citizen, Government should not act as enemy of the Citizen by harassing them particularly with the properties treated the same as enemy under a law which has already died long about 37 years before. In this judgment we have referred to a number of decisions and it is our belief that government is aware of these judgments but still we find that citizens being harassed in the name of a law which is no more. We hope that government should act properly and instruct at least the vested property cell so that no other citizen should be harassed in the name of law which has already dead.</u>

18. Let copy of this judgment-be sent to the Hon'ble Minister, Ministry of law, justice and parliamentary affairs, Government of Bangladesh.

19. Send down the lower Court record.

Communicate this Order at once.

End.

full_judgment:
Farid Ahmed J : This Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the acquisition proceeding in LA Case No. 8 of 1992 by the Land Acquisition Officer, Comilla, acquiring the petitioner's land measuring 0.20 acres being Dag No. 647 Khatian No. 312. Mouza-Homna J L No. 51. Thana Homna, District-Comilla, should not be declared to have been passed without any lawful authority and to be of no legal effect and or such other or further order or orders passed as to this court may seem fit and proper.

2. The facts as stated in the petition are that the petitioner is the owner of the homestead land measuring 0.20 acres where he was living with his family members and also has been running a tea stall in the small part of it. He filled up a ditch of about 25 x 30 feet by collecting earth from various places and erected two houses of 24' x 12' and 44' x 12' as corrugated tinshed. The covetous eyes of an influential mighty person of the society fell on the said land who made an offer to purchase the same at a consideration of Taka 10 lac and having failed he forcibly hanged a signboard of the then ruling party. The petitioner then removed the signboard from his land. On 29-7-90 a meeting of Upazila Parishad under the Chairmanship of the then Upazila Chairman Mr. Amzad Hossain was held and in the said meeting a resolution was adopted to the effect that 0.20 acres land of plot No.647 is required for expansion of Homna Upazila Complex. As per said resolution the then Upazila Nirbahi Officer (UNO) prepared a specific proforma for the requisition and acquisition of the property and the same was sent to the Land Acquisition Officer, Comilla, who started LA Case No.8 of 1992-93 for the acquisition of the land in question. On 12-12-92 a notice under section 3 of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 was issued in favour of the petitioner asking him to submit objection, if any against the said proposal for acquisition. The petitioner submitted his objection on 29-12-92 and on 7-2-93 his objection was rejected. The authority found that the property is required for public purpose and for public interest and sent the proposal to the Divisional Commissioner for approval. Thereafter notice under section 6(I)(3) of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, was served upon the petitioner vide Memo dated 19-6-93 duly signed by the Deputy Commissioner. Finding no other alternative, the petitioner instituted Title Suit No. 16 of 1993 in the Court of Assistant Judge. Homna, Comilla, for declaration that the acquisition of the land of the petitioner is null and void and that the same is malafide, and not for public purpose or public interest.

3. The respondents have contested the suit by filing written statements alleging that the acquisition is for bona fide public purpose for the public interest. The learned Assistant Judge on 26-8-96 decreed the suit.

4. Against the said judgment and decree of the trial Court, the respondents preferred Title Appeal No. 219 of 1996 before the learned District Judge Comilla and the learned Joint District Judge, 3rd Court, Comilla by Judgment and decree dated 31-1-02 allowed the appeal and dismissed the suit holding that the suit challenging the proceeding started under the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance. 1082 was not maintainable.

5. By tiling two separate supplementary affidavits dated 1-3-06 and 15-3-06 the petitioner has also contended that though the requiring body i.e. Thana Nirbahi Officer (TNO), gave their proposal to acquire the land in question to protect the Upazila Parishad Bhaban and administrative sanction was also given for the said purpose by the Ministry of Local Government Rural Development and Co-operatives but the notice under section 3 of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982, signed by the Land Acquisition Officer was issued mentioning that the property is needed or likely to be needed to expand the Homna Thana Parishad. The petitioner also stated that the local administration and the land acquisition authority have proceeded to acquire the land of the petitioner in question under the pressure and to meet the sweet will of a Cabinet Secretary who thereafter became the Commerce Minister, thereafter the Minister or Waster Transport of the then Government and thereafter the Minister of Industry or the present Government, whose proposal of buying the said homestead land was not accepted by the petitioner and that the said facts would be evidenced from the letter dated 21-4-92 issued by the Ministry of Local Government. Rural Development and Co-operatives to the Upazila Nirbani Officer, Homna, according administrative approval for the acquisition of the property (Annexure-F) and from the letter dated 16-9-93 (Annexure-H) issued by the TNO to the Deputy Commissioner, Comilla for receiving fund for compensation against acquisition and to deliver physical possession of the land, copy of the said letters were served upon the Private Secretary to the then Minister of Commerce and thereafter Private Secretary to the Minister of Water Transport, though the said Ministry is not the concerned Ministry for requisition and acquisition of the property. The petitioner also stated that there are vast vacant Government high lands available in front side and in the east and west side of the Upazila Bhaban, the proposal for acquisition of the petitioner's land for the expansion of the Upazila Parish ad Bhaban is malafide, unjustified and not reasonable. The said acquisition proceedings have not been finalised and a declaration of the acquisition of the property by the Deputy Commissioner has yet not been published in the Official Gazette. The property in question is still vacant and no building or foundation for construction was undertaken in the said land, except a boundary wall in the north end of the land was constructed in the year 2003 after issuance of the Rule by this Court.

6. It is further contended by the petitioner that ex-Upazila Complex building has been expanded by constructing a two-storied building a few years ago adjacent to the western side of the Upazila building whereof the office of the UNO and temporary Paurashava Offices are working. And a new three-storied building also has been erected in the south eastern side of the Upazila Parishad field. Whereat offices of Agriculture, Youth Development, Education, Fishery, Accounts, etc. have been transferred from the old Upazila Parishad, Homna. A vast vacant Government land towards the south is still lying unused in front of the ex-Upazila Parishad building measuring about I (one) acre of land which is more than enough to expand the Upazila Complex if, at all, is necessary.

7. The petitioner, being aggrieved by the acquisition proceedings under I-A case No. 6 of 1991-92 started by the respondents has preferred the writ petition and obtained the instant Rule.

8. Mr AKM Fazlul Hoque, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner, submits that the reason for the acquisition of the property must have been stated definitely and specifically. When the requiring body needs the property for one reason and the property is acquired or notified to be acquired for another reason, it is a sign of arbitrary and whimsical use of statutory power by the authority and therefore, the notice under section 3 of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 and the proceedings for acquisition is liable to be declared as unlawful and without any jurisdiction. Mr Fazlul Hoque also submits that in the notice under section 3 of the Ordinance it has been mentioned that the property is needed or likely to be needed for the public purpose whereby it has been kept open for both the alternatives, though the law requires that the Deputy Commissioner will have to choose one, and, as such, the acquisition proceedings should be declared as illegal and without lawful authority, Mr Fazlul Hoque thereafter submits that keeping vast land unused within the campus of the Upazila complex, the purpose of acquisition is malafide and for private interest to meet the sweet will of an influential person and not for the bonafide  public interest or public purpose and, as such, the Rule is liable to be made absolute.

9. Mr Zaman Akhter, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing on behalf of the respondents, without tiling any affidavit-in-opposition, submits that the land in question is required for the expansion of Upazila Parishad for the public interest and the acquiring authority after observing all formalities as required under the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982, acquired the property, the objection of the petitioner made under section 4(1) of the Ordinance, was considered by the Divisional Commissioner and found that the property proposed to be acquired for the public purpose for the expansion of Upazila Parishad, the land in question is necessary and, as such, it cannot be said that the proceedings for acquisition of the property is a malafide action and the same is not for public purpose and, as such, the Rule is liable to be discharged.

10. It appears from Annexure-E that a proforma (proposal for acquisition was filled up by the TNO on 9-9-92 and stated that the said 0.20 acres land which is a ditch is required for the protection of the Homna Parishad Bhaban and that by filing up the said land, the main Upazila Parishad Bhaban would be protected. Annexure-F, a letter dated 21-4-92 issued by the Assistant Secretary, Ministry of Local Government, Rural Development and Co-operatives intimating the TNO Homna Upazila, Comilla, that administrative approval was given for the acquisition of the land in question to protect the building of the Upazila Parishad Bhaban. Annexure-G is the notice dated 12-1-92 under section 3 of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance 1982 hereinafter referred to as the Ordinance issued by the Land Acquisition Officer Comilla, wherein it has been mentioned that the land in question is required to be acquired for the public purpose for the expansion of Hornna Upazila Parishad Bhaban and the said land is required. and likely to be required for acquisition and asked the petitioner to file objection, if any, within 15 days from the date of receipt of the said notice. The notice issued under section 3 of the Ordinance reads as follows:

যেহেতু নিম্নোক্ত তফশীলে বর্নিত সম্পত্তি হোমনা থানা পরিষদ সম্প্রসারন জন কল্যান মূলক উদ্দেশ্যে এবং গণ স্বার্থে প্রয়োজন অথবা প্রয়োজন হইতে পারে, সেহেতু এক্ষনে ১৯৮২ সনের স্থাবর সম্পত্তি অধিগ্রহনও হুকুম দখল অধ্যাদেশ (১৯৮২ সনের ২নং অধ্যাদেশ) এর ৩ পারার বর্ণিত্তত সিদ্ধান্ত অনুযায়ী এতদ্বারা সংশ্লিষ্ট সকলকে ও অবগতির জন্য নোটিশ জারী করা হইল যে, উক্ত সম্পত্তি সরকার কর্তৃক অধিগ্রহনের প্রস্তাব করা হইয়াছে।

উক্ত সম্পত্তিতে স্বার্থবান যে কোন ব্যক্তি এই নোটিশ জারী হওয়ার পর ১৫ (পনের) দিনের মধ্যে প্রস্তাবিত সম্পত্তি অধিগ্রহনের বিরুদ্ধে নিম্নস্বাক্ষরকারীর নিকট আপত্তি দায়ের করিতে পারেন।”

11. From the contents of the said notice it appears that the land was proposed to be acquired for the expansion of the Hornna Upazila Parishad for the public purpose which is required or likely to be required for the said purpose and by this notice it has been kept open for both the alternatives, though the law requires that the Deputy Commissioner will have to choose one and in the said notice the purpose tor acquisition shall have to be specifically mentioned. It also appears from the said notice that the Land Acquisition Officer signed the notice 12-12-92 though under section 3 of the said Ordinance it is the Deputy Commissioner who has to cause a notice to be published under the said Ordinance.

<u>12. The learned Deputy Attorney-General has failed to satisfy us from the record that the' Deputy Commissioner authorised the land acquisition officer to issue such letter or the law empower, that Land Acquisition Officer to issue such letter Under the provisions of section 3 of the Ordinance the Deputy Commissioner has to say whether the property in question is needed or alternatively whether it is likely to be needed but he cannot say at the same time that it is both needed or likely to be needed. On considering the notice under section 3 of the Ordinance (Annexure-G) we find that the same was not issued for any specific purpose and the same has not been issued by a proper authority i.e. the Deputy Commissioner who is authorised by law to issue such letter. The learned Advocate for the petitioner has cited the case of Sankar Gopal Chatterjee vs Additional Commissioner. Dhaka Division reported in 41 DLR 326 and the case of Abdul Kader vs Masaddar Ali reported in 3 BLC (AD) 211. In the case reported in 41 DLR 326 it has been held.</u>

<u>" ..... A property is either needed or it is likely to be needed, but while acquiring a property the Deputy Commissioner cannot keep both the alternatives in his pocket. He has to choose between the two. If he keeps both the options open, then the does not know whether the property is needed for immediate use or it is likely to be needed for some future use. The use of both these alternative expressions in the notice under section 3 is indicative of a lack of application of mind and the notice under section 3 is liable to be struck down on that ground as well"</u>

13. This view of the High Court Division has been approved by our Appellate Division in the case reported in 3 BLC (AD) 21. After the issuance of the notice under section 6 of the Ordinance, the petitioner instituted Title Suit No. 16 of 1993 in the Court of learned Assistant Judge, Homna, Com ilia, for declaration that the acquisition proceeding is illegal, malafide and the same is without jurisdiction. The learned Assistant Judge decreed the suit by judgment and decree dated 20-8-96 declaring that the acquisition of property is mala tide and not for public purpose.

14. The respondents against the said judgment and decree of the trial Court preferred Title Appeal No. 219 before the learned District Judge, Comilla. The learned Joint District Judge 3rd Court Comilla by judgment and decree dated 31-1-02 allowed the appeal holding that the suit is barred under section 44 of the Ordinance and that the proceeding initiated under the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Act cannot be called in question before any Civil Court.

15. The petitioner has annexed a sketch map as Annexure-'Ll' along with his supplementary affidavit dated 15-3-06. In the said sketch map it has been shown that the Upazila Complex is situated adjacent to big public road from two sides i.e. from the east and the west 7-8 feet wide public roads have connected the Upazila Complex with the main road and around the said two connected roads there are available vacant lands of the Upazila Parishad. It also appears from the said sketch map that a big vacant land is lying in front of the Upazila Parishad Bhaban, The area of the said land according to the petitioner is about one acre. In the northern side of the Upazila Bhaban the proposed land for acquisition is situated. From the sketch map, we find that the extension of Upazila Parishad can be easily done in the vacant land of the Upazila Parishad. The respondents have mentioned in their proposal for acquisition that the lands is required for the protection of the building and in the notice under section 3 it has been mentioned that for the extension of the Upazila Parishad, the land is required or likely to be required. So, we find that respondents are not sure or definite about their purpose for the acquisition of the property. The proposal was made in the year 1990 for the acquisition of the property till today there is no allegation from the side of the respondents within these 15 years that without the proposed land the protection of the main building or Upazila Parishad is being hampered. It has not been denied by the respondents that there is no available vacant land of the Government south of the Upazila Parishad or within Upazila Complex. The petitioner has asserted that a Cabinet Secretary who thereafter became an influential Minister of the then political party in power tried to purchase the land in question by creating pressure upon the petitioner and having failed he has influenced the acquisition authority to take steps for the acquisition of the property in the name of expansion of the Upazila Parishad Bhaban and to show the involvement of the said influential Minister, the learned Advocate has drawn our attention to Annexures-Il and III which show that copy of the said annexures were forwarded to the Private Secretary of the said Minister, though the said Minister or Ministry has nothing to do on the question of the land in question. This action of the respondents also shows the malafide intention of the respondents in acquiring the property. The petitioner has also made statements on oath annexing some photographs to show the present position of the proposed acquired land and the vacant land situated within the complex of the Upazila Parishad. From the said photographs it seems to us that a vacant land is available in front of the Upazila Parishad.

16. From the above discussions, we find that the proposal for acquisition of the land in question was not bonafide and the notice for the acquisition of the property is a mala fide action of the respondents and the same was not for a specific purpose or tor public purpose. The notice under section 3 of the Ordinance, was not issued by a competent officer and, as such, the proceedings of LA Case No. 8 of 1992-93 is declared to be illegal and without lawful authority and the same has got no legal basis.

17. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs.

Send down the records to the concerned authority.

<u>Md Muzammel Hossain J : I respectfully agree with my learned brother in making the Rule absolute Since my learned brother has stated the facts of the case, and the points involved in making the Rule absolute I would like to add a few words of my own and to focus on the intention of the requiring body as a proforma was submitted by the Thana Nirbahi Officer on 9-9-1992 (Annexure-E). On perusal of Annexure E it appears that the purpose of the proposal was to acquire the land in question tor the protection of the Upazila Parishad Bhaban. It also appears from the memo dated 21-4-92 issued by the Ministry of Local Government, Rural Development and Co-operatives (Annexure F) and possession certificate (Annexure 1) issued by the Land Acquisition Officer that the purpose, of the acquisition was for the protection of the Upazila Parishad Bhaban whereas from the notice dated 12-12-1992 under section 3 of the Ordinance (Annexure G) it appears that the land in question is required for the extension of the Upazila Parishad Bhaban. Section 3 of the Acquisition and Requisitions of Immovable Properties Ordinance 1982 empowers the Deputy Commissioner to publish a notice at a convenient place on or near the property which is needed or likely to be needed for any public purpose or in the public interest stating that the property is proposed to be acquired. In the case of Shankar Gopal Chatterjee vs Additional Commissioner; Dhaka Division reported in 41 DLR 326 a Division Bench of this Hon'ble Court held that the Law of Acquisition gives the Deputy Commissioner power to acquire property in two likely situations, Firstly, if the property is needed and secondly, if the property is likely to be needed. A property is either needed or it is likely to be needed, but while acquiring a property the Deputy Commissioner cannot keep both the alternatives in his pocket. He has to choose between the two, if he keeps both the options open, then he does not know whether the property is needed for immediate use or it likely to be needed for some future use. The use of both these alternative expressions in the notice under section 3 is indicative of a lack of application of mind and the notice under section 3 is liable to be struck down on that ground as well. In the case Abdul Quadir vs Masaddar Ali reported in 3 BLC (AD) 211 the Appellate Division held that when the two alternatives are kept open then there was total non-application of mind and the whole exercise by the petitioner was a malafide move to get the land aequired illegally when he himself failed to purchase the same as has been found by the High Court Division. In the instant case since the respondents, requiring authority and acquiring authority, expressed different purpose if cannot be said clearly for which purpose the land in question is going to be acquired. It appears that there is a total non-application of mind on the part of the authority which makes the order liable to be struck down. The petitioner in the; Supplementary-Affidavit stated that there is no precise or definite purpose for the acquisition of the land in question in as much as the respondents purported to acquire the land on the one hand for the protection of the Upazila Parishad Bhaban and on the other hand, for the extension of the Upazila complex. Since the very purpose of the acquisition is ambiguous or otherwise uncertain, the Acquiring Body did not know or does not know for what purpose the land was or is required to be acquired. It has been asserted on behalf of the petitioner that the local administration and the Acquiring Body proceeded to acquire the land in question at the behest of a mighty person who is a former secretary and presently an influential Minister of the Government holding different portfolios and whose proposal of buying the said homestead land was not accepted by the petitioner. The learned Advocate for the petitioner has brought to our notice some other correspondences namely; Memo dated 21-4-1992 (Annexure F), Memo dated 16-9-1992 (Annexure-H), Memo dated 18-11-2000 [ Annexure-H(1)] forwarded to the Private Secretary to the Hon'ble Minister stating the name of the Ministry. There is no rhyme and reason to understand why these memos should be addressed to the Private Secretary to the Hon'ble Minister who was or is not at all involved or in-charge of the Ministry or who is not concerned as to the acquisition of the land under the Acquisition and Requisition of Immoveable Property Ordinance, 1982 and the Rules framed thereunder. From the statements of the petitioner and the sketch map annexed to the Supplementary-Affidavit, it is evident that there is a big vacant land measuring one acre in front of the Upazila Parishad Bhaban. The petitioner asserted that extension of the Upazila Parishad could be easily done in the said vacant land. The petitioner has also asserted that a mighty person being an influential Minister having failed to grab the property, impressed upon the Acquiring Authority to take steps for the acquisition of the property in question. Since these statements of the petitioner have not been controverted by the respondents it is deemed to have been admitted to be true. In that view of the matter. We find that the acquisition proceedings have been started with malafide intention to deprive the petitioner in the absence of any bonafide requirement. Though the proposal for acquisition was made in 1990 yet till today there is no material evidence on record to show that in the absence of the acquisition of the property in question the existence of the Upazila Parishad haban is in jeopardy. It is well established that rnalafide vitiates everything. Malatide has been defined by the Indian Supreme Court in the decision of the case of Jaichand VWD AIR 1967 SC 483 in the following terms:</u>

" ......malafide exercise of power does not necessarily imply any moral turpitude as a matter of law. It only means that the statutory power is exercised for purpose foreign to those tor which it is in law intended."

We may profitably refer to the decision in the case of Abdur Rouf vs Abdul Hakim. reported in 17 DLR (SC) 515 where it has been observed:

"A malafide act is by its nature an act without jurisdiction. No legislature when it grants power to take action or pass an order contemplates a mala fide exercise of power. A Malafide order is a fraud on the statute. It may be explained that a mala fide order means one which is passed not for the purpose contemplated by the enactment granting the power to pass the order, but tor some other collateral or ulterior purpose."

In the case of Khandoker Moshtaque Ahmed I"S Bangladesh reported in 34 DLR (AD) 22 it has been observed.

"Power has not been given to exercise it illegally or with mala fide intention Malafide actions do not get any protection from any court of law."

When any action is taken or proceeding is initiated with mala tide intention without formation of any opinion as to the purpose of the acquisition the entire proceedings should be vitiated and, as such, the acquisition proceedings should be declared to be without any lawful authority. For the aforesaid reasons. I also concur with my learned brother in holding that the acquisition proceedings have been made without lawful authority and are of no legal effect. We have also noticed that the respondents Acquiring Authority with malafide intention started the acquisition proceedings in respect of the property in question without any public purpose or without any public interest and, as such, the acquisition proceedings are declared to be without lawful authority. With the aforesaid findings and observations. I concur with my learned brother in making the Rule absolute.

End.

parties:
Begum Khaleda Zia----- Petitioners
Vs.
Government of Bangladesh and others----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Nazmun Ara Sultana J : This Rule was issued at the instance of Begum Khaleda Zia, former Prime Minister and now Leader of the Opposition in Parliament calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the impugned notice dated 24-5-2009 (annexure C-2) asking the petitioner to return the demised property during the subsistence of a registered lease in perpetuity dated 8-7-1981 situated at 6, Shaheed Moinul Road, Dhaka Cantonment, Dhaka without due process of law shall not be declared to have been made without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and also violative of the fundamental rights guaranteed to the petitioner under Articles 27, 31 and 42 of the Constitution and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. At the very out-set it requires to be mentioned here that this writ petition was initially filed impugning a notice dated 20-4-2009 (annexure-C) asking the petitioner to return the property situated at 6, Shaheed Moinul Road, Dhaka Cantonment stating the reasons that there was no law for transferring the military property in question to any civilian and that there was also no reason of any public nature for transferring the said property as per rule 26 of Cantonment Land Administration Rules (CLA Rules) 1937 and also stating that the petitioner conducted political activities during the last 27 years from that house situated in the restricted area of Dhaka Cantonment. When the writ petition was waiting for motion hearing the respondents served a supplementary notice dated 7-5-2009 upon the petitioner (annexure-C1) asking her to show cause as to why she should not be directed to return the property in question within 15 days stating further reasons that the land in question being Class A- J military land as per rule 5(i) of CLA Rules, 1937 the leasing of the ame in favour of the petitioner was "void ab-initio" being in contravention of the statutory rules and stating also that after the death of petitioner's husband President Ziaur Rahman the Government, in a meeting of Council of ministers headed by President held on 12-6-1981, took decision to give huge financial and other benefits including a house with all modern amenities in Gulshan or other posh area of Dhaka City to the petitioner and her sons and that when that decision of the Government was being materialized (and ultimately on 17-7-1982 a house on 1 bigha 10 Katha & 11 chhatak land in Gulshan Model Town was transferred to the petitioner) the leasing out of the property in question which includes 2.72 acres of land and the buildings standing thereon to the petitioner without any decision of the Government was illegal, unethical and against public interest. The respondents served the 3rd final notice dated 24-5-2009 annexure C-2 on the petitioner asking her to hand over the possession of the house in question to the Military Estate Officer by 30.06.2009 when the writ petition was still pending for motion hearing.
