case_source: (From the judgment and order dated the 9th day of August 1999 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No.5392 of 1996).
full_judgment:
MM Ruhul Amin CJ: I had the advantage of going through the judgments proposed to be delivered by my learned brothers Md Fazlul Karim, J and Md Joynul Abedin, J. I concur with the judgment of my brother Md Joynul Abedin, J.

Md Fazlul Karim J: These Appeals, by leave, arising from the same judgment and order, taken together to hear analogously, are directed against the judgment and order dated the 9th day of August, 1996 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 5392 of 1996 making the Rule absolute.

<u>3. The facts of the case, in short, are that the respondents other lands had earlier been acquired by the Government for the purpose of construction of Dhaka-Chittagong Highway and thereafter only the case plots are left to them and they want to develop the same for the purpose of setting up industry on these lands. If the lands in the case plots are acquired they will have no means of livelihood and will be thrown to the street as landless people. It is further asserted that the writ-respondent No.5 has 3.49 acres of land on the other side of Dhaka-Chittagong Road near the case land but the writ-respondent No.5 instead of setting up the industry on his own land managed to get the said property acquired by influencing local administration to grab the properties of the petitioners at a low cost. It is further asserted that although it is shown in paper that the case plots have been acquired by the Government and possession of the same has been handed over to the requiring body but, in fact, the petitioners are still in possession of the respective case plots and it was never taken over by the respondent No.5. It is further contended that the acquisition case has been started with malafide intention as the writ-respondent No. 5 could set up his industry on his own land which is sufficient for establishing the industry in question. It is further alleged that even after acquisition of the case land the writ-respondent No. 5 is not utilising the same for over the long 9 years and, as such, the acquisition order is liable to be struck down on this count as well.</u>

4. The writ-respondent No. 5 contested the writ petition contending, inter alia, that the land in question was acquired under Ordinance No. 2 of 1982 for setting up an industry which is for public purpose. It has further asserted that according to the provisions of the Ordinance, objection was filed in response to the notice served under section 3 of the Ordinance and the same was heard and thereafter, the report was sent to the Divisional Commissioner who rejected the objection and duty accorded his approval. The publication of the Gazette Notification was made on 31-12-1992 vesting the land in the Government and the Government thereafter handed over vacant possession of the case land to the requiring body and they are in possession of the same since 31-12-1991. It is also asserted that an agreement has been concluded on 14-8-1990 in accordance with section 15 of the Ordinance. It appears that the Ministry of Land by its memo dated 4-9-1990 asked the Deputy Commissioner to take necessary steps to acquire at least 2.50 acres of land by LA Case No. 60 of 1987-88 or any other land for Mullah Industrial Estate and subsequently LA Case No.1 of 1990-91 was started. Thus, the case property was acquired for the writ-respondent No.5 in accordance with law. The added writ-respondent No. 5 also filed an affidavit-in-opposition wherein they denied the material allegations made in the writ petition and contended, inter alia, that as per recommendation of the Ministry of Industry, Ministry of Land and the District Land Allotment Committee, Comilla, started LA Case No.1 of 1990-91 after complying with all the procedures as per law. The case land has been acquired for setting up an export oriented industry and transferred the acquired land to the writ-respondent No.5. It is asserted that the land has been acquired for the purpose of public interest and public purpose and the writ-respondent No.5 requires an area of 2.50 acres of land and writ- respondent No.5 has already set up the said industry for producing tooth brush-D-sticks, staple pins, gem clips, educational toys, etc. and the possession of the land has duly been handed over to writ-respondent No. 5 whereupon a portion of the land has been developed and structures raised thereon for running the industry. It further appears that this writ- respondent filed title suit No. 72 of 1996 on 28-5- 1996 against the writ-petitioners of Writ Petition No. 5392 of 1996 for permanent injunction in the Court of Assistant Judge, Daudkandi, Comilla over the selfsame property and an order for maintaining status quo was passed on 28-5-1998 in respect of the suit land and the proceeding of the suit has been stayed.

<u>5. Leave was granted to consider the submission of the learned Counsel for the appellant that "the petitioners took the selfsame grounds before us to assail the order of the High Court Division. They have urged that the acquisition was for public purpose and that the High Court Division erred in law in finding it malafide, inasmuch as the requiring body had allegedly had some land near the acquired land. They have also urged that the High Court Division erred in finding that the acquisition was made at the behest of the Ministry of Land and the High Court Division failed to notice that the writ petition was an inordinate belated one."</u>

6. Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Counsel, appearing for the appellant, submitted that the acquisition is for public purpose and in public interest; that the High Court Division erred in finding malafide only because the petitioner allegedly had some land nearby the acquired land and the acquisition proceeding had been started on the order passed by the Ministry of Land; that no malice of the Government or officials against the writ-petitioner having been alleged or established by adequate materials, the High Court Division erred in holding the acquisition proceeding to be malafide. The learned Advocate further submitted that the High Court Division erred in exercising inordinate delay in challenging the acquisition, ignoring that a vested right had accrued to the appellant having acted bonafide on such acquisition for long time. Furthermore, the learned Advocate submits that the acquisition has been made in accordance with the law and not at the behest of any other inasmuch as the writ petition was filed as a measure of afterthought long after the industry has already been set up.

7. Mr Faruque Ahmed, learned Counsel, appearing for the respondent, submitted that the High Court Division has committed no wrong in making the Rule absolute declaring that requisition has been initiated and started without any lawful authority; that the proceeding of Land Acquisition Case No. 1 of 1990-91 at the office of the respondent No.4, insofar it relates to the acquisition of the property of the writ-petitioners of Mouza Uzar Bhanga JL No. 165, Police Station Daudkandi, District-Comilla appertaining to RS Khatian No. 202 Plot No. 380 measuring 0.7 acre out of 0.14 acre of land as evidenced by Annexure-C, the writ petition is required to be declared to have been made without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect.

8. It appears from the record that an application was filed by the writ petitioners for the local inspection of the case land to ascertain as to whether there is any structure in the case land and for what purpose it was being used. The learned Advocates for the respective parties were directed to make a local inspection of the case land and to submit a report to the Court and all the learned Advocates have submitted their individual report to the Court. From the report it appears that only a small portion of the acquired land has been raised and developed by the writ-respondent No. 5 wherein a two semi-pucca construction has been built wherein the work of the industry is being carried out and vast adjunct is vacant.

9. From the inspection report one fact has clearly emerged, that only a portion of the acquired land is being used by the writ-respondent No. 5 for the purpose of the industry, an export-oriented one and no paper has been produced before the High Court Division to show that the writ-respondent No. 5 has ever exported products like tooth pick of any kind, etc. for the manufacturing of which the land in question was acquired by the Government.

10. The case of the writ-petitioner is that the appellant has his own land in the vicinity where he could set up the industry in question has not been looked into by the District Land Allotment Committee in deciding to allot the land to the writ-respondent No.5 through LA Case No. 1 of 1990-91.

11. It has been alleged by the respondent that no notice under section 7 was served in respect of Plot No. 342 and the writ-petitioners had not received any compensation in respect of the case land but the law provides that the notification has to spell out whether the land is acquired on the satisfaction of the Deputy Commissioner or Divisional Commissioner or the Government as the case may be and in the present case though it has been mentioned that on the satisfaction of the Government the land has been acquired but the Divisional Commissioner has accorded final approval to the acquisition proposal.

12. The writ-respondent, in affidavit-in-opposition, has categorically asserted as to requirement of the land in question for setting up an industry but there is nothing tangible to show that the authority in consideration of the same has taken step for acquiring the land, inasmuch as the possession of respondent No. 5 of 3.49 acre self acquired in the vicinity of land which could be used for the alleged industry, in spite of the fact that his own land is not used for any such purpose but instead an application for acquiring was filed for 2.50 of land in the area leaving aside his own land in the vicinity for the purpose of setting up of an industry.

13. Upon notice under section 3 dated 2-7-1990 an objection was filed on 15-7-1990 Annexure-D. The appellant did not state about his possession of any land in the vicinity of the acquired land. The respondents accordingly filed a representation to the Ministry alleging that the appellant has 3.49 acres of land in the vicinity of the acquired land.

14. The writ-respondents though asserted that they have been using the acquired land for the purpose of industry but no paper had been placed before the High Court Division to show that the appellant has ever produced any product by setting up an export-oriented industry for which the land has been acquired. It further appears from the Annexure-F in the writ petition that the appellant has certain plots of land measuring an area of 3.89 acres as detailed therein on the other side of the Dhaka-Chittagong Highway in the close vicinity of the acquired land. It appears from the affidavit-in-opposition filed by the appellant before the High Court Division that they did not deny the said assertion of the writ-petitioner but only gave an evasive reply that it is not correct.

15. In view of the specific mention about the plots and area of the land owned by the appellant which could be utilised for the purpose instead of acquiring the land, I do not find any reason whatsoever for the appellant to go for acquisition of land in the vicinity for setting up an alleged export oriented industry leaving aside his own land in the vicinity totaling an area of 3.49 acres of land on the side of Dhaka-Chittagong Highway and this aspect of the case was overlooked by the District Land Allotment Committee in deciding the allotment of the land in favour of appellant through LA Case No. 1 of 1990- 91. The respondents herein have also brought to the notice of the said fact by Annexure-H in the writ- petition to the authority concerned but the authority gave a deaf ear to the said representation. It appears from the submission of the learned Assistant Attorney-General before the High Court Division that though it is apparent from the record that the notices were duly served on some persons but the real owner of Plot No. 342 of the case land has not admittedly been served with the notices of acquisition of the suit land. Thus, the said non-service of notices for acquisition vitiated the acquisition proceedings itself.

16. It is also apparent to note from the contents of the report to the Court filed by the learned Advocates regarding the local inspection at the instance of the respondents that only a small portion of the acquired land has been raised and developed by the appellant where he built two semi-pucca construction for the alleged work of the industry and the rest of the land is still lying vacant and under water. It is also in the report that a vast portion of the case land was not developed which is a low lying area with waist-deep water. It is clear from the report of the learned Advocate who went for inspection that structure of any kind on the vast portion of the acquired land was built as claimed by the respondent.

17. The High Court Division accordingly arrived at a finding that only a portion of the acquired land is being used by the appellant for the purpose of industry and there is no paper of his own land where he could set up an industry in question has been looked into by the District Land Allotment Committee authority in deciding allotment of the land to the appellant through LA Case No. 1 of 1990-91. The reports of the local inspection, therein, where the ward Commissioner was present could not identify three other acquired plots which were admittedly under water and there is no structure of any kind on those plots which appertain to show that the appellant could not give the detail of possession of the vast portion but the same were not even in possession of the appellant.

18. It may be noted that no notice under section 7 was ever served in respect of Plot No. 342 and the respondent had not received any compensation in respect of the said case land. Although it has been clearly provided by law that the notification must contain the satisfaction of the Deputy Commissioner or Divisional Commissioner or the Government as the requirement of the acquired land, but in the instant notice it appears that the Authority has simply given a mechanical nod regarding acquisition without applying its mind on the facts and circumstances of the case. The infirmity in the notice could not be remedied or corrected even though the gazette notification for acquisition of the land has been effected giving alleged validity of the acquisition. Thus it appears from the record that the non- issuance of the mandatory notice under the provision of the Ordinance No. II of 1982 has vitiated the acquisition proceeding and in that view of the matter, illegal publication of gazette could not be a sufficient ground for covering any defect in the acquisition proceedings.

19. The High Court Division was also mindful about the fact on perusal of the attached materials that the appellant has not set up an export-oriented industry in the case land and till date, have not developed the area but a simple portion of land has been raised beyond the water where the two semi-pucca structure have been raised.

20. As to the assertion of the writ-petitioner that the appellant possesses 3.49 acres of land on the other side of the road which has been not denied by making any statement in the affidavit-in-opposition except by way of a general, vague and evasive reply and without even denying specifically that the said plots do not belong to him or that he has no right, title and interest in those plots. This aspect of the respondent's case has not been considered by the Authority or the Land Allotment Committee. But contrary to the provision of Article 29(2)(d) of the Requisition and Acquisition of Property Act, 1982 which cast duty upon the authority to see even if it is possible for the requiring body to set up the industry on its own land measuring 3.49 acres of land in proximity of the acquired land, the appellant had acquired 2.50 acres of land belonging to the respondents. Furthermore, no attempt was ever taken by the appellant to approach the respondent for purchase of the land in question and there is nothing on the record to show why these particular plots of land have been found suitable for the said industry.

21. The High Court Division has detailed the circumstances and the speed by which the acquisition proceeding was undertaken and completed. It is apparent from a Government Memo dated 9-4-1990 whereby the Deputy Commissioner, Comilia was asked to take necessary steps to acquire at least 2.50 acres of land in LA Case No. 65 of 1987-88 or any other land for the appellant. Thereafter, the appellant filed an application on 3-6-1990 for acquiring 2.50 acres of land and the allotment committee soon thereafter on 21-6-1990 approved the proposal by initiating LA Case No.1 of 1990-91. The proceeding at such hot haste clearly shows the speed and the motive behind acquisition of the land and completing the entire drama of acquisition within such unusual and short period.

22. These circumstances manifest the non- application of the mind of the District Allotment Committee and the acquiring authority in the matter of acquisition of the land in question for the appellant.

23. The High Court Division also took note of the malafide in the matter of initiating and conducting the requisition proceeding and on the principle that malafide vitiated everything declared the acquisition proceeding illegal and without any jurisdiction.

<u>24. It is important for the authority concerned to arrive at a finding that the acquisition is expedient for a public purpose or public interest and to cause a public notice to be given for acquisition and requisition of the property but as it could be gathered from the circumstances and speed, the proceeding was undertaken and disposed of by the authority giving deaf ear to the stages of proceeding of the acquisition of property pursuant to the provisions of the Act. It is also a glaring example of evading the process of law by directing Deputy Commission to take necessary steps for acquiring 3.49 in LA Case No. 65 of 1987-88 or any other case for the petitioner on 9-4-1990 and soon thereafter completing acquisition proceeding in such a hot haste initiating afresh the LA Case No.1 of 1990-91 after the said alleged proposal incidentally on LA Case No. 65 of 1987-88.</u>

Accordingly, the appeals are dismissed.

Md Tafazzul Islam J : I agree with the judgment proposed to be delivered by my learned brother Md Joynul Abedin J.

Md Joynul Abedin J : These four appeals by leave are directed against the common judgment and order dated 9-8-1999 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division in Writ Petition Nos. 5392 of 1996 and 576 of 1998 making both the Rules absolute.

28. The respondents, as writ petitioners, filed Writ Petition Nos. 5392 of 1996 and 576 of 1198 challenging the proceeding of Land Acquisition Case No.1 of 1990-91, insofar it relates to the acquisition of property of the writ petitioners of Mouza Ozar Bhanga, JL No.165, Police Station-Daudkandi, Cornilla comprising 2.50 acres of Plot Nos. 342 and 381 being the subject matter of Writ Petition No. 5392 of 1976 and Plot No. 380 being the subject matter of Writ Petition No. 576 of 1998 hereinafter called the case land as without lawful authority and for a direction on the writ-respondent appellants to drop the said proceeding.

29. The common case of the writ petitioners is that the Government has already acquired their other lands for the construction of Dhaka-Chittagong Highway and they are only left with the case land which they wanted to develop for the purpose of setting up their own industry. If the case land is acquired they will be thrown out on to the street. The writ respondent No. 5, M/s Mollah Industrial Estate, on the other hand, has 3.49 acres of land in the vicinity of the case land on the other side of Dhaka- Chittagong Highway. Despite this, the writ-respondent No. 5, without setting up its aforesaid industry on its own land managed the case land to be acquired for setting up its industry by influencing the local administration. Although the case land is shown in paper to have been acquired by the Government and possession handed over to writ- respondent No.5 as the requiring body but, in fact, the writ petitioners are still in possession of the case land and the same are not taken over and utilised by the writ-respondent No. 5. It is also stated that the acquisition of the case land is malafide as the same is caused to have been acquisitioned by the Government for the purpose of setting up of the industry of the writ-respondent No.5, although writ respondent has its own land across the Dhaka-Chittagong Highway within the vicinity of the case land.

30. The writ-respondent No. 5 contested the Rule issued in both the writ petitions, contending that the case land was acquired by the Government to enable the writ-respondent No. 5 to set up their export-oriented industry, which was for public purpose, by issuing notice under section 3 of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 inviting objections from all the concerned, including the writ-petitioners and the Deputy Commissioner, Comilla, after due hearing of the objections, submitted the record of the proceedings with his opinion to the Divisional Commissioner for his decision. The Divisional Com- missioner, thereafter, on consideration of the said report of the Deputy Commissioner, made a decision for acquisition of the case land and the Deputy Commissioner then issued a public notice under section 6 inviting claims for compensation informing all the concerned that the Divisional Commissioner took a decision to acquire the case land and would take possession of the same followed by a notice under section 7 for awarding compensation. All the concerned received payment of compensation except the writ-petitioners, who purposely refused to take compensation. Subsequently Gazette notification under section 11 of the Ordinance was published on 31-12-1992 vesting the case land on the Government and thereafter the possession thereof was handed over to the writ- respondent No. 5 i.e. the requiring body on 31-12- 1991.

31. The High Court Division, thereafter, on hearing the parties made the Rules absolute on the grounds that the acquisition of the case land is not for public purpose. The case land insofar as it belonged to the writ-petitioners has not been utilised by the requiring body i.e. the writ respondent No.5 and the same is still in possession of the writ-petitioners and that the acquisition is malafide, inasmuch as the case land is managed to have been acquired leaving aside 3.49 acres of land of the writ- respondent No. 5 in the vicinity. Accordingly, the delay in filing the writ-petitions under reference shall not prejudicially affect the right of the writ- petitioners to have the case land dropped from the said LA Case No. 1/90-91.

32. Against this backdrop, leave was granted to consider whether the acquisition in question is for public purpose, whether the acquisition of the case land is malafide for procuring acquisition of the case land leaving aside the land of the writ-respondent No. 5 situated in the vicinity on whether the delay in filing the aforesaid two writ-petitions by the writ- petitioners was inordinate and fatal for both the acquiring and the requiring body and thus rendering the writ petitions as not maintainable.

33. We have heard the learned lawyers for both the appellants and respondents in support of their contentions against and in favour of the impugned judgment of the High Court Division.

34. It is noted from the record that the writ respondent No. 5, Mollah Industrial Estate, as the requiring body, approached the Government and made a proposal for acquisition of land for them to the extent of 2.50 acres at the present site to enable them to set up export-oriented industry and entered into an agreement dated 14-2-1990, in this regard with the Government under section 15 of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982. Consequently, the Deputy Commissioner, Comilla published a notice under section 3, proposing to acquire lands mentioned, therein including the case land for public purpose to enable the writ-respondent No. 5 to set up an export- oriented industry inviting objections from the affected persons against such acquisition. The writ- petitioners filed objection on 15-7-1990 to the Deputy Commissioner. The Deputy Commissioner thereafter on due hearing of the objections submitted the record of the proceedings held by him to the Divisional Commissioner, Chittagong along with his report for his decision. The Divisional Commissioner thereupon on due consideration of the report together with the objections of the writ- petitioners gave his decision in favour of acquisition of the said land as contemplated under section 5 of the said Ordinance after rejecting the objections. The Deputy Commissioner thereafter issued a public notice under section 6 dated 2-3-1991 intimating the said decision of the Divisional Commissioner, inviting claims for compensation from all the concerned including the writ petitioners.

35. The writ-petitioners, in response thereto, submitted their objection dated 22-10-1991 to the Ministry of Land pointing out for the first time that the writ-respondent No. 5 had their own land measuring 3.49 acres across the Dhaka-Chittagong Highway which is close to the acquired land, with a request not to acquire their land. Their objection was rejected on due enquiry. The writ-respondent No.5 thereupon deposited compensation money to the Government, as per the estimate furnished by the Government and thereafter the Deputy Commissioner arranged for payment of compensation to the affected. All the concerned received the compensation money for their land but the writ-petitioners refused to receive compensation for the case land. Accordingly, the compensation money has been kept in the public account of the Republic. The case land, consequently, finally stood acquired and vested in the Government and the Government there- after handed over possession of the same to the writ-respondent No.5 on 2-12-1991 and the Deputy Commissioner then published a declaration of the acquisition of the case land and other land in the official Gazette on 31-12-1992. The writ-petitioners then filed Writ Petition No. 5392 of 1996 after 2 years and Writ Petition No. 576 of 1998 after 7 years of the final vesting of the case land to the Government on publication of the said official Gazette.

<u>36. A property is said to be needed for public purpose or in the public interest when it is acquisitioned in furtherance of the general interest of the community as opposed to the particular interest of the individuals. When the Divisional Commissioner makes a decision for acquisition of a property under section 5(1) of the Ordinance such decision is conclusive evidence that the property is needed for public purpose or in the public interest. In this view of the legal position and when it could not be established by the writ-petitioners that payment of compensation was withheld by the Government after the decision of acquisition of the case land was made or taken by the Divisional Commissioner the proceedings of the said LA Case No.1 of 1990-91 shall not abate. The case of Alauddin Khandker vs Secretary, Ministry of Land, 4 BLC (AD) 25 may be profitably referred to in this regard.</u>

<u>37. Since in the present case, the case land was finally vested in the Government on publication of the official Gazette under section 11, the filing of the said two writ-petitions challenging the acquisition proceeding in question was abortive, ineffectual and meaningless, inasmuch as such inordinate delay in filing the writ-petitions disentitled the writ-petitioners relief sought for. In fact, the writ-Court erred in entertaining such delayed writ-petitions, inasmuch as the rights which accrued to the Government and the writ-respondent No.5 by reason of such delay were not liable to be disturbed and interfered with; case of Bangladesh vs Golam Azam 46 DLR (AD) 192 can be cited on the point.</u>

<u>38. Now the only pertinent question that falls for consideration is, whether the acquisition under consideration is malafide. The answer to this question depends on whether the case land was acquisitioned despite the fact that the writ-respondent No.5 has sufficient quantum of land in the neighbourhood of the case land. It is already noticed that the writ-petitioners did not make this allegation in their written objection to the notices issued under section 3 as well as under section 6 by the Deputy Commissioner. They only made a belated objection on 22-10-1991 in this regard to the Ministry of Land, much after the decision was taken by the Divisional Commissioner for acquisition of the case land. Moreover, the writ-petitioners could not establish the allegation about the existence of any land of the writ-respondent No. 5 in or about the vicinity of the acquired land by producing any authentic or official document when the writ-respondent No. 5 denied the same. It is therefore, clear that the allegation of the malafide acquisition stands disproved. On the other hand, in the face of denial of this allegation by the writ-respondent No.5 the writ-petitions under reference could be said to have involved disputed question of fact making the writ-petitions not maintainable.</u>

<u>39. It is already noticed that the acquisition proceeding in the present case already reached its finality with the case land vested in the Government long before the said writ petitions were filed. Now even after this if the writ-respondent No. 5 is allegedly found to have failed to utilise or use the case land for the purpose it was acquired, the Court cannot provide any relief by way of restoration of possession of the case land to the writ-petitioners by setting aside the acquisition proceeding which acquisition was long complete and legally made. When any land is otherwise validly acquisitioned such acquisition cannot be interfered with, except on the ground that the acquisition was malafide and/or compensation for the land was not paid. No such case has been made out by the writ-petitioners. In a case where it is established that the requiring body has failed to use or utilise the acquired land for the purpose it was acquired the Government can make the requiring body surrender such land to the Deputy Commissioner and, in that case, on the application made by the real owners of the land, the Government in its discretion may restore possession of such land to them.</u>

In view of the foregoing discussions the appeals are allowed without any order as to costs.

Md Abdul Matin J : I agree with the judgment proposed to be delivered by my learned brother Md Joynul Abedin J.

Order of the Court:

These appeals are allowed by majority Judgment.

End.

full_judgment:
Md Awlad Ali J: This Rule issued under section 115(4) of the Code of Civil Procedure against the order dated 14-5-2005 passed by the District Judge Chittagong was initially heard by a Division Bench comprising Mr Justice ABM Khairul Haque and Mr Justice ATM Fazle Kabir and a preliminary question of law arose as to the maintainability of revisional application before the District Judge against an order passed by the Subordinate Judgment suit the valuation of which is 3,77,61,255 and the said Bench in view of the conflicting decisions given by other Benches referred the case to the Hon'ble Chief Justice for constitution of a larger Bench and the Hon'ble Chief Justice constituted this full Bench in accordance with the provision of rule 4 of Chapter VII of the High Court Rules for final decision.

2. The questions as formulated by the Court referring the case at the time of hearing of the Rule are, (1) Whether the pecuniary jurisdiction of the District Judge under section 115(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure is unlimited, if not, (2) Whether the High Court Division, under section 115(1) of the Code can entertain revisional application bearing valuation of more than Taka 5 lac, in respect of Orders passed by the Joint District Judges."

3. The background and the facts from which the questions arose are that the petitioner in the revision case instituted a suit being Other Suit No. 96 of 2003 on 3-6-2003 in the Second Court of Joint District Judge, Chittagong against the opposite party Nos. 1-8 praying for declaration of title in the suit properties. In the suit in pursuance of an application the defendant opposite party No.9 was impleaded as defendant by an order dated 13-2-2005 and the said defendant began to interfere with the possession of the plaintiff and, as such, an application was filed on behalf of the plaintiffs praying for an order of temporary injunction, and until hearing of the said application, prayed for ad interim order of injunction. The learned Joint District Judge by his order No. 56 dated 27-2-2005 issued notice upon the defendant opposite party No. 9 to show cause as to why injunction shall not be granted and since no ad interim order was passed another application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure was moved on 6-3-2005 praying for an order restraining the said defendant from interfering with the possession or otherwise dispossessing the tenants of the plaintiff-petitioners from the disputed property, but the learned Joint District Judge after hearing the petitioner by his order dated 6-3-2003 fixed the date of hearing of the said application on 12-3-2005. Being aggrieved by the order dated 27-2-2005 and 6-3-2005 the plaintiff petitioners preferred a revisional application under section 115(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure in the Court of District Judge, Chittagong, but the learned District Judge by his order dated 14-5-2005 without entering into the merit of the revisional application rejected the application holding that since the valuation of the suit is above 5 lac Taka he does not have the pecuniary jurisdiction to entertain the revisional application under section 115(2) of the CPC. The petitioners being aggrieved by the order dated 14-5-2005 passed by the learned District Judge moved this court and obtained the Rule.

4. The defendant opposite party No.9 filed a counter-affidavit to oppose the Rule.

5. Mr Rafique-ul-Huq, at the very outset of the hearing of the Rule issued under section 115(4) of the Code of Civil Procedure brought to the notice of the referring court two judgments one passed in Civil Order No. 1105 of 2005 dated 5-4-2005 and the other one in Civil Order No. 2345 of 2005 passed on 2-7-2005. In Civil Order No. 1105, a Division Bench took the view that under the amended section 115(2) of the Code, a revisional application valued above 5 lac Taka is not maintainable before the District Judge, rather the High Court is a proper forum under section 115(1) of the Code to dispose of such revisional application. A conflicting view was taken by another Division Bench presided over by Mr Justice Md Arayesuddin and it was held by that Bench that since no valuation has been mentioned in any of the provisions of section 115 of the Code, the revisional application with the valuation of any amount, would lie before the District Judge under section 115(2) against an order passed by a Joint District Judge from which no appeal lies. In view of the above conflicting decisions, Mr Rafique-ul Huq submitted that the matter should be referred to the Hon'ble Chief Justice for forming a larger Bench to consider the question of pecuniary jurisdiction of the District Judge under section 115(2) of the Code. After hearing Mr Huq, the learned Counsel for the petitioners and Mr Shafique Ahmed who appeared on behalf of the opposite parties submitted that in view of the words "from which no appeal lies" the question of valuation is immaterial and, relying on the decision in Civil Order No. 2345 of 2005, he concluded that all revisional applications irrespective of the valuation are maintainable before the District Judge and the reference to the Hon'ble Chief Justice to constitute a larger Bench will only cause delay in disposal of the revisional application. The concluding portion of the order dated 14-5- 2005 passed by the learned District Judge Chittagong is to the following effect: "So, since this Revisional application arose out of a suit which was valued for Taka 3,77,61,225 and exceeds pecuniary jurisdiction of Taka 5,00,000 of the District Judge in which the District Judge has no appellate jurisdiction, this Civil Revision is not maintainable".

6. The Bench referring the case observed that the question of jurisdiction of the Court has to be decided at the earliest opportunity and referred to section 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure which is in the following terms:

"Save insofar as is otherwise expressly provided nothing herein contained shall operate to give any Courts jurisdiction over suits the amount or value of the subject matter of which exceeds the pecuniary limits (if any) of its ordinary jurisdiction".

Then observed that since the suit is valued at much above Taka 5 lac then the revisional application can only be. disposed of by a Court which has got the necessary pecuniary Jurisdiction. It has been further observed by the referring Bench that sub-section (1) of section l is does not empower the High Court Division to call for the records in connection with an 'order' passed by the Joint District Judge, since the provision does not include an 'order' passed by the Joint District Judge"

7. We have noticed from the submissions of the learned Counsel for the petitioners that two Division Benches, one presided over by Mr Justice Syed Amirul Islam and another presided over Mr Justice Md Abdul Quddus took the view that the District Judge cannot entertain any revisional application under section 115(2) of the Code beyond its pecuniary jurisdiction which is fixed at 5 lac Taka being the appellate jurisdiction. In the judgment of Civil Revision No. 3318 of 2004 dated 31-7-2005 in the case of Joysna Ara Amin and others vs Sudhangshu Bimal Dhar and others. Mr Justice Syed Amirul Islam sitting with Mr Justice Sheikh Abdul Awal, considering the relevant provisions of the Civil Courts Act, 1887 and the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure, observed that the court which is not invested with appellate power cannot also exercise revisional power. Only that court which has appellate jurisdiction can exercise revisional power as per law. It has further been observed that in view of the provision of section 115(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure there is nothing in the sub-section expressly providing that a revision will lie against an order of a Joint District Judge before the District Judge irrespective of the value of the subject matter of the suit or proceeding pending in the Court of Joint District Judge where ordinarily suit or proceeding of unlimited valuation are filed. It has been further. observed that always revisional forum has been determined with reference to the pecuniary jurisdiction of the appellate court. The District Judge can exercise his power of revision under section 115(2) of the Code where his pecuniary jurisdiction in revisional matter is co-extensive with that of his appellate jurisdiction. The conclusion drawn by their Lordships is that the learned District Judge cannot entertain an application under section 115(2) of the Code beyond its pecuniary jurisdiction which is fixed for appellate jurisdiction.

8. Another Division Bench presided over by Mr Justice Md Abdul Quddus in Civil Order No. 1105 of 2005 by Judgment dated 5-4-2005 again considering the provision of section 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure and section 115(2) of the Code expressed the view that Civil Revision against an order of Joint District Judge in a suit or proceeding pending before it the value of the subject matter of which is above and beyond Taka 5 lac being the pecuniary jurisdiction of District Judge can never be preferred in the court of District Judge without any express provision in that regard being provided in the amended section 115(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure.

9. Conflicting decision was given by a Division Bench comprising Mr Justice Md Arayesuddin and Mr Justice SM Emdadul Hoque in the Judgment dated 2-7-2005 in Civil Order No. 2345 of 2005 and their Lordships expressed the view that in view of the 3rd amendment of the Code of Civil Procedure (Act No. 40 of 2003) the learned District Judge under section 115(2) of the Code has been empowered to entertain revisional application against the order passed by the Joint District Judge, Senior Assistant Judge from which no appeal lies. In this regard no pecuniary jurisdiction has been maintained in the aforesaid Act.

10. For proper elucidation of section 115( 1) and (2) of the Code of Civil Procedure as amended by the Code of Civil Procedure (Third Amendment) Act, 2003 and in determining the revisional jurisdiction of the District Judge with reference to other provision of law namely, Civil Courts Act, 1887 as amended, the Suit Valuation Act and the provision of the Civil Procedure Code, we reproduce sub-section (1) and (2) of section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure which reads as follows:

"115 Revision (1) The High Court Division may, on the application of any party aggrieved, call for the record of any suit or proceeding in which a decree or an order has been passed by a Court of District Judge or Additional District Judge or a decree has been passed by a Court of Joint District Judge, Senior Assistant Judge or Assistant Judge from which no appeal lies; and if such Court appears to have committed any error of law resulting in an error in such decree or order occasioning failure of justice, the High Court Division may, revise such decree or order and, make such order in the suit or proceeding as it thinks fit.

(2) The Court of District Judge may, on the application of any party aggrieved, call for the record of any suit or proceeding in which an order has been passed by a Court of Joint District Judge, Senior Assistant Judge or Assistant Judge from which no appeal lies; and if such Court appears to have committed any error of law resulting in an error in such order occasioning failure of justice, the Court of District Judge may, revise such order and, make such order as it think fit".

11. We need to discuss firstly, certain provisions of the Civil Courts Act, 1887 as amended by the Civil Courts (Amendment) Act, 2001.

Section 19. Extent of Jurisdiction of Senior Assistant Judge, etc Save as otherwise provided by any enactment for the time being in force, the jurisdiction of a Senior Assistant Judge and Assistant Judge shall extend to all suits of which the value does not exceed four lac taka and two lac taka respectively.

Section 21(1)Save as aforesaid, an appeal from a decree or order of a Joint District Judge shall lie-

(a) to the District Judge where the value of the original suit in which or in any proceeding arising out of which the decree or order was made did not exceed five lac Taka, and

(b) to the High Court Division in any other case.

(2) Save as aforesaid and appeal from a decree or order of Senior Assistant Judge or Assistant Judge shall lie to the District Judge.

12. Section 19 of the Civil Courts Act provides for the pecuniary jurisdiction of Senior Assistant Judge and Assistant Judge in respect of suit. Sub-section 2 of section 21 indicates that an appeal shall lie to the District Judge against a decree or order passed by the Senior Assistant Judge or Assistant Judge. Order as employed in sub-section (2) implies appealable order as contemplated under Order XLIII, rule (1) of the Code of Civil Procedure or any order passed in any proceeding like pre-emption proceeding. Suits or proceedings of which the vahie exceeds four lac Taka will lie to the Joint District Judge having unlimited pecuniary jurisdiction. But, according to the provision of sub-section (1) of section 21 appeal from a decree or order passed by the Joint District Judge will lie to the District Judge in which the value of the original suit or proceeding did not exceed Taka five lac. Therefore, in a suit filed before the Joint District Judge the value of which does not exceed five lac Taka, if a decree or order, as the case may be is passed appeal will lie to the District Judge. As per Clause (b) of sub-section (1) of section 21 appeal will lie to the High Court Division in any other cases i.e. when the value does exceed Taka 5 lac.

13. Incidentally, it may be mentioned that the District Judge and the Joint District Judge have equal pecuniary jurisdiction over all original suits cognisable by the Civil Courts save as otherwise provided by any enactment yet suits shall be instituted in the court of the lowest grade competent to try them as indicated in section 15 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

14. Section 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure, as we have already noted, indicates the pecuniary jurisdiction of any Court over suits. Therefore, the pecuniary value will determine the forum and the jurisdiction over the subject matter of' the proceedings in the Civil jurisdiction. Importantly, section 6 of the Civil Procedure Code is inextricably linked to section 8 of the Suit Valuation Act, 1887 which is as under:

"8. Court Fee value and Jurisdictional value to be the same in certain suits-Where the suits other than those referred to the Court Fees Act 1870 (VII of 1870), section 7, Paragraphs (v), (vi) and (ix) and paragraph (x) clause (d), Court Fees are payable ad valorem under the Court Fees Act, 1870 the value as determinable for the computation of court-fees and the value for purposes of jurisdiction shall be the same."

15. the above provision indicates that the value for the purpose of jurisdiction and Court-Fees should be same.

16. With advantage, we may also .refer to section II of the Suit Valuation Act, 1887 where provisions have been made in respect of procedure where objection is taken on appeal or revision that a suit or appeal was not properly valued for jurisdictional purposes. And it is indicated there that the objection as to the valuation for jurisdictional purposes shall be taken at the first instance, and such objection as regards valuation for jurisdictional purpose can also be taken in revisional jurisdiction under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

<u>17. Reading section 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure, sections 8 and 11 of the Suit Valuation Act and the relevant provisions of the Civil Courts Act as stated above the conclusion would follow that the value of the suit or proceeding would conclusively determine the forum where a suit or proceeding will be filed and tried and the appeal will be heard and disposed of Thus the forum of appeal is to be determined according to the value of the suit or proceeding and the value of appeal consequently will lead to the revisional forum and jurisdiction and that would be the basis for determining revisional forum.</u>

18. The provision of sub-section (1) of section 115 is not our concern as from the plain reading it would appear that the power is the revisional power of the High Court Division. But the question has arisen as to whether the High Court Division under sub-section (1) is empowered to call for the records in connection with an "order" passed by the Joint District Judge, since the provision does not include the 'order' passed by the Joint District Judge.

<u>19. Mr Rafique-ul-Huq, has pointed out that under the original section 115 and also in the amended section 115(1) and (2) as introduced by the Law Reforms Ordinance, 1978, the words by any court subordinate to the High Court Division were employed, which have been omitted in the newly enacted sub-sections (1) and (2) of section 115 of the Code and thereby confusion has been created about the power of the High Court Division in calling for the records of any suit or proceeding in which an order has been passed by a Court of Joint District Judge. Although some of the Courts including the Courts of Additional District Judge and Joint District Judge are subordinate to the District Judge but all the courts are undoubtedly, subordinate to the High Court Division under the Constitutional Scheme (Articles 109 and 114 of the Constitution) and in view of the provision of section 9 of the Civil Courts Act, 1887 and some provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure. Therefore, in a proper case the High Court Division, in exercise of the power of superintendence and control, may call for the records of any suit or proceeding in which an order has been passed by a Court of Joint District Judge, particularly when the value of the suit or proceeding is above five lac Taka, and that against an order passed by the Joint District Judge in a suit or proceeding the value of which exceeds Taka four lac but does not exceed Taka 5 lac revision will be to the District Judge.</u>

<u>20. Section 115(2) was enacted by the Code of Civil Procedure (Third Amendment) Act, 2003 to prevent the overflowing effect of revision cases in the High Court Division in Civil Jurisdiction and to obviate the sufferings of the litigants. But in enacting such provision the legislature has not expressly amended the other provisions of law such as section 6 of the Code, the provisions of Civil Courts Act and the Suit Valuation Act and the effect of those provisions remained unaffected after the introduction of sub-section (2) of section 115. Therefore, unless specific rules to the contrary have been framed the revisional jurisdiction must be determined according to the value of the suit or proceeding. The Courts having jurisdiction to entertain an appeal shall have jurisdiction on revisional application as per valuation of the original suit or proceeding. In the instant case, the plaintiff valued the suit at Taka 3,77,61,225 and the order proposed to be revised was passed by the Joint District Judge, and a revisional application was taken to the District Judge and the learned District Judge rejected the application summarily by his order dated 14-5-2005 on the ground of pecuniary jurisdiction. In view of our above discussion, the learned District Judge rightly turned down the revisional application.</u>

21. Besides the order as aforesaid, which is revisable by the High Court Division, some other orders passed by the Joint District Judge may be revised by the High Court Division, as for instance, an order of temporary injunction is or has been passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, or the Assistant Judge as the case may be against that order an appeal will lie to the District Judge and if such appeal is transferred to the Joint District Judge and the appeal is heard and disposed of by the Joint District Judge, judgment or order in such appeal is to be understood as judgment or order passed by the District Judge. Therefore, appeal arising out of an order filed before the District Judge transferred to the Joint District Judge for disposal, the Joint District Judge exercises the power of the District Judge in such appeal. District Judge and Joint District Judge in such case exercises concurrent jurisdiction. In this regard section 22 of the Civil Courts Act, 1887 is relevant which is in the following terms:

"22(1) A District Judge may transfer to any Joint District Judge under his Administrative Control any appeals pending before him from the decree or orders of Assistant Judges.

(2)……………..

(3) Appeals transferred under this section shall be disposed of subject to the rules applicable to like appeals when disposed of by the District Judge.

22. Similar power is exercised by the District Judge under section 24 of the Code of Civil Procedure. It is provided under that section that on the application of may of the parties or of its own motion the District Court may at any stage transfer any suit, appeal or other proceedings before it for trial or disposal to any court subordinate to it and competent to try or dispose of the same.

23. Considering the above provision, the proposition has been settled in the case of Mohammad Eshaque vs Ruhul Amin and others reported in 34 DLR 342 and 33 DLR 141, Abdus Salam vs Bangladesh.

Ordinarily the forum choice is dependent on the pecuniary value of the subject matter of suits or proceedings unless there is contrary provision. Procedure for filing revisional application will require the petitioner to state the value of the suit from which it arises.

24. In the "note" of Chapter 11 of Part 1 of the High Court Rules, it has been stated that "Every memorandum of appeal from orders and every application for revision should state the value of the suit from which it arises".

25. In the absence of any prescribed rules or procedure for filing revisional application before the District Judge the aforesaid provision may be the guideline for presenting a revisional application before the District Judge, under section 115(2) of the Code.

<u>26. In view of our above discussions the question No. 1 as formulated by the court referring the case is answered in the negative i.e. the District Judge has not unlimited pecuniary jurisdiction in entertaining revisional application under section 115(2) of the Code. The Second question is answered in the affirmative. The High Court Division under section 115(1) of the Code can entertain revisional application against the order passed by the Joint District Judges in a suit or proceeding the value of which is more than Taka five lac in exercise of the power of Superintendence and Control over the Subordinate Courts.</u>

27. Therefore, the revisional application under section 115(2) against the orders dated 27-2-05 and 6-3-05 filed before the District Judge, Chittagong was not maintainable. The consequence would follow that the Rule issued under section 115(4) of the Code of Civil Procedure against the order dated 14-5-2005 passed by the learned District Judge will be discharged. The petitioner may however, bring an application under section 115(1) of the Code before the High Court Division against the order of the Joint District Judge, if so advised.

28. The reference is thus disposed of.

A copy of this judgment may be sent to the concerned Ministries.

End.

Vs.
Social Investment Bank Ltd and others ------- Respondents
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 11th December, 2001 passed by the High Court Division in Matter No. 78 and 86 of 2001).
full_judgment:
Md FazluI Karim J : These appeals by leave arose out of the impugned judgment and order dated 11th December, 2001 passed by the learned Company Judge of the High Court Division dismissing the Company Matter Nos.79 and 86 of2001 holding the same to be not maintainable in the Company Court rejecting an application for direction upon the respondents to serve notice of Board meeting to the appellants-Directors in compliance of section 95 of the Companies Act, 1994 to enable the appellants to attend the meeting of the Board of Directors of the respondent No.1 Social Investment Bank Ltd. The appeals involve same question of law on the self- same fact and disposed of by the same judgment by the High Court Division, and have been taken up together for hearing and accordingly, disposed of by this single judgment.

2. The facts relevant for disposal of these appeals are as under:

The said applications were filed in the High Court Division stating, inter alia, that the Social Investment Bank Ltd. hereinafter called "the Bank" was incorporated under the Companies Act with 4 types of directors namely, Group-A Bangladesh sponsor directors, Group-B foreign sponsor directors, Group C Government nominated directors and Group-D member of general public. The Bank had four foreign sponsor-directors in Group B, who live outside Bangladesh namely, Mr Ahmed Saleh Jamjoom, Mr Md Aminuddin, Dr Abdullah Omar Naseef and Dr Hamid Al Gabid holding shares at 7592, 4492, 449 and 1997 respectively. At present the Bank has three foreign sponsor-directors in Group-B namely, Mr Ahmed Saleh Jamjoom, Mr Abdullah Omar Naseef and Dr Hamid-al-Gabid who were re-elected as directors in the 5th Annual General Meeting of SIBL held on 1st August, 2000. In the said Annual General Meeting it was resolved that the Board of Directors would nominate 5 persons to represent the said foreign sponsor-directors as alternate directors (Annexures B, B-1). Accordingly, in the Board of Directors of the Bank the appellant No.1, Abdul Muhit, appellant No.2, Major (Rtd) Ekhtiar Hossain, appellant No.3 Dr Ataur Rahman Talukder, appellant No.4, Nargis Mannan and one Abul Bashar Bhuiyan were nominated to represent the original directors (Annexure C). Since then the appellants as alternate directors had been receiving notices for attending meetings of Board of Directors. But by four separate letters dated 8-5- 2001 the Bangladesh Bank directed the appellants under section 45 of the Banking Companies Act not to act as alternate directors (Annexures E, E-1, E-2 and E-3) and pursuant to that direction the Bank, the respondent No.1, also issued letters dated 9-5-2000 asking the appellants not to act as alternates to foreign directors (Annexures F to F-3). Being aggrieved by the said letters of Bangladesh Bank dated 8-5-2001 and of the Bank dated 9-5-2001 the appellants separately filed writ petition Nos. 1889 of 2001,1873 of 2001, 1872 of 2001 and 1871 of 2001 and obtained Rules and ad-interim orders staying the operation of Bangladesh Bank's letters dated 8- 5-2001 but no stay was given against the letters of the Bank (Annexures G, G-1, G-2 and G 3) pending hearing of the Rule. On the basis of the stay order in the aforesaid writ petitions, two Board Meetings of the Bank were held on 8-7-2001 and 11-7-2001 without giving any notice to the appellants. The appellants, however, managed to obtain copies of the said notice (Annexures H and I). Despite the Court's order of stay, the Bank at the initiative of its present Chairman illegally called 64th Board Meeting on 8-7-2001 (Annexure J) and in that meeting a resolution was adopted to cancel the directorship of the aforesaid original directors. Upon receiving the information about holding of the Board Meeting on 8-7-2001, the appellants went to attend the meeting but the Chairman of the Bank did not allow them to attend it. Thereafter, the appellants separately moved Contempt Petition Nos. 73, 74, 75 and 72 of 2001 against the respondents for violating the order of stay dated 21-6-2001 and Rules were issued directing the Chairman and Managing Director of the Bank to show cause as to why contempt proceedings should not be drawn up against them (Annexures K, K-1, K-2 and K-3). The respondents again called a meeting of the Board of Directors on 25-8-2001 without giving notices to the appellants, though they were entitled to such a notice as the Bangladesh Bank's direction has been stayed by an order of the Court. Therefore, the appellants moved this application on the last day before summer vacation and the matter was admitted. By an order dated 23-8-2001 the Court stayed the meeting of the Board of Directors of the Bank scheduled to be held on 25-8-2001 and all other meetings to be held later on.

3. In Matter No.78 of 2001 an application was filed under section 95 read with section 233 of the Companies Act for allowing the appellants to attend the meeting of the Board of Directors and in Matter No. 86 of 2001 the application was filed under section 95 read with Article 72 of the Memorandum of Articles of Association.

4. The matters have been contested by respondents stating, inter alia, that the Directors of the Bank are not classified into four groups as contended by the appellants. All the four foreigners mentioned in the petition are no longer directors of the Bank as they have vacated their office by reason of absence from Board meetings for a continuous period of three months and/or for not attending three consecutive Board meetings under section 108 of the Companies Act, 1994 read with Article 82 of the Articles of Association of the Bank. The office of the above mentioned directors falling vacant was confirmed in a resolution at the 64th Board meeting of the Bank held on 8-7-2001 (Annexure J). Consequently, the appointment of the appellants as alternate directors are no longer valid. Section 101 (2) of the Companies Act provides that an alternate director appointed under sub-section (1) shall not hold office for a period longer than that permissible to the original director in whose place he has been appointed and shall vacate the office. Sub-section (3) further provides that if the term of the original directors is determined, any provision for reappointment of retiring directors in default of another appointment, shall apply to the original and not to the alternate directors. The last Annual General Meeting in which the original directors retired and got re-elected was held on 1-8-2000 but there was no authorisation from the original directors for the appellants to act as alternate directors for them. The appellants also by letter dated 3-12-2000 admitted that they have been holding the appointment as alternate directors for the original directors since 1997 on the basis of letter issued in the year 1997 (Annexures X, XI, X2 & X3). Since there was no fresh nomination from the original directors in favour of the appellants after their election as directors there was no appointment of the appellants as alternate directors. The Annual General Meeting has no authority under the law and the Articles of Association to appoint alternative directors and as such the proceeding of the AGM held on 1-8-2000 is to that extent ultra vires the section 101 of the Companies Act. There was no need for such a resolution to be passed in the AGM as the Articles have authorised the Board to appoint an alternate director for a director who is absent for more than 3 months. Therefore, the Board resolution dated 1-8-2000 in respect of appointment of alternate directors is not valid. It was merely a rectification of the appointment of alternate directors by the Annual General Meeting, which had no authority to make such an appointment. In the circumstances, by the retirement and the re-election of the original directors at the 5th Annual General Meeting the alternate directors were not automatically re-appointed.

5. The learned Company Judge rejected the application with direction:

"that the Companies Act specifically provided the jurisdiction of the Company Court to be applied under specific provisions the Court does not have any general, plenary or residuary jurisdiction to deal with other matters and questions arising under the Companies Act. Section 95 does not specifically provide jurisdiction to this Court. Therefore, the only remedy available to the petitioners is the Civil Court and not this Court."

6. Leave was granted upon the submission of the learned Counsel as to whether considering the applications made to the Company Court under the substantive provision of the Companies Act, the Company Court is entitled to exercise its inherent jurisdiction wherever there is manifest breach of law and Article to prevent injustice and the provisions of the Companies Act are not subservient to proceedings in any other forum and pendency of civil litigation is held to be no bar to initiate proceedings under the Companies Act, inasmuch as section 3 of the Companies Act has not barred rather gives certain jurisdiction to the High Court in order to resolve dispute under the Companies Act under its original jurisdiction. Though section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure gives jurisdiction to Civil Court to try all civil disputes unless they are expressly or impliedly barred but in view of the provision of section 3 of the Companies Act direction by the Company Court could be given to enforce the provision of section 95 of the Companies Act to resolve the dispute which is not a civil dispute but to enforce the said provision under inherent jurisdiction, inasmuch, as the said dispute not being a civil dispute has not barred the jurisdiction of the Company Court.

7. Mr Shafique Ahmed, the learned Counsel appearing for the appellants, has submitted with reference to the order granting leave that the right that has been sought to be enforced in an application under section 95 of the Companies Act is a right conferred by the Companies Act i.e., a right secured to the director under the Act to get a notice of the Board's meeting and if the same is denied the appellant has right to move the High Court Division to vindicate his right, inasmuch as section 95 of the Companies Act specifically provides that the High Court Division unless otherwise provided by gazette notification the dispute not being a civil dispute the Court could direct issuance of a notice which the appellant is entitled in law, the learned Judge of the High Court Division erred in law in holding that these applications are not maintainable before the Company Court, inasmuch as the Court lost sight of inherent jurisdiction to see compliance or due observance of mandatory provision of Companies Act while considering the application made to it under section 95, a substantive provision of the Company Act.

8. Mr Rafique-ul-Huq, the learned Counsel appearing for the respondents, has however, submitted that the issuance of a notice under section 95 of the Companies Act not being a substantive provision of the Companies Act and there is no reference to the Court i.e., the High Court Division, for enforcement of the right to receive the notice, the Company Court could not exercise its inherent jurisdiction.

The learned Counsel has further submitted that section 95 of the Companies Act is not an enactment conferring jurisdiction on the High Court Division like other sections in the Companies Act providing for resort to the Court i.e., the High Court Division, and, as such, could not invoke the said provision or complaint regarding non-compliance of the provision of section 95 of the Companies Act.

9. As regards the provision under section 95 of the Companies Act providing notice to be given is a right to be enforced by or/under section 95 of the Companies Act by resorting to the jurisdiction of the High Court Division or on the Civil Court, the learned Counsel for the appellants has referred to a decision in the case of British India Corporation vs Robert Menzies reported in 1936 Company Cases 250 wherein a special Bench held that "the Courts referred in section 3 of the Companies Act have inherent jurisdiction to compel due observance of the mandatory provisions of the Act and thus the Company Judge, therefore, can order a company to deliver to a shareholder a copy of its register of members on payment of copying charges even though there is no express provision in the Companies Act authorising the Court to make such an order".

10. The learned Counsel has referred to a decision in the case of Kishore Y Patel vs Patel Engineering Co Ltd reported in AIR 1992 Bombay 114 wherein it has been held that Rule 9 of Companies (Court) Rules 1959 has to be interpreted in the light of the enabling provision of section 643 of the Act. While considering applications made to the Company Court under the substantive provisions of the Act, the Company Court is entitled to mould the relief and exercise its inherent jurisdiction whenever found necessary to prevent injustice.

11. Mr Rafique-ul-Huq, the learned Counsel appearing for the respondents, has, however, submitted that the application under section 95 of the Companies Act is not a substantive one but a procedural one and with reference to rule 10 of the Companies Rules providing for substantive provision authorising the Court to assume jurisdiction to decide the disputes, inasmuch as sub-section (3) of section 233 of the Companies Act provided that the remedy sought could be given by the Court under section 2D of the Companies Act but the learned Judges have lost sight of the said provision in the case of British India Corporation Co vs Menzies that under section 95 of the Companies Act, no inherent power could be resorted to even for any relief by the Company Judge, for the Company Court could not invoke the provision of section \5\ of the Code of Civil Procedure regarding enforcement of the provision of section 95 itself.

12. Mr Rafiq-ul-Huq has next submitted that section 3 of the Companies Act mentioned about the Court having power under its statutory jurisdiction and referred to a decision in the case of Dhaka Jute Mills Ltd vs Satish Chandra Banik reported in 19 DLR 735 which arose out of an application under sections 76(3) and 79(3) of the Companies Act wherein it has been held that the High Court Division does not exercise any ordinary original civil jurisdiction and cases under the Companies Act are decided by way of special statutory jurisdiction conferred upon the High Court Division by the Act itself and it would be misnomer to describe such jurisdiction as ordinary original civil jurisdiction.

13. Mr Rafique-ul-Huq has next referred to a decision in the case of Md Shamsuzzaman Khan vs MS Islam reported in 28 DLR 101 and submitted that section 3 of the Companies Act only gives certain jurisdiction to the High Court for resolution of the disputes under Companies Act under its original jurisdiction and section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure has expressly provided that all civil disputes should be tired by civil Courts unless the jurisdiction is expressly or impliedly barred and in that view of the matter the relief under section 95 of the Companies Act cannot be grounded on any provision under the Companies Act in order to take the dispute to the jurisdiction of the company Court and has relied also upon a decision in the case of Chahia Fibre Co vs Abdul Jabbar reported in 20 DLR (SC) 335 wherein Mr Hamoodur Rahman, J as his Lordship then was, stated that:

''It is a well settled rule that the ouster of jurisdiction of a civil Court in respect of a civil suit is not to be readly inferred. Unless that jurisdiction has been either expressly or impliedly taken away by some other law it will continue to vest in the civil Court."

14. Section 2(a) of the Companies Act 1994 provides that the Court means the Court having jurisdiction under this Act. Section 3 of the Companies Act provides that the Court having jurisdiction under this Act shall be the High Court Division provided that the Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette and subject to such restrictions and conditions as it thinks fit, empower any District Court to exercise all or any of the jurisdictions by this Act conferred upon the Court, and in that case such District Court shall, as regard the jurisdiction so conferred, be the Court in respect of all companies having their registered office in the district.

15. Section 2(g) of the Companies Act 1994 provides that "District Court" means the Principal Civil Court of original jurisdiction in a district, but does not include the High Court Division in the exercise of its ordinary civil jurisdiction.

16. Even by analogy to Rule 9 of the Companies Rules 2000 which has not yet been given effect to which provides that :

"In all Courts having jurisdiction under this Act shall be kept and maintained a book called "The Register of Company Matters" in which shall be entered and numbered serially all applications made under sections 13, 15,41,43,59, 71,81,82,85,89,115,151,153,171,175,176, 193, 203, 228, 229, 230, 231, 233, 245, 248, 251, 253, 255, 258, 259, 261, 262, 263, 264, 265, 293, 294, 296, 299, 300, 301, 302, 303, 305, 309, 311, 312, 314, 316, 326, 328, 331, 333, 338, 339, 340, 342, 346, 349, 395, 396 and any other original proceeding under the Act in relation to a company."

17. The said Rule though has not yet been given effect to but goes to show that the jurisdiction arising out of any dispute regarding section 95 of the Companies Act is not conferred on the High Court Division but the dispute being a civil dispute the ordinary civil Court namely, District Court, has been vested with the jurisdiction.

<u>18. From the above discussion, it is clear that unless section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure bars the jurisdiction of the Civil Court expressly or impliedly under any enactment, the said provision gives jurisdiction to file a suit/litigation of any civil nature in any civil Court of competent jurisdiction. Thus section 95 of the Companies Act providing no forum thereunder, any dispute arising thereto is to be resolved as a civil dispute resorting to the ordinary civil Court of competent jurisdiction and, as such, the inherent jurisdiction under the Companies Act in the absence of any specific provision therein would not be invoked to enforce the provision of section 95 of the Companies Act, as the said provision is providing procedural matters only and not substitutive provision. It is also clear that under section 95 of the Companies Act, the High Court Division could not also invoke the provision of section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure sitting as a Company Court under the Companies Act, 1994.</u>

19. In view of the above, we do not find any substance in the submission of the learned Counsel for the appellants for our interference with the impugned order.

These appeals are accordingly, dismissed without any order as to costs.

End.

lawyer:
M Amir-ul Islam with Ms Tania Amir, Dr Shirin S Chaudhury and Shamsul Hasan, Advocates ----- For the Petitioners in WP Nos. 2120103, 2189103 
Abdul Baset Majumder with SB Bhandari, Advocates ----- For the Petitioner in WP No. 1978/03.
