parties:
Muhibur Rahman Manik and others ----- Petitioners
Vs
Bangladesh and others ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Md. Hamidul Haque, J: These Rules were issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why section 6 of Druto Bichar Tribunal Ain, (Act No. 28 of 2002) and the Notification vide SRO No. 38-Law/2003 so far it relates to the petitioners concerned should not be declared to be unconstitutional and void and also why the transfer of the cases of the petitioners to the Druto Bichar Tribunal should not be declared to have been done without lawful authority and is of no legal effect.

2. As in these three Rules, the vires of section 6 of Druta Bichar Tribunal Ain (hereinafter referred to as the Ain) has been challenged; all these Rules were heard together and now be governed by this single judgment.

3. In these Rules facts are not very much relevant. The petitioners of these writ petitions are accused in some cases. Their cases were transferred from the trial Courts to Druto Bichar Tribunal which was set up in view of the provisions of section 4 of the above Ain.

4. Mr. M. Amirul Islam, the learned Advocate appeared on behalf of the petitioners of WP Nos. 2120 and 2189 of 2003 and Mr. Abdul Baset Majumder, the learned Advocate appeared on behalf of the petitioners of WP No. 1978 of 2003. Their submissions are almost the same. However, let us start with the submissions of Mr Amirul Islam. Gist of his submission is that section 6 of the above Ain does not provide any principle or guideline for exercise of the power given to the Government under that section and, as such, in the absence of such guideline or any objective criterion, there is ample scope of discrimination between same classes of people and also a scope of exercising the power arbitrarily in transferring cases to Druto Bichar Tribunal. He has given much emphasis on the fact that the section confers unfettered power upon the Government to "pick and choose" any accused of a case for harassment and political victimisation and this power violates the equality clause as guaranteed under Article 27 of the Constitution.

5. Mr. Amirul Islam, in support of his argument, at first has taken us through the relevant section of the above Ain and thereafter cited two cases, one of Indian jurisdiction and another of our jurisdiction. First case cited by him is the case of State of West Bengal vs Anwar Ali and others as reported in AIR 1952 SC 75. The other case cited is the case of Waris Mea vs State reported in 9 DLR (SC) 117 He has taken us through both the cases and with reference to the case reported in AIR he has submitted that the principle laid down in that case fully applies in the instant cases before us. As he has given much emphasis on the case of the Indian Jurisdiction, let us first consider whether the principles laid down in that case have any manner of application in the instant cases before us. In AIR case, vires of section 5 of the West Bengal Special Courts Act, 1950 was challenged. Section 5 of that Act is quoted below:

"5(1) A Special Court shall try such offences or classes of offences or cases or classes of cases, as the State Government may by general or special order, in writing, direct.

(2) No direction shall be made under sub- section (1) for the trial of an offence for which an accused person was being tried at the commencement of this Act before any Court but, save as aforesaid, such direction may be made in respect of an offence, whether such offence was committed before or after the commencement of this Act."

6. It appears that respondent Anwar Ali of that case and 49 others were charged with various offences and the case was sent for trial by the Governor of West Bengal to the Special Court established under the above Act. The vires of the section was challenged on the ground that it was violative of the right of equal protection of law as enjoined under Article 14 of the Indian Constitution. It further appears from the judgment that the new Act laid down substantially different rules for trial of offences and cases than laid down in the Code of Criminal Procedure. So, the Court has observed that it deprived the respondents of the safeguard of the committal procedure and of the trial with the help of jury or assessors and it also deprived them of the right of "de novo" trial in case of transfer. By taking into consideration these departures from the procedure of trial as laid down in the Code of Criminal Procedure, their Lordships in the majority judgment. Held the view that the law violated the provision of Article 14 of the Constitution.

7. Mr. Amirul Islam tried to impress upon us that the principle laid down in the above case may be applied in the facts and circumstances of the present cases.

8. Let us now consider the case reported in 9 DLR (SC) 117. On perusal of this case we find that the vires of section 23(A) and 23(B) of the Foreign Exchange Regulations Act, 1947 was challenged on the ground that these sections has offended the provisions of Article 5 of the Constitution i.e., provisions relating to equality before law or equal protection under the law. We find that three forums were set up for the trial of the offenders under the Act, namely, (1) the Courts under the ordinary law (2) Adjudication officers and (3) Tribunals to pass sentence after trial of an offence under that Act. The vires of the sections was challenged mainly on the ground that the sections did not contain any guideline as to which class or classes of cases were to go before the court and which cases before the Tribunal and which cases before the Adjudication Officer. So, their Lordships found that those sections were unconstitutional and violative of the provisions of equality before law as contained in Article 5 of the Constitution. Mr Islam has argued that similar view may be taken in the instant cases before us because here also there is no guideline as to which cases can be transferred to the Tribunal.

9. Next, Mr. Islam has argued that transfer of the cases of the present petitioners to the Tribunal is malafide. He referred to ground no. III of Writ Petition No. 2120/03 and has submitted that the petitioner was a lawmaker in the Awami League Government and, as such, his case was transferred at the behest of the interested quarters only to victimise and harass him.

10. Mr. A. Baset Majumder, the learned Advocate who appeared on behalf of the writ petitioner in Writ Petition No. 1978/03 has also made similar submission that the transfer of case of the petitioners was malafide because transfer was made at the instance of a Minister of the area. So, he has argued that the power exercised by the Government in transferring the case of the petitioners was nothing but colourable exercise of power. The other arguments of Mr. Baset Majumder are similar to the arguments of Mr. Amirul Islam.

11. Mr. A.F. Hasan Ariff, the learned Attorney- General, appeared on behalf of the respondents. The learned Attorney General has submitted that the principles laid down in the case reported in AIR 1952 SC 75 and the case reported in 9 DLR (SC) 117 have no manner of application in the facts and circumstances of the present cases. At the very outset he has pointed out that procedure for trial now followed in the Courts where the cases were pending and the procedure for trial in the Druto Bichar Tribunal are basically the same and, as such, there is no reason for the petitioners to be apprehensive. He has emphasised on the point that by the transfer of the cases, the petitioners are not at all adversely affected or in any way prejudice. He has also referred to Article 35(3) of the Constitution and has submitted that every person accused of a criminal offence has a right to get speedy trial, According to him to ensure that right; the legislature enacted the above Ain. He has given emphasis on the point that an accused has a right to get speedy trial but he has no right to delay the trial. He clarified his argument by stating that in the normal criminal courts due to increase of the volume of cases and due to various other causes, sometimes 8/10 years are taken to conclude the trial of a case. So, according to him, there is no illegality or nothing wrong in the Ain itself, the purpose of which it is ensure speedy trial. He has also invited our attention to the fact that now it is a universally accepted idea that an accused should get speedy trial.

12. After submission of the learned Attorney- General, Mr. Amirul Islam made his last submission. According to him, right of transferring a case from one Court to another Court cannot be exercised by the Government or any executive authority. He has pointed out that such right has been given to the higher courts under different laws now in force. Next, he has given emphasis on the fact that it is the Government who chooses the cases, the Courts and the Judges. So, according to him, this unfettered power as given to the Government not only is violative of fundamental rights but it also amounts to interference with the conception of independence of judiciary. This law, according to Mr. Islam, has given a power to the Government to interfere with the criminal administration of justice in the country. In this connection, he also referred to section 15 of the Ain which, according to him, provides that if the Tribunal fails to conclude the trial within the time limit as provided in section 10, the Tribunal is to account for this failure to the Government. This, according to Mr Islam, is a naked interference in the Judiciary. According to him, the Tribunal is also under a constant fear that it is accountable to the Government.

13. We have perused the different sections of the Ain. However, to appreciate the arguments as advanced by the learned Advocates of both the parties, sections 5 and 6 are reproduced below:

‘৫।এখতিয়ার-সরকার, সরকারী গেজেটে প্রজ্ঞাপন দ্বারা, যে মামলা দ্রুত বিচার ট্রাইব্যুনালে স্থানান্তর করিবে শুধু সেই মামলাই এই ট্রাইব্যুনাল বিচার করিবে।

৬। মামলা “স্থানান্তর-সরকার, সরকারী গেজেটে প্রজ্ঞাপন দ্বারা, জনস্বার্থে, হত্যা, ধর্ষণ, আগ্নেয়াস্ত্র, বিস্ফোরক দ্রব্য মাদকদ্রব্য সংক্রান্ত অপরাধের বিচারাধীন কোন মামলা উহার যে কোন পর্যায়ে ক্ষেত্রেমত, দায়রা আদালত বা বিশেষ আদালত বা ম্যাজিস্ট্রেট আদালত হইতে বিচারের জন্য দ্রুত বিচার ট্রাইব্যুনালে “ স্থানান্তর করিতে পারিবে।”

14. Section 5 provides that only those cases which are transferred by Gazette Notification to a Tribunal are to be tried by the Tribunal and section 6 provides that cases relating to offences of murder, rape, firearms, explosive substances and drugs may be transferred by the Government in public interest by making a notification in the Gazette to a Tribunal from the Court of Sessions or Special Court or from a Court of Magistrate, as the case may be. So, from section 6 we find that a case which relates to the offences as mentioned in the section and pending for trial in the Courts as mentioned in the section may be transferred by the Government to a Tribunal.

15. Now, the most pertinent question is whether such transfer amounts to denial of the protection given to the citizens under Article 27 of the Constitution. Article 27 is similar to Article 14 of the Indian Constitution and Article 5 of the then Pakistan Constitution. We may mention here that Anwar Ali's case as reported in AIR 1952 was decided at the time when the original Code of Criminal Procedure was in force in India but thereafter so many amendments and changes were made in the Code in India. At that time there was committal procedure and trial by jury or by assessors. When these procedures were there in the Code, the Act of West Bengal Special Courts was enacted. Obviously, the Hon'ble Judges of the Supreme Court of India noticed the departures as contained in the new Act from the existing procedure for trial as was in force in the various provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Naturally, due to the departures, there was violation of equality clause because the persons who committed offences of same class had to face trial in two different forums under two separate procedures of trial. In one procedure, there was provision of committal procedure, trial by jury or assessors. In another procedure, the committal procedure and trial by jury or assessors were abolished.

16. Let us now consider the question whether petitioners will be treated differently from those accused of the same footing who will be tried by the Courts from which the cases of the petitioners were transferred to the Tribunal. If we find that there are major departures from the procedure of trial followed in those Courts, then the question of differential treatment will arise. We made a query to Mr Islam to point out what departures he could find. Mr Islam has pointed out three departures. With reference to section 9, he has pointed out that as regards the trial of the cases that section provides that the procedure as laid down in Chapter XX of the Code shall be followed whereas the same procedure relates to trial by Magistrates. He has also pointed out that sub-section (2) of section 9 provides that if the punishment does not exceed imprisonment for more than 7 years, the accused may be tried summarily under the provisions of Chapter XXII of the Code. Next, he has pointed out that photographs taken at the time of the occurrence or the recorded conversation have been made admissible in evidence under section 16 of the Ain.

<u>17. We have perused the whole Ain and we have found that even the departures as pointed out by Mr Islam have not in any way affected the rights of the present petitioners. It is true that in sub-section (I) of section 9. Chapter XX of the Code has been mentioned but the reference of Chapter XX cannot be considered as a departure affecting the rights of the petitioners. Moreover, we have noticed that in section 7 of the Ain it has been clearly mentioned that the Tribunal shall be deemed to be a Court of Session. When Tribunal shall be deemed to be a Court of Session it will act as a Court of Sessions. Section 17 clearly provides that the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure shall apply in respect of trial of a case in the Tribunal so far those are not inconsistent with any provisions of the Ain. The learned Advocate for the petitioners could not show any provision of the Ain which has in any way curtailed the right of the petitioners to get fair trial. Even we find from sub-section (3) of section 9 that the same procedure of granting bail which is applicable in the Court from whom the cases are transferred shall continue to apply in the Tribunal if an application for bail is made before that Tribunal. So, we find that no stringent provision has been incorporated in the new law even regarding bail.</u>

18. As regards section 16, we may say that the section only empowers that Tribunal to admit such evidence. In the Evidence Act or in the Code of Criminal Procedure, there is no bar to admission of such evidence. Moreover, from the proviso to section 16, it is clear that such evidence cannot be the basis for conviction.

<u>19. So, on perusal of the Ain itself we find that an accused whose case is transferred to the Tribunal will get similar opportunities to defend himself like an accused facing trial in the other Courts from where the cases were transferred to the Tribunal. However, we find that there is a departure in respect of time frame as given in the Ain from the time frame given in the Code. Under section 339 of the Code, a Magistrate is required to conclude the trial of the case within 120 days and a Sessions Judge within 360 days. Here, in this Ain, the Tribunal is to conclude the trial within 135 days. This is evident from section 10 of the Act. So, the only difference we find is that in the Ain time limit is reduced to 135 days. We find no reason how this reduction of the time limit will affect the petitioners when the other conditions relating to trial remains the same. Here comes the application of Article 35 of our Constitution. The learned Advocate of both the sides has submitted that there is no Article in the Indian Constitution which is similar to clause (3) of Article 35 of our Constitution. Clause (3) of Article 35 clearly provides that a person accused of a criminal offence shall have the right to a speedy trial. This aspect of a constitutional guarantee of getting speedy trial was not discussed in any of the cases cited by Mr Amirul Islam.</u>

20. When our Constitution itself provides that a person accused of an offence shall have a right to get a speedy trial, it is the duty of the Parliament to enact the law to ensure such right. The learned Attorney-General has explained that the instant Ain was enacted with that end in view. We have no doubt in our mind that the principles laid down in the cited cases could be applied in the instant cases before us if it could be found that accused persons of the same footing or standing are being tried in separate forums under separate procedures of trial. Obviously, in that case, that would have been violation of equality cause of Article 27. We have found that an accused tried by the Tribunal and an accused tried by the other Courts as mentioned in the Ain are being tried under the same procedure. Moreover, we find that the enactment was made in consonance with the provisions of the Constitution itself. Someone has said long ago that "justice is like a train that's nearly always late." Now it is a universal demand that such bad name should be erased and we find that the new Ain is one step towards that goal.

21. Mr. Amirul Islam, while referring to the Anwar Ali's case reported in AIR 1952 SC 75 and taking us through paragraph 23 of the judgment delivered by Fazl Ali, J. has pointed out that according to the gravity of the offences, different provisions are there is the Code of Criminal Procedure. He has argued that in the Code itself procedure is given for trial of grave offences and the purpose is to give the accused every opportunity to defend him properly. We are afraid that with the change in time, the observations made by Fazl Ali, J. in the above case may not be considered as applicable today. The Code of Criminal Procedure in India has also been amended and the trial by jury has been abolished. In Bangladesh, the Code of Criminal Procedure has also been amended several times. At present, there is no procedure of trial by jury or by assessors or there is no "de novo" trial. So, the observations made by Fazl Ali, J. though were applicable at that time, cannot be applied now in 2003.

22. Moreover, we like to add that the conception of speedy trial was always there. Sessions triable cases implies that a trial in a Court of Sessions was to be concluded in one session. Unfortunately, due to various reasons, a session’s triable case cannot be concluded in one session, even it cannot be concluded in several sessions due to the adjournments taken both by the prosecution side and by the defence side. This is not due to any infirmity of the law itself but due to the practice that has developed to cause delay. So, we are of the view that the introduction of special provisions for speedy trial of cases cannot be considered as totally a new conception.

23. Mr. Islam has given much stress on the fact that there is no guideline in the Ain itself to transfer a case and, as such, the Government has the opportunity to transfer cases on "pick and choose" basis. it is not fully true that there is no guideline in section 6 of the Ain. We find that at least there are three guidelines-first, only those cases which are pending for trial can be transferred, because in the section the word ‘বিচারাধীন’ has been used. Next, guideline is that only cases which involve five kinds of offences as mentioned in the section can be transferred and thirdly, such transfer can be made only in public interest. In Anwar Ali's case, Hon'ble Judges took exception as to the constitutionality of the provisions of section 5 of the West Bengal Special Courts Act mainly on the ground that class or classes of offences are not mentioned in the Act. Here, in section 6 of the Ain, class or classes of the offences are clearly mentioned.

24. The learned Attorney General has submitted that by this time many cases have already been transferred to nine Tribunals which were set up and cases were transferred to those tribunals taking into consideration the public interest. According to him, it is not true that the cases have been transferred with a view to politically victimise some persons. In this connection he referred to the cases of Trisha murder, Bappi murder, Mohima rape and other cases and has submitted that the trial of these cases were concluded within a reasonable time and has ensured speedy justice. As regards the argument of "pick and choose", as advanced on behalf of the petitioners, the learned Attorney-General has submitted that hundreds of cases are pending for trial in different Courts and it is not possible to transfer all those cases to the Tribunal due to shortage of Judges and other logistic support. We also agree with the above view of the learned Attorney-General. It is not possible to transfer all the cases as mentioned in section 6 to the Special Tribunals because that may require dozens of Tribunals which cannot be manned with existing number of Judges. Moreover, if at a time, suppose one hundred cases are transferred to one Tribunal, it will not be possible for that Tribunal to dispose of such number of cases within the time limit fixed by the Ain.

25. As regards the departure made in sub- section (2) of section 9 of the Ain, we are of the view that due to this departure, the petitioners will not be prejudiced in any way. In Writ Petition No. 2120, the allegation is that of making bombs, the punishment for which extends to imprisonment for twenty years and the other two cases are under section 302 and some other sections of the Penal Code. So, in all the cases, the punishment is imprisonment for more than seven years and, as such, there is no scope of trying the petitioners under the summary procedure as provided in section 260 of the Code in view of the provision of sub-section (2) of section 9 of the Ain. If someone is actually aggrieved by this departure and challenges the provisions of sub-section (2), then the question as to whether incorporation of that provision has taken away his right of getting equal opportunity of trial with another who is on the same footing but is being tried in a different forum, and the question whether that sub- section (2) is violative of Article 27, would arise.

26. The last argument of Mr. Islam was that the Government chooses the cases, Tribunals and also the Judges and in this way the Government has unfettered power to influence criminal justice and to cause harassment to political rivals. Perhaps Mr. Islam was not fully informed of the fact as to the appointment of Judges in those Tribunals the Judges were appointed in consultation with the Supreme Court vide Notification No. 624-Bichar- 3/1A-2/2002 dated 13-11-02. So, it is not true that judges have been appointed by the Government according to its choice

<u>27. As regards the argument of accountability of the Judges we find that this is also not correct. Section 15 provides that a Tribunal is to send a report to the Supreme Court if it cannot conclude trial within the specified time. So, the Tribunal is accountable to the Supreme Court not to the Government. It is provided that only a copy of the report is to be forwarded to the Government. However, sub-section (2) of section 15 provides that the Public Prosecutor and the concerned police officers will be required to submit report to the Government and in that case, copy shall be forwarded to the Supreme Court. Sub-section (3) provides that after perusal of the reports, the authority concerned may take necessary action against the person responsible for not concluding the trial within the specified time. In case of a Judge, the concerned authority, obviously, is the Supreme Court, not the Government. So, it is not true that the Judges have been made accountable to the Government. Moreover, from sub-section (4) of section 10, we find that if the Tribunal cannot conclude that trial within the specified time, the Tribunal is to send back the case to the Court from where it was transferred to the Tribunal. No provision has been made in the Ain to the effect that the case shall be concluded at any cost within the specified time by giving go-bye to the established principles of trial causing prejudice to an accused.</u>

28. Both Mr. Amirul Islam and Mr. Abdul Baset Majumder have submitted that the purpose of setting up the Tribunals is to ensure conviction to the accused persons whose cases are transferred to such Tribunals. This is a general remark not substantiated by any statistics. The learned Advocates could not produce any statistics as to how many cases were tried during this period by the Tribunals and in how many cases the accused were convicted and in how many cases the accused were acquitted. In the absence of such statistics, we do not like to give any opinion on this point. However, the learned Attorney-General has submitted that there are many instances of acquittal by the Tribunals. For the same reason, we do not like to give any opinion on his remark also.

29. As regards the argument of malafide, the learned Attorney-General has submitted that by this time several dozens of cases have been transferred. He has submitted that the case of petitioner Muhibur Rahman Manik is of the year 1999 and the case of the petitioners of the other writ petition is of the year 1993. According to him, the transfer of the cases were not made on any political purpose. On this point, our view is that even after the transfer when the petitioners will get the same opportunity in the same way like an accused who will be tried in the Courts from where their cases have been transferred, the question of mala fide is not relevant.

30. In view of our discussion made above, we find that provisions of section 6 of the Ain do not in any way infringe the right of getting equal protection of law.

In the result, the Rules are discharged without any order as to cost. The orders of stay granted earlier are vacated.

End.

Rokanuddin Mahmud, Senior Advocate instructed by SU Chaklader; Advocate-on-Record  ------- For the Appellant (In CA 40 of 1999).

full_judgment:
Md Ruhul Amin J: These two appeals, by leave, are against the judgment and order of the High Court Division dated 13th August, 1997 passed in Writ Petition No. 362 of 1997 making the Rule absolute.

2. Respondent Nos. 1 and 2 in both the appeals filed the aforementioned writ petition seeking for Rule Nisi upon the respondents in the following term:

8. The averments made in the writ petitions in support of the relief sought, in short, are that petition No. 1, i.e. respondent No. 1 in the appeals, a Co-operative Society, members whereof were refugees, was registered in 1951 for the welfare of its members, the Mohazir, by way of providing residential accommodation and ill 1952 the Society applied to the Government for allotting lands for the construction of residential accommodation of the Mohazir Members of the Society and thereupon Government allotted 25 acres of land from the land which was earlier acquired by the Government and delivered possession thereof in July, 1952. The Government by a deed of conveyance of October 1956, registered in November, 1956 conveyed the land for a consideration of Taka 38,047. The Society got the land so conveyed by the Government recorded in its name in SA Khatian No.2 and that was paying Government Revenue regularly. The Society also acquired 6.97 acres of land from the Government. While the society was in possession of the land got from the Government by deed of conveyance of October, 1956, the Building Research. Institute (BRI, later on HBRI) in 1962 forcibly entered into some portion of the land of the Society and started construction of building.

9. The Society having failed to dissuade BRI from proceeding with the construction filed Title Suit No. 187 of 1962 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka on 24th December, 1962 seeking declaration of title with the prayer for injunction restraining the defendants from disturbing the peaceful possession of the Society and that from raising construction. The Court of Subordinate Judge passed an order dated 18-4-1963 restraining the defendants from going for construction in new areas but permitted to complete construction of the structure already started. Thereafter, Government started negotiation with, the Society for amicable settlement and as negotiation was going the society did not take any step in the suit and consequently the suit was dismissed for default. At one stage of negotiation a compromise formula was evolved to the effect that the society would be allowed to retain its land except the portion occupied by the BRI and that as some more land will be necessary for the completion of BRI scheme and for that the society may be allotted more or less equal area of land contiguous of their land so that none may be inconvenienced, Although time passed but because of the procedural matters involved towards the materialisation of the formula evolved on 27th August, 1970 and finality was not reached in spite of series of meetings and exchange of different letters. In the month of January, 1992 in a meeting held under the Chairmanship of the then Minister in-Charge of the Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs decision was taken calling for a detailed report for the purpose of implementation of the formula evolved on 27th August, 1970. In 1993 in a meeting held on 27th October 1993 decision was taken that out of the 25 acres of land 14 acres will be given to the Society and that the land measuring 6.67 acres acquired by the society would also be given out of the 25 acres of land and thereby the Society will finally get 20.97 acres of land and that to materialise this decision a deed of exchange would be executed between the Society and HBRI. Thereafter, in a meeting on 26th December, 1995 the decision that was taken on 27th October, 1993, was revised and that it was decided that the society would get 19 acres of land from the 25 acres of land and it was also decided that land which the Society will give to HBRI, will be acquired for the Society from the neighbouring land, that while negotiation to arrive at a compromise formula was going on then all on a sudden a notice was issued on 23rd November, 1996 by the Ministry of Housing and Public Works for the eviction of the residents of the Housing Estate by police force. In the notice it was stated that the eviction would be made from the land of HBRI upon demolition of unauthorised construction and evicting the unauthorised occupants, that in the light of the notice dated 23rd November, 1996 the occupants, who were the members of the Society, of different plots of the land of the Society were evicted upon demolition of the structures.

10. It is the case of the writ petitioners that they acquired 25 acres of land by deed of conveyance from the Government and that later on acquired further 6.97 acres of land and that while they were in possession BRI in 1962 illegally encroached upon certain portion of land of the Society and thereupon Society filed civil suit wherein there was an order of injunction. Thereupon, the Government came forward to compromise with the Society and because of that suit having not been proceeded with the same was dismissed. That to arrive at a compromise there were several meetings and there were negotiations and that from time to time formulae were evolved though ultimately, because of procedural complications could not be given final shape and that while the negotiation was going on Government by police force evicted the occupants, who are the members of the Society, of the land of the Society.

11. The Rule was opposed by filing affidavit-in-opposition by the respondent No.5, the Executive Engineer, Public Works Division, Mirpur, Dhaka. The said respondent stated, inter alia, that although the Society on incorrect representation obtained the land for providing residential accommodation to its members, the Mohazir, by way of constructing colony and residence to rehabilitate the Muhazirs but instead of constructing colony and residential accommodation for rehabilitating the Muhazirs the office-bearers of the Society gave the land to some other persons who were not Muhazirs, that with the liberation of Bangladesh purpose of the Society became non est and that Society having ceased to function the same was wound up by the Gazette Notification dated 3rd January, 1974. That as back as 1962 BRI went into possession of the substantial portion of the land out of the 25 acres that was conveyed by the Government and that at one stage of negotiation it was agreed upon by the Society that the land that would be required for implementation of the scheme of BRI would be surrendered and in exchange thereof Government would acquire land for the Society. It was the case of the replying respondent that as the unauthorised persons upon erecting structures were in occupation of the land of HBRI, the Government has evicted those persons from the land of HBRI.

12. The High Court Division on consideration of the submissions of the learned Advocates of the parties and that as well as upon consideration of the papers annexed to the writ petition and affidavit-in-opposition made the Rule absolute upon observing as follows;

(a) 	that the petitioner society is the owner by purchase from the Government through registered sale deed of the land in question and these annexures, documents the society is still the owner of the land in question.

(b) that the HBRI as well as the Government themselves accepted the petitioner society as the lawful owner of the land in question.

(c) 	since the Government had accepted the petitioner society as the lawful owner of the land in question and since the prima facie documents of title are there, that is, the sale deed, the mutation papers of SA Record of rights and the letters and correspondences of the Government admitting the petitioner society as owner of the land in question and since respondents were trying for long time to make amicable settlement with the petitioner society, it cannot be said that the petitioner society is not the owner of the aforesaid land. Further, when the compromise matter was progressing we failed to understand as to what led the respondents to evict the occupants by force and demolish their structures from the land. It was neither a Government land nor land of HBRI. It appears that in the year 1962 this HBRI occupied some portions of the lands of the society. Such occupation is also illegal and without jurisdiction in views of the fact that HBRI is not the owner of any portion of the land in question till today.

(d) In view of the registered documents and other papers we are of the view that the Government had no scope to challenge the right and title of the petitioner society at such a later stage ill the year, 1997 while the deed of transfer was executed in the year, 1952.

(e) that the respondents illegally evicted the allottees of the petitioner society and demolished their structures and, as such, their actions are not at all lawful. As such, their order dated 23-11-1996 vide Annexure-Wand order dated 23-9-1996 vide Annexure-A annexed with the writ petition are liable to be declared illegal and without jurisdiction.

13. The High Court Division finally made the order as follows;

"In the result, this Rule is made absolute and the order as contained in Annexures-W and X of the writ petition are hereby declared to have been passed and/or issued without lawful authority and of no legal effect and it is also declared that all actions taken by the respondents in pursuance of the aforesaid orders as contained in Annexures- W and X are also illegal and without jurisdiction”.

14. It may be mentioned the High Court Division in the last paragraph of its judgment has expressed the view that, "this judgment will not be a bar for the parties to effect the compromise for greater interest of both the parties, and the parties may proceed with the proposal of the compromise and ultimately the compromise may be given effect to according to the terms and conditions to be settled between the parties. In this view of the matter, the parties may proceed with in accordance with the compromise proposal".

15. As against the judgment and order of the High Court Division respondent Nos. 1 and 3 in the writ petition filed separate leave petitions to appeal and leave was granted to consider the submissions of the learned Counsel appearing for the HBRl and the learned Attorney-General that the writ petition having raised several disputed question of facts relating to the title and possession of the respondent society in respect of the land in question and for the resolution of such question there are pending civil suits filed by the Society itself for declaration of their title to the disputed land was dismissed for default, the learned Judges of the High Court Division erred in deciding those disputed question of facts under the writ jurisdiction and in not holding that the petition itself was not entertain able, that impugned Annexure- W being an office order issued by the Chief Engineer, Public Works Department, appointing Mr Zahirul Huq Khan, an executive Engineer of PWD to conduct the eviction work of the unauthorised occupants from the approved land of HBRI given by PWD and Annexure-X being a letter issued by the Executive Engineer, PWD to the Deputy Police Commissioner to depute required number of police force to evict unauthorised occupants from 13 acres of land from the HBRI complex and the said office order and the official letter having been issued with the lawful authority by the concerned officials in their official capacity in the performance of their executive functions of the Government the learned Judges of the High Court Division erred in declaring the said Annexure to have been issued without lawful authority and the actions taken in pursuance thereof evicting the unauthorised occupants from the land of the Government were also illegal, that the original society having been liquidated through Gazette Notification dated 3rd December, 1973 (Published in the Gazette on 3rd January, 1974) and the writ-petitioner-respondent society having become non est the present fake society has no locus standi to challenge the propriety of Annexures-W and X under the writ jurisdiction and, as such, the High Court Division is wrong in not holding that the writ petition itself was not maintainable.

16. In the writ. petition it was averred that PWD has undertaken a project for construction of 3000 residential flats in the Dhaka City and as a part of a said project the Ministry of Works has instructed the Housing and Building Research Institute to transfer some land of the Darus-Salam Co-operative Housing Society Ltd. comprising CS Plot Nos. 8, 9, 10, 16, 17 and 47 area more or less 4.64 acres to Public Works Department for construction of some flats-under the above scheme in exchange of @ Taka 30 lac per bigha in utter violation of the decision of the inter-Ministerial meeting dated 22-7-1990 held under the Chairmanship of the Secretary.

17. The respondent No. 1 to make his aforesaid statement relating to eviction from the plots stated in the writ petition emphatic and expressive has filed Annexure-D (Map) in the Additional Paper Book. The sole purpose, as appears to us, of filing the said Annexure-D is to substantiate respondent No. 1’s claim that the occupants of the Society's land measuring 4.64 acres have been evicted from the plots as stated in the writ petition. But on perusal of the Map Annexure-D in the Additional Paper Book it is seen that plot No. 10 has not been shown as the plot from which eviction has been made. In the Annexure-D in the Additional Paper Book plots those are subject matter of writ petition has been shown by light red colour but Plot No. 10 has not been shown as the subject matter of writ petition or in other words, not the land from which eviction has been made pursuant to annexures W and X in the writ petition. From the averments as have been made in the writ petition it is seen that the plots wherefrom eviction was said to have been made were in the occupation of the Society of in other words, were not in the occupation of HBRI. In the writ petition it was averred that plots where from the Society was evicted comprise land measuring 4.67 acres. It is seen from Annexure-T to the writ petition that the plots stated in the writ petition comprise in total 6.012 acres of land and the said plots are in occupation of the HBRI. In the afore state of the matter the averment of the Society that eviction that was made by the authorised Magistrate in the light of Annexures W and X was of the members of the Society from the plots and quantity of land averred in the writ petition was of the kind that need adjudication or determination upon going through the elaborated process of collection of materials and sifting thereof. There is another important aspect of the matter. The society in its suit, Title Suit No. 187 of 1962 accepted the fact of HBRI's going into possession of the land. Although the Society has not specified the land that was taken over by HBRI, but from Annexure- T to the writ petition it is seen plots as are now being claimed by. the writ petitioner and some other plots were taken over by HBRI and started construction. In the aforesaid suit while the court was making the order in an interlocutory matter it was agreed upon by the Society that land already taken into possession by HBRI and making construction would remain with HBRI and that HBRI would proceed with the construction already undertaken. From Annexure-H to the writ petition it is seen that the Society was requested to transfer the land in the occupation of HBRI. From Annexure-J to the writ petition it is seen that 22.48 acres out of 25 acres of land of the society comprises the area upon which HBRI was established. From Annexure-O to the writ petition it is seen that although 25 acres of land was conveyed to the Society but the Society was in possession of 15.96 acres and the balance of the land is in possession of other organisations including the HBRI. It is seen from Annexure-P to the writ petition that in total 56.16 acres of land was acquired for BRI (later on HBRI) in the year 1962 and that Society's 22.78 acres of land was within the 56.16 acres of land of HBRI and that later on in the: year 1975, although upon excluding the Society’s land 33.38 acres of land was acquired for utilisation of BRI but Society's 22.78 acres of land could not be restored to the Society as because the HBRI, made construction as per previously approved scheme in the land of the Society.

18. In the background of the facts stated therein before it is seen that the writ petitioner in the garb of challenging the legality of Annexure W and X has, in fact, approached the High Court Division to obtain possession of the land said to be of the Society, although since 1962 the Society could not have the same. It is also seen from the papers annexed to writ petition and the Additional Paper Book that the Society's claim of eviction of its members from its land pursuant to the Annexures W and X is uncertain as because the society claimed that the area of the plots from which its members have been evicted pursuant to the Annexures W and X is more or less 4.65 acres but from Annexure-T it is seen that the area of the said plots is 6.012 acres. So, it is evident from the materials brought on record by the Society, its claim as to eviction of its members from the plots and the area as mentioned in the writ petition are totally uncertain and unspecified. Furthermore from the Annexures referred to herein before it is seem that the Society was not in possession of the substantial portion of land claimed by it, rather the same are in the possession of the HBRI, some other organisations as well as unauthorised persons and trespassers and that unauthorised persons and trespassers in the land of HBRI were evicted pursuant to the Annexures-W and X. There is another noticeable aspect of the matter. There is no material on the record to substantiate the claim of the Society that the lands of the plots as claimed by the Society in the writ petition were allotted to any member of its Society. From Annexure T in the writ petition the plots mentioned in the writ petition are in the possession of HBRI It is seen from the Annexure-T to the Writ petition that in connection with the construction of 3600 residential flats decision was taken to purchase 13 acres of land of HBRI on payment of 30 lac per bigha and it appears that in connection thereof the eviction that has been challenged in the writ petition was made. So, it is evident that the land from which eviction was made was not in the possession of the Society.

19. The entire thrust of arguments of the appellants, was that the High Court Division was in serious error in deciding disputed question of facts, particularly the question of possession of the land wherefrom eviction was made in the light of Annexures-W and X to the writ petition. In refusal of the argument of the appellants relating to deciding of the disputed question of facts the learned Counsel appearing for the respondent No. 1 has submitted that no disputed question relating to possession of the land, particularly the plots as stated in the writ petition, was involved in the writ petition as because those plots were conveyed to the Society by the Government as back as 1956, although possession was made over in 1952. The learned Counsel for the respondent No. 1 has also submitted that the Civil Suits mentioned in the leave granting order are in no way related to the plots of land which are subject matter of the writ petition. He has further submitted that from Annexure-D, to the Additional Paper Book it is clear that eviction was made from the plots shown in Annexure-D marked with light red colour and in the said Annexure the plots where from the members of the society have been evicted specifically shown.

20. It is seen from the judgment of the High Court Division that the said Division proceeded primarily with the question of title of the Society in the plots which were the subject matter of the writ petition and thereupon arrived at the finding as the title and possession of the plots wherefrom eviction has been made pursuant to the Annexures W and X is of the Society and as eviction was not legal and as the land wherefrom eviction made was neither of the Government nor HBRI the eviction was unauthorised. It is noticed from the judgment of the High Court Division that Annexures relating to possession were not brought to the notice of the learned Judges of the said Division and had those Annexures been placed before the High Court Division disputed question of possession would have not been gone into by the said Division and the point raised by the respondents in the writ petition as to non-maintainability of the writ petition involving disputed question of facts would have received proper consideration of the High Court Division.

21. There is also one more important aspect of the matter. The Society was established for the welfare of the Mohazirs by making available to them residential accommodation and for that purpose the society approached the Government for allotment of land which was allotted and that finally conveyed by registered deed in the year 1956. But before utilisation of the land by the Society, for the establishment of the BRI major portion of Society's land along with other land was acquired and made over to the BRI and that while BRI was making construction at a certain portion of the land made available to HBRI, the Society filed Title Suit No. 187 of 1962 impleading Government as the defendant and prayed for injunction and while disposing of the injunction matter by the Court of Subordinate Judge it was agreed upon between the parties that the land in which BRI has gone into possession would be retained by it but no new construction would be made in the position whereupon construction has yet not been made and that construction that has been started would be completed.

22. After the liberation of the country the Society became non est and thereupon by a notification dated 3rd December, 1973 (published in the Gazette on 3rd January, 1974) was liquidated by the Registrar of the Co-operative Society. The society was revived by the Gazette Notification dated 15th January, 1980. It is contended by the appellants that from the papers on record it is seen that after the revival of the Society question was raised as to the genuineness of the membership thereof and that it has remained a matter of uncertainty in between December, 1973 and 14th January, 1980, the land that was made available to the Society in the year 1952 was managed by whom and looked after by whom.

23. It is seen from the papers on record that major part of the land is in possession of the HBRI The High Court Division solely proceeded on the question of title of the Society but did not consider the question of possession of the land that was transferred to the Society in the background of the papers on record. In the background of the papers on record serious dispute as to how much land the Society actually got and that question of possession between the Society and the HBRI is quite apparent and present. It is the contention of the appellants that the High Court Division was in serious error in deciding the disputed question relating to the quantity of land and possession of the parties in the writ petition. In our view, in the background of the papers on record the High Court Division ought not to have gone for adjudication of the quantity of land and the question of possession of the parties in the writ petition upon merely referring to the Annexure-B (deed of conveyance) to the writ petition showing transfer of 25 acres of land and some other lands to the Society upon totally oblivious of the question of actual possession. As it appears though the writ petition has been filed in the garb of challenging legality of the Annexures-W and X and the action taken thereunder but as a matter of fact resort has been made by the writ petitioners to obtain the possession of the land as to which they had never been in actual possession.

24. The petitions instead of approaching the proper forum for the adjudication of their claim as transpires from the materials on the record, they in a camouflaged manner impugning the Annexure 'W' and the action taken in the light of the contents of the said Annexure and Annexure-X have filed the writ petition to secure the relief sought upon adjudication of facts which are seriously contentious. The writ petition has been camouflaged with the sole object of obtaining the possession of the land that was once given to the Society, but the Society could not have the possession, entire of the same, by way of a declaration that the members of the Society have been evicted from their land while the fact of possession of the Society of the plots and area stated in the writ petition is not definite rather in correct in the background of the materials in the annexures in the writ petition. The High Court in making the Rule obtained by the writ petitioners absolute proceeded primarily and solely on the question of title of the Society in the land that was conveyed by the government to the Society in 1956 as well as on the premise that title follows possession. The proposition that title follows possession is one of general in nature. There are cases of exceptional nature and character to which general proposition title follows possession has no application or, in other words, there are cases which are exception to the general proposition that title follows possession. In the present case in the light of the Ext. B (the deed of conveyance of 25 acres of land to the Society) to the writ petition although apparently there appears the Society has title to the said 25 acres of land but there is no material on the record to substantiate the contention of the Society as to possession thereof or of the plots mentioned in writ petition wherefrom members of the Society, as claimed by the Society, to have been evicted by the respondents in the writ petition in the light of Annexures 'W' and 'X'. Rather from the materials on the record it is seen, if not from before but at least from 1962, dispute as to possession between the Society and BRI, later on HBRI, was going on and there were negotiations as well as meetings to reach at a compromise even upon reducing the quantity of land to be made available to the Society but did not reach finality up to the date on which the eviction impugned in the writ petition was made. There is no tangible and reliable material on record that Society went for the execution of its object of providing accommodation to its members-the Mohazirs. From the papers on the record it is seen that decision was made at the level of policy making authority that 13 acres of land would be made available to the Public Works Department from the area of the HBRI and in the implementation of the said policy decision, decision was made to have the said land available from the land of HBRI upon eviction of the trespassers and unauthorised occupants. There is also no material on the record wherefrom with certainty it can be seen or said that plots and quantity of land mentioned in the writ petition were or are in the possession of the Society or its Members.

25. We are of the view High Court Division was in error in making the Rule absolute upon proceeding on the general proposition that title follows possession on overlooking the facts in the background of the materials on record that the said general proposition does not hold good in the present case.

26. There is no material on the record to show that Chief Engineer acted in violation of provision of law or in other words was not competent to vest the officer named in Annexure 'W' with Magisterial power to do the work of eviction of unauthorised occupant of the land of Public Works Department or of any other organisation under the Ministry of Public Works. By Annexure 'X' officer who was vested with magisterial power to do the work of eviction, request was made to the Police Department to make available required number of police personnel. The requisition for police so made or request for police personal made by Annexure X can in no way be considered not legal or that the said request or requisition cannot be said to have been made in violation of law of any kind. That being the position in law the High Court Division was in error in declaring the said Annexures 'W' and 'X' to the writ petition illegal.

27. On consideration of the facts and circumstances of the petitioner's case in the writ petition and the materials annexed to the writ petition it is quite clear that petitioners camouflaged the writ petition by way of impugning the Annexure 'W' and action taken thereunder to obtain the object which they were not having at least since 1962 because of non- settlement of dispute over the possession of the land conveyed by Annexure 'B' to the writ petition between the society and HBRI. The High Court Division was in error in making the Rule absolute and consequent thereupon giving the relief sought in the writ petition in spite of the unresolved serious dispute as to possession of the land claimed by the Society. In the background of the facts as in the writ petition we are of the view petitioners remedy lies either at the level as has been observed by the High Court Division in the concluding part of its judgment or at some other proper forum where contentious facts legally can be adjudicated. But not the writ jurisdiction since law is settled by now that matter seriously contentious in nature requiring adjudication on the basis of evidence of detail nature is outside the scope of writ jurisdiction as because in the said jurisdiction in general matters are disposed of in summary manner on the basis of affidavit evidence except in an exceptional case where a person may be called by the Court to give his testimony as to a matter which is not seriously contentious or disputed in kind or nature. The instant case does not come within the ground of exceptional cases where writ court may dispose of a matter by calling one to give one's testimony as to the subject matter of the case before the writ court, particularly as to matter of possession of the plots and quantity of the lands comprised by the said plots mentioned in the instant writ petition.

28. The plots and the quantity of land claimed by the writ petitioners to have been in their possession and that they have been evicted in pursuance of the Annexures-W and X finds place in paragraph 27 of the writ petition. But the fact in the light of the papers on record as to actual number of plots and the actual quantity of land of the plots from which the writ petitioners said to have been evicted is totally uncertain and that even from Annexure-D to the Additional Paper Book it is seen that one of the plots i.e. plot No. 10, from which writ petitioners were said to have been evicted, as stated in paragraph 27 of the writ petition, is not one of those plots. This shows that quantity of the land and the plots from which writ petitioners were said to have been evicted is unspecified and uncertain.

29. In view of the discussion made herein above, we find merit in appellants contention that the High Court Division was in error in deciding the disputed question of facts, particularly question of possession of the land claimed to have been evicted, in writ jurisdiction which is not permitted.

In the result the appeals are allowed. There is no order as to costs.

End.

Abdul Quyaum with Tapash Kanti Biswas and Md Ali Reza, Advocates------ For the Opposite Parties.
